Action Sports.overview: Action Sports covers skateboarding and snowboarding safety, equipment maintenance, park/slope etiquette, fundamental and intermediate maneuvers, and outdoor stewardship.

requirements.topic_heading: Hazards, Safety Gear & First Aid in Action Sports
requirements.lead_text: Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards you may encounter while participating in action sports (skateboarding or snowboarding) and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Review prevention, symptoms, and first-aid treatment for hypothermia, frostbite, dehydration, sunburn, heat exhaustion, heatstroke, blisters, sprains, strains, fractures, head/concussion injuries, and spinal injuries. (c) Show your helmet, wrist guards, knee/elbow pads, boots, and bindings, and explain how to inspect and fit them properly.

common_misconception_pair.fact: Rubbing frostbitten skin causes severe tissue damage from ice crystals, so affected areas should instead be rewarmed gently using lukewarm water or body heat (p. 12).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Before dropping into a concrete skatepark bowl on a skateboard or riding a BMX track, how should you verify that your helmet and protective pads meet Action Sports safety standards?
quiz_item.question: Before dropping into a concrete skatepark bowl on a skateboard or riding a BMX track, how should you verify that your helmet and protective pads meet Action Sports safety standards?
options: A. Wear a lightweight road-cycling helmet tilted back on the forehead and skip wrist guards so your hands can grip the coping.
B. Fit a CPSC or ASTM F1492 certified skate or BMX helmet level across the brow with a snug chin strap, paired with knee pads, elbow pads, and wrist guards.
C. Use an unpadded hard-shell construction hat and wrap elastic athletic tape around your ankles and wrists.
D. Loosen the helmet chin strap by three finger-widths so it can slide off easily during a fall and wear only shin guards.

quiz_item.question: According to the Skier/Snowboarder Responsibility Code, who has the right-of-way on a mountain trail?
options: A. The faster rider traveling straight down the fall line
B. Snowboarders riding regular stance over goofy-footed riders
C. The rider ahead or downhill of you
D. Whichever rider shouts loudest before entering an intersection
choices: A. The faster rider traveling straight down the fall line
B. Snowboarders riding regular stance over goofy-footed riders
C. The rider ahead or downhill of you
D. Whichever rider shouts loudest before entering an intersection
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. The rider ahead or downhill of you

quiz_item.correct_answer: A. The urethane bushings mounted on the kingpin

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What is the safest technique to reduce injury if you lose balance and fall while skateboarding or snowboarding?
quiz_item.question: What is the safest technique to reduce injury if you lose balance and fall while skateboarding or snowboarding?
options: A. Reach both hands straight down with locked elbows to brace against the ground
B. Stay completely rigid and fall flat onto your back
C. Lower your center of gravity, tuck your chin and arms in, and roll onto fleshy areas
D. Jump high into the air away from the board while twisting your ankles
choices: A. Reach both hands straight down with locked elbows to brace against the ground
B. Stay completely rigid and fall flat onto your back
C. Lower your center of gravity, tuck your chin and arms in, and roll onto fleshy areas
D. Jump high into the air away from the board while twisting your ankles
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Lower your center of gravity, tuck your chin and arms in, and roll onto fleshy areas
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Crouching low, tucking your arms against your chest, and rolling across your shoulders or padded joints spreads out the force of impact and protects your wrists (p. 12).

B. Inspect the approach, takeoff, and landing zone, and confirm the landing is clear with a spotter
C. Remove wrist guards and elbow pads to reduce wind resistance in the air
D. Cut ahead of riders waiting at the top of the park so your muscles stay warm
choices: A. Ride at top speed on the very first run without inspecting the feature
B. Inspect the approach, takeoff, and landing zone, and confirm the landing is clear with a spotter
C. Remove wrist guards and elbow pads to reduce wind resistance in the air

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Inspect the approach, takeoff, and landing zone, and confirm the landing is clear with a spotter

options: A. The faster rider traveling straight down the fall line
B. Snowboarders riding regular stance over goofy-footed riders
C. The rider ahead or downhill of you
D. Whichever rider shouts loudest before entering an intersection
choices: A. The faster rider traveling straight down the fall line
B. Snowboarders riding regular stance over goofy-footed riders
C. The rider ahead or downhill of you
D. Whichever rider shouts loudest before entering an intersection
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. The rider ahead or downhill of you
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Riders ahead of you have the right-of-way because their field of vision is directed downhill, making it your responsibility to avoid them (p. 12).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which component inside a skateboard truck absorbs lean pressure and returns the hanger to center after a turn?
options: A. The urethane bushings mounted on the kingpin
B. The abrasive grip tape bonded to the top ply
C. The inner bearing spacers inside the wheel hub
D. The metal mounting bolts holding the baseplate
choices: A. The urethane bushings mounted on the kingpin

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Urethane bushings sit around the kingpin inside the truck, compressing when the rider leans and rebounding to return the wheels to center (p. 16).

B. Public ownership of factories, elimination of market competition, state-allocated consumer goods, and interest-free national banking.
C. Private ownership of property, freedom of enterprise and choice, the profit motive, and open market competition regulated by supply and demand.
D. Barter-only trade networks, monopolistic industry trusts, mercantilist export tariffs, and lifetime employment contracts.
choices: A. Centralized government price controls, guaranteed corporate profits, mandatory union membership, and fixed production quotas.
B. Public ownership of factories, elimination of market competition, state-allocated consumer goods, and interest-free national banking.

quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Private ownership of property, freedom of enterprise and choice, the profit motive, and open market competition regulated by supply and demand.

quiz_item.question: According to the American Business pamphlet, how should a for-profit company balance its obligation to investors with its duty to society?
options: A. Maximize short-term profit at any cost and let government agencies handle safety later
B. Earn a profit for owners and investors ethically while safeguarding customers, employees, and natural resources
C. Avoid making any profit at all so that product prices remain below manufacturing cost
D. Focus exclusively on shareholder dividends and ignore product safety testing
choices: A. Maximize short-term profit at any cost and let government agencies handle safety later
B. Earn a profit for owners and investors ethically while safeguarding customers, employees, and natural resources
C. Avoid making any profit at all so that product prices remain below manufacturing cost
D. Focus exclusively on shareholder dividends and ignore product safety testing
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Earn a profit for owners and investors ethically while safeguarding customers, employees, and natural resources
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): For-profit firms owe investors a return, but profit must be earned ethically while protecting customer safety, treating workers fairly, and stewarding natural resources (p. 20).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why must a business leader plan to invest more money than a tool's original purchase price when that tool eventually wears out?
quiz_item.question: Why must a business leader plan to invest more money than a tool's original purchase price when that tool eventually wears out?
options: A. Because federal law requires companies to buy two identical machines for every broken one
B. Because inflation often raises the replacement cost of tools above their original price, and businesses must also invest to improve products
C. Because accounting rules forbid companies from repairing or replacing any tool under $10,000
D. Because worn-out tools automatically increase a company's stock price
choices: A. Because federal law requires companies to buy two identical machines for every broken one
B. Because inflation often raises the replacement cost of tools above their original price, and businesses must also invest to improve products
C. Because accounting rules forbid companies from repairing or replacing any tool under $10,000
D. Because worn-out tools automatically increase a company's stock price
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Because inflation often raises the replacement cost of tools above their original price, and businesses must also invest to improve products
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Due to inflation, replacing a worn $5,000 tool might cost $7,000, and leaders must also invest beyond basic maintenance to improve products and stay competitive (p. 38).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which combination accurately describes the four foundational features of the American free enterprise system covered in Requirement 1?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which combination accurately describes the four foundational features of the American free enterprise system covered in Requirement 1?
options: A. Centralized government price controls, guaranteed corporate profits, mandatory union membership, and fixed production quotas.
B. Public ownership of factories, elimination of market competition, state-allocated consumer goods, and interest-free national banking.
C. Private ownership of property, freedom of enterprise and choice, the profit motive, and open market competition regulated by supply and demand.
D. Barter-only trade networks, monopolistic industry trusts, mercantilist export tariffs, and lifetime employment contracts.
choices: A. Centralized government price controls, guaranteed corporate profits, mandatory union membership, and fixed production quotas.
B. Public ownership of factories, elimination of market competition, state-allocated consumer goods, and interest-free national banking.
C. Private ownership of property, freedom of enterprise and choice, the profit motive, and open market competition regulated by supply and demand.
D. Barter-only trade networks, monopolistic industry trusts, mercantilist export tariffs, and lifetime employment contracts.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Private ownership of property, freedom of enterprise and choice, the profit motive, and open market competition regulated by supply and demand.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The U.S. free enterprise system rests on private property rights, freedom of choice for producers and consumers, the incentive of profit, and competition driven by supply and demand.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which financial statement shows a company's assets, liabilities, and owner's equity at a specific moment in time?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which financial statement shows a company's assets, liabilities, and owner's equity at a specific moment in time?
options: A. The statement of cash flows
B. The quarterly marketing budget
C. The balance sheet
D. The income statement
choices: A. The statement of cash flows
B. The quarterly marketing budget
C. The balance sheet
D. The income statement
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. The balance sheet
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The balance sheet reports what a business owns (assets), what it owes (liabilities), and the remaining net worth (owner's equity) on a specific date (p. 48).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: According to the American Business pamphlet, how should a for-profit company balance its obligation to investors with its duty to society?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to the American Business pamphlet, how should a for-profit company balance its obligation to investors with its duty to society?
options: A. Maximize short-term profit at any cost and let government agencies handle safety later
B. Earn a profit for owners and investors ethically while safeguarding customers, employees, and natural resources
C. Avoid making any profit at all so that product prices remain below manufacturing cost
D. Focus exclusively on shareholder dividends and ignore product safety testing
choices: A. Maximize short-term profit at any cost and let government agencies handle safety later
B. Earn a profit for owners and investors ethically while safeguarding customers, employees, and natural resources
C. Avoid making any profit at all so that product prices remain below manufacturing cost
D. Focus exclusively on shareholder dividends and ignore product safety testing
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Earn a profit for owners and investors ethically while safeguarding customers, employees, and natural resources
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): For-profit firms owe investors a return, but profit must be earned ethically while protecting customer safety, treating workers fairly, and stewarding natural resources (p. 20).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which federal law requires employers to provide a workplace free from recognized, serious hazards and is enforced through workplace inspections?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which federal law requires employers to provide a workplace free from recognized, serious hazards and is enforced through workplace inspections?
options: A. The Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA)
B. The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA)
C. The Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA)
D. The Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSH Act)
choices: A. The Employee Retirement Income Security Act (ERISA)
B. The Fair Labor Standards Act (FLSA)
C. The Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA)
D. The Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSH Act)
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. The Occupational Safety and Health Act (OSH Act)
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): The Occupational Safety and Health Act requires employers to maintain workplaces free from serious recognized hazards, enforced by OSHA inspections and cooperative programs (p. 60).

requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following, choosing a different group for each: (a) Go to a festival, celebration, or other event identified with one of the groups. (d) Learn a song, dance, poem, or story that is traditional to one group, and teach it to a group of your friends. (e) Go to a library or museum to see a program or exhibit featuring one group's traditions. Report on what you see and learn.

quiz_item.question: When comparing three different cultural groups in the United States for Requirement 1, what is the primary goal of examining their traditions, customs, and historical contributions?
options: A. To understand how diverse cultural backgrounds shape American society, build mutual respect, and recognize shared human values alongside distinct heritages.
B. To rank cultural groups by the century they arrived in North America and determine which group should set uniform national customs.
C. To prove that regional differences in language, food, and holidays have completely disappeared in modern metropolitan areas.
D. To replace local cultural celebrations with a single standardized set of civic traditions across all states.
choices: A. To understand how diverse cultural backgrounds shape American society, build mutual respect, and recognize shared human values alongside distinct heritages.
B. To rank cultural groups by the century they arrived in North America and determine which group should set uniform national customs.
C. To prove that regional differences in language, food, and holidays have completely disappeared in modern metropolitan areas.
D. To replace local cultural celebrations with a single standardized set of civic traditions across all states.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. To understand how diverse cultural backgrounds shape American society, build mutual respect, and recognize shared human values alongside distinct heritages.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): American Cultures Requirement 1 emphasizes exploring how distinct cultural groups contribute to the nation, helping Scouts overcome stereotypes and appreciate both diversity and shared civic life.

Multi Country Family Origins: Many Americans can trace their origins back to several countries (p. 40).

Blended Family Heritage Traditions: It's common for an American to have a multicultural heritage, that is, to keep family traditions or customs that have been passed down from several cultures (p. 40).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When comparing three different cultural groups in the United States for Requirement 1, what is the primary goal of examining their traditions, customs, and historical contributions?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When comparing three different cultural groups in the United States for Requirement 1, what is the primary goal of examining their traditions, customs, and historical contributions?
options: A. To understand how diverse cultural backgrounds shape American society, build mutual respect, and recognize shared human values alongside distinct heritages.
B. To rank cultural groups by the century they arrived in North America and determine which group should set uniform national customs.
C. To prove that regional differences in language, food, and holidays have completely disappeared in modern metropolitan areas.
D. To replace local cultural celebrations with a single standardized set of civic traditions across all states.
choices: A. To understand how diverse cultural backgrounds shape American society, build mutual respect, and recognize shared human values alongside distinct heritages.
B. To rank cultural groups by the century they arrived in North America and determine which group should set uniform national customs.
C. To prove that regional differences in language, food, and holidays have completely disappeared in modern metropolitan areas.
D. To replace local cultural celebrations with a single standardized set of civic traditions across all states.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. To understand how diverse cultural backgrounds shape American society, build mutual respect, and recognize shared human values alongside distinct heritages.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): American Cultures Requirement 1 emphasizes exploring how distinct cultural groups contribute to the nation, helping Scouts overcome stereotypes and appreciate both diversity and shared civic life.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: According to the American Cultures pamphlet, what would be true of a community that had always lived in complete isolation from all other cultural groups?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to the American Cultures pamphlet, what would be true of a community that had always lived in complete isolation from all other cultural groups?
options: A. It would possess no technology borrowed from other groups and no awareness that other cultures exist
B. It would automatically adopt international trade laws without outside contact
C. It would speak every major world language fluently
D. It would rely entirely on imported agricultural tools
choices: A. It would possess no technology borrowed from other groups and no awareness that other cultures exist
B. It would automatically adopt international trade laws without outside contact
C. It would speak every major world language fluently
D. It would rely entirely on imported agricultural tools
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. It would possess no technology borrowed from other groups and no awareness that other cultures exist
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In complete isolation, a society would have zero borrowed technology or ideas from outside peoples and would not even know other cultures exist (p. 46).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What does the American Cultures pamphlet mean when it states that many Americans have a multicultural heritage?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What does the American Cultures pamphlet mean when it states that many Americans have a multicultural heritage?
options: A. They must hold dual citizenship in at least three foreign nations
B. They keep family traditions and customs passed down from several different cultures
C. They change their religious affiliation every calendar year
D. They only celebrate holidays that were created within the last decade
choices: A. They must hold dual citizenship in at least three foreign nations
B. They keep family traditions and customs passed down from several different cultures
C. They change their religious affiliation every calendar year
D. They only celebrate holidays that were created within the last decade
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. They keep family traditions and customs passed down from several different cultures
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Many Americans trace their roots to multiple countries and preserve a blend of traditions and customs inherited from several cultures (p. 40).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: According to the Declaration of Independence discussed in Requirement 1, from where do legitimate governments derive their just powers, and what unalienable rights are named?
quiz_item.question: According to the Declaration of Independence discussed in Requirement 1, from where do legitimate governments derive their just powers, and what unalienable rights are named?
options: A. From hereditary monarchs and parliamentary charters, guaranteeing property ownership, military protection, and tax exemption.
B. From the federal judiciary and state legislatures, guaranteeing trial by jury, interstate commerce, and municipal voting.
C. From colonial trade treaties and martial law, guaranteeing public education, national banking, and frontier land grants.
D. From the consent of the governed, instituted to secure the unalienable rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
choices: A. From hereditary monarchs and parliamentary charters, guaranteeing property ownership, military protection, and tax exemption.
B. From the federal judiciary and state legislatures, guaranteeing trial by jury, interstate commerce, and municipal voting.
C. From colonial trade treaties and martial law, guaranteeing public education, national banking, and frontier land grants.
D. From the consent of the governed, instituted to secure the unalienable rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. From the consent of the governed, instituted to secure the unalienable rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): The Declaration of Independence states that all people are endowed with unalienable rights including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Select two individuals from American history, one a political leader (a president, senator, etc.) and the other a private citizen (a writer, religious leader, etc.). Find out about each person's accomplishments and compare the contributions each has made to America's heritage. (b) With your counselor's approval, choose an organization that has promoted some type of positive change in American society. Find out why the organization believed this change was necessary and how it helped to accomplish the change. Discuss how this organization is related to events or situations from America's past. (c) With your counselor's approval, interview two veterans of the U. S. military. Find out what their experiences were like. Ask the veterans what they believe they accomplished. (d) With your counselor's approval, interview three people in your community of different ages and occupations. Ask these people what America means to them, what they think is special about this country, and what American traditions they feel are important to preserve.

requirements.description: Do TWO of the following: (a) Select two individuals from American history, one a political leader (a president, senator, etc.) and the other a private citizen (a writer, religious leader, etc.). Find out about each person's accomplishments and compare the contributions each has made to America's heritage. (b) With your counselor's approval, choose an organization that has promoted some type of positive change in American society. Find out why the organization believed this change was necessary and how it helped to accomplish the change. Discuss how this organization is related to events or situations from America's past. (c) With your counselor's approval, interview two veterans of the U. S. military. Find out what their experiences were like. Ask the veterans what they believe they accomplished. (d) With your counselor's approval, interview three people in your community of different ages and occupations. Ask these people what America means to them, what they think is special about this country, and what American traditions they feel are important to preserve.

requirements.lead_text: Do TWO of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do TWO of the following: (a) Explain the National Register of Historic Places and how a property becomes eligible for listing in the National Register of Historic Places. Make a map of your local area, marking the points of historical interest. Tell about any National Register properties in your area. Share the map with your counselor, and describe the historical points you have indicated. (b) Research an event of historical importance that took place in or near your area. If possible, visit the place. Tell your counselor about the event and how it affected local history. Describe how the area looked then and what it now looks like. (c) Find out when, why, and how your town or neighborhood started, and what ethnic, national, or racial groups played a part. Find out how the area has changed over the past 50 years and try to explain why. (d) Take an active part in a program about an event or person in American history. Report to your counselor about the program, the part you took, and the subject. (e) Visit a historic trail or walk in your area. After your visit, share with your counselor what you have learned. Discuss the importance of this location and explain why you think it might qualify for National Register listing.

pamphlet_excerpts: Selective Historic Property Listing: The National Register does not list all historic properties (p. 40).
Strict Eligibility Evaluation Criteria: There are very specific criteria for a property to be listed (p. 40).
Historical and Architectural Significance: Above all, the property must be significant in American history, architecture, archaeology, and culture (p. 40).
Plotting Local Register Sites: Once you have found what National Register properties are in your area, plot them on a map (p. 40).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Verify Property Historical Significance: Above all, the property must be significant in American history, architecture, archaeology, and culture (p. 40).
Step 2 - Plot Sites on Map: Once you have found what National Register properties are in your area, plot them on a map (p. 40).
Step 3 - Label Streets and Waterways: Your map does not have to be exact, but it should identify major streets, highways, and natural resources such as lakes and rivers (p. 40).
Step 4 - Obtain Base Town Map: Your local library, chamber of commerce, or realty office might be able to provide you with amap of your town (p. 40).

options: A. It must be owned and operated by the federal government
B. It must charge admission fees to out-of-state tourists
C. It must be significant in American history, architecture, archaeology, or culture
D. It must have been built before the signing of the U.S. Constitution

quiz_item.correct_answer: C. It must be significant in American history, architecture, archaeology, or culture
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): To qualify for the National Register of Historic Places, a property must meet specific criteria demonstrating significance in American history, architecture, archaeology, engineering, or culture (p. 40).

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Watch two motion pictures (with the approval and permission of your counselor and parent or guardian) that are set in some period of American history. Describe to your counselor how accurate each film is with regard to the historical events depicted and also with regard to the way the characters are portrayed. (b) Read a biography (with your counselor's approval) of someone who has made a contribution to America's heritage. Tell some things you admire about this individual and some things you do not admire. Explain why you think this person has made a positive or a negative contribution to America's heritage. (c) Listen to recordings of popular songs from various periods of American history. Share five of these songs with your counselor, and describe how each song reflects the way people felt about the period in which it was popular. If a recording is not available, have a copy of the lyrics available.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to the Declaration of Independence discussed in Requirement 1, from where do legitimate governments derive their just powers, and what unalienable rights are named?
options: A. From hereditary monarchs and parliamentary charters, guaranteeing property ownership, military protection, and tax exemption.
B. From the federal judiciary and state legislatures, guaranteeing trial by jury, interstate commerce, and municipal voting.
C. From colonial trade treaties and martial law, guaranteeing public education, national banking, and frontier land grants.
D. From the consent of the governed, instituted to secure the unalienable rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
choices: A. From hereditary monarchs and parliamentary charters, guaranteeing property ownership, military protection, and tax exemption.
B. From the federal judiciary and state legislatures, guaranteeing trial by jury, interstate commerce, and municipal voting.
C. From colonial trade treaties and martial law, guaranteeing public education, national banking, and frontier land grants.
D. From the consent of the governed, instituted to secure the unalienable rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. From the consent of the governed, instituted to secure the unalienable rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): The Declaration of Independence states that all people are endowed with unalienable rights including life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.

Sun-Dried Adobe Bricks: Rio Grande Indians constructed their homes from adobe bricks of sun-dried earth mixed with straw (p. 7).

quiz_item.question: Why did American Indian nations across regions such as the Pacific Northwest, the Great Plains, and the Desert Southwest develop markedly different housing, diets, and clothing prior to European contact?
options: A. All tribes followed a single continental council that assigned different crafts and housing styles to each region by lottery.
B. Each Indigenous nation adapted its technology, shelter, food ways, and social organization to the specific geography, climate, and natural resources of its homeland.
C. Tribes in every region relied exclusively on imported European iron tools and domesticated horses for thousands of years before 1492.
D. Differences in shelter and diet were caused solely by proximity to Spanish missions established along the Atlantic seaboard.
choices: A. All tribes followed a single continental council that assigned different crafts and housing styles to each region by lottery.
B. Each Indigenous nation adapted its technology, shelter, food ways, and social organization to the specific geography, climate, and natural resources of its homeland.
C. Tribes in every region relied exclusively on imported European iron tools and domesticated horses for thousands of years before 1492.
D. Differences in shelter and diet were caused solely by proximity to Spanish missions established along the Atlantic seaboard.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Each Indigenous nation adapted its technology, shelter, food ways, and social organization to the specific geography, climate, and natural resources of its homeland.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): American Indian cultures developed distinct lifeways (such as cedar plank houses in the Pacific Northwest, bison hide tipis on the Plains, and adobe pueblos in the Southwest) adapted directly to local ecosystems and resources.

pamphlet_excerpts: Columbia River Canoe Trade: Using dugout canoes, Plateau tribes traveled and traded widely along the Columbia and Fraser river systems (p. 57).
Coastal Pelts and Shells: From the west came sea otter pelts and ornamental shells (p. 57).
Interior Skins and Bitter root: Deer skins, hemp for basket making, and bitter root were brought from the interior (p. 57).
Salmon and Carved Wares: Dried salmon, candle fish oil, baskets, carvings, even the canoes in which the traders carried their wares (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Gather Interior Trade Goods: Deer skins, hemp for basket making, and bitter root were brought from the interior (p. 57).
Step 2 - Exchange Salmon and Canoes: Dried salmon, candle fish oil, baskets, carvings, even the canoes in which the traders carried their wares (p. 57).
Step 3 - Raise and Trade Horses: When horses came to the Plateau in the early 18th c entury, tribes like the Yakima, Nez Perce, and Cayusebecame expert horse raise rs and traders (p. 57).
Step 4 - Practice Traditional Tribal Ceremonies: The Plateau Indians had a complex system of beliefs and ceremonies (p. 57).

pamphlet_excerpts: Reviving Languages and Traditions: Indians are relearning lost traditions and languages and reviving their arts and crafts, their songs, dances, and stories (p. 17).
Reclaiming Tribal Self-Determination: Many have chosen not to disappear into America's "melting pot." Indians are reclaiming control over what happens to them (p. 17).
Choosing Modern Tribal Futures: They want to decide for themselves how they will live in the modern world (p. 17).
Balancing Heritage and Modernity: The question is, how can they keep cultural roots alive and protect and preserve tribal identities, yet still be a part of modern society (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Support Tribal Self-Determination: They want to decide for themselves how they will live in the modern world (p. 17).
Step 2 - Preserve Living Cultural Roots: The question is, how can they keep cultural roots alive and protect and preserve tribal identities, yet still be a part of modern society (p. 17).
Step 3 - Examine Modern Community Challenges: There is no easy answer, and no one knows what the future holds (p. 17).
Step 4 - Research Influential Indigenous Leaders: They may have been renowned leaders, peacemakers, or lawmakers (p. 17).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why did American Indian nations across regions such as the Pacific Northwest, the Great Plains, and the Desert Southwest develop markedly different housing, diets, and clothing prior to European contact?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why did American Indian nations across regions such as the Pacific Northwest, the Great Plains, and the Desert Southwest develop markedly different housing, diets, and clothing prior to European contact?
options: A. All tribes followed a single continental council that assigned different crafts and housing styles to each region by lottery.
B. Each Indigenous nation adapted its technology, shelter, food ways, and social organization to the specific geography, climate, and natural resources of its homeland.
C. Tribes in every region relied exclusively on imported European iron tools and domesticated horses for thousands of years before 1492.
D. Differences in shelter and diet were caused solely by proximity to Spanish missions established along the Atlantic seaboard.
choices: A. All tribes followed a single continental council that assigned different crafts and housing styles to each region by lottery.
B. Each Indigenous nation adapted its technology, shelter, food ways, and social organization to the specific geography, climate, and natural resources of its homeland.
C. Tribes in every region relied exclusively on imported European iron tools and domesticated horses for thousands of years before 1492.
D. Differences in shelter and diet were caused solely by proximity to Spanish missions established along the Atlantic seaboard.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Each Indigenous nation adapted its technology, shelter, food ways, and social organization to the specific geography, climate, and natural resources of its homeland.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): American Indian cultures developed distinct lifeways (such as cedar plank houses in the Pacific Northwest, bison hide tipis on the Plains, and adobe pueblos in the Southwest) adapted directly to local ecosystems and resources.

options: A. Dogsleds pulled across frozen tundra trails
B. Dugout canoes navigated along the Columbia and Fraser river systems
C. Sailing vessels built from bound balsa logs along the coast
D. Wheeled wooden carts drawn along stone-paved highways
choices: A. Dogsleds pulled across frozen tundra trails
B. Dugout canoes navigated along the Columbia and Fraser river systems
C. Sailing vessels built from bound balsa logs along the coast
D. Wheeled wooden carts drawn along stone-paved highways
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Dugout canoes navigated along the Columbia and Fraser river systems
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Before horses reached the region in the early 1700s, Plateau tribes used dugout canoes to travel and trade widely along the Columbia and Fraser river systems (p. 57).

pamphlet_excerpts: Open-Minded Management Communication: They want management to listen to the workers with an open mind and to consider that their claims are valid (p. 12).
Transparency During Company Sales: If the company is for sale, employees expect management to share information about terms and conditions so the workers can make appropriate plans (p. 12).
Advance Notice of Outsourcing: If the company plans to outsource jobs, employees want to know if the employer plans to transfer or lay them (p. 12).
Protection From Job Displacement: Workers want assurances that they will not be displaced by machinery and technology or replaced by guest workers (p. 12).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Evaluate Outsourcing Transfer Plans: If the company plans to outsource jobs, employees want to know if the employer plans to transfer or lay them (p. 12).
Step 2 - Assess Technological Displacement Risks: Workers want assurances that they will not be displaced by machinery and technology or replaced by guest workers (p. 12).
Step 3 - Balance Jobs and Benefits: Workers try to strike a balance between keeping their jobs and protecting fringe benefits (p. 12).
Step 4 - Examine Executive Worker Pay: However, today's corporate executives may earn many times more than the workers in the same company (p. 12).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: During a troop discussion on workplace rights for Requirement 1, a Scout asks why nineteenth and early twentieth century workers organized labor unions. Which explanation is historically accurate?
quiz_item.question: During a troop discussion on workplace rights for Requirement 1, a Scout asks why nineteenth and early twentieth century workers organized labor unions. Which explanation is historically accurate?
options: A. Workers organized primarily to abolish hourly wages in favor of unpaid agricultural apprenticeships and longer seven-day factory schedules.
B. Labor unions were created by railroad corporations to set nationwide retail prices and eliminate interstate freight tariffs.
C. Workers joined together to bargain collectively for safer working conditions, an eight-hour workday, fair living wages, and laws ending exploitative child labor.
D. Early unions were formed by federal courts to ban strikes and require employees to purchase their own heavy factory machinery.
choices: A. Workers organized primarily to abolish hourly wages in favor of unpaid agricultural apprenticeships and longer seven-day factory schedules.
B. Labor unions were created by railroad corporations to set nationwide retail prices and eliminate interstate freight tariffs.
C. Workers joined together to bargain collectively for safer working conditions, an eight-hour workday, fair living wages, and laws ending exploitative child labor.
D. Early unions were formed by federal courts to ban strikes and require employees to purchase their own heavy factory machinery.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Workers joined together to bargain collectively for safer working conditions, an eight-hour workday, fair living wages, and laws ending exploitative child labor.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The American labor movement arose so workers could use collective bargaining to address workplace hazards, excessive hours, low pay, and child labor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Guild-Based Craft Training: Craft unions provide training to their members based on the model of medieval craft guilds (p. 19).
Apprenticeship School and Work: A trainee begins as an apprentice, learning a trade at a union sponsored school and acting as an assistant on the job (p. 19).
Advancing to Journey Worker: After successfully completing a training period of four or more years, the apprentice becomes a fully qualified skilled worker, or journey worker (p. 19).
Private and Public Sectors: The private sector and the public sector (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Complete Multi-Year Apprenticeship Training: After successfully completing a training period of four or more years, the apprentice becomes a fully qualified skilled worker, or journey worker (p. 19).
Step 2 - Distinguish Economic Employment Sectors: The private sector and the public sector (p. 19).
Step 3 - Identify Private Sector Enterprises: The private sector refers to the aspects of the economy that are under the control of individuals and privately owned businesses (p. 19).
Step 4 - Identify Public Sector Agencies: The public sector is under the control of the federal, state, or local governments (p. 19).

Step 3 - Identify Emerging Workplace Disputes: Did you notice how fast a simple plan becomes complicated (p. 49).
Step 4 - Compare Bargaining Resolution Styles: Situations like that happen every day in businesses (p. 49).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How does the 21st-century global economy differ from the international economy of the previous 200 years?
quiz_item.question: How does the 21st-century global economy differ from the international economy of the previous 200 years?
options: A. National governments now control every aspect of cross-border commerce without corporate input
B. International shipping of manufactured goods has been completely replaced by local barter
C. Corporations, investment bankers, and traders treat the world as one big market, outpacing government regulation
D. Tariffs have eliminated all foreign competition for American manufacturing workers
choices: A. National governments now control every aspect of cross-border commerce without corporate input
B. International shipping of manufactured goods has been completely replaced by local barter
C. Corporations, investment bankers, and traders treat the world as one big market, outpacing government regulation
D. Tariffs have eliminated all foreign competition for American manufacturing workers
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Corporations, investment bankers, and traders treat the world as one big market, outpacing government regulation
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Previously, trade occurred between nations under government-set rules, whereas today corporations and investors treat the world as one big market changing faster than governments can regulate (p. 12).

pamphlet_excerpts: Owner Focus on Profitability: The foremost concern of a company owner (an individual or a group of investors) is to make a profit (p. 46).
Profit-Driven Investment Decisions: They make decisions about whether to continue to invest in the companies based on the profitability of those businesses (p. 46).
Cutting Costs and Selling: Just as management may shut down a division in a company to cutcosts and improve profitability, the owner may sell an unprofitable company to protect (p. 46).
Institutional and Individual Stockholders: Financial institutions, investment groups, and individuals often buy shares of stock in a company (p. 46).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Evaluate Division Closure Decisions: Just as management may shut down a division in a company to cutcosts and improve profitability, the owner may sell an unprofitable company to protect (p. 46).
Step 2 - Identify Company Stockholder Groups: Financial institutions, investment groups, and individuals often buy shares of stock in a company (p. 46).
Step 3 - Understand Share Ownership Percentages: Each share represents a piece of the company, a percentage of ownership (p. 46).
Step 4 - Examine Employee Stock Options: Some companies offer an employee stock-option plan that allows employees to acquire shares of company stock and receive stock distributions (p. 46).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: During a troop discussion on workplace rights for Requirement 1, a Scout asks why nineteenth and early twentieth century workers organized labor unions. Which explanation is historically accurate?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: During a troop discussion on workplace rights for Requirement 1, a Scout asks why nineteenth and early twentieth century workers organized labor unions. Which explanation is historically accurate?
options: A. Workers organized primarily to abolish hourly wages in favor of unpaid agricultural apprenticeships and longer seven-day factory schedules.
B. Labor unions were created by railroad corporations to set nationwide retail prices and eliminate interstate freight tariffs.
C. Workers joined together to bargain collectively for safer working conditions, an eight-hour workday, fair living wages, and laws ending exploitative child labor.
D. Early unions were formed by federal courts to ban strikes and require employees to purchase their own heavy factory machinery.
choices: A. Workers organized primarily to abolish hourly wages in favor of unpaid agricultural apprenticeships and longer seven-day factory schedules.
B. Labor unions were created by railroad corporations to set nationwide retail prices and eliminate interstate freight tariffs.
C. Workers joined together to bargain collectively for safer working conditions, an eight-hour workday, fair living wages, and laws ending exploitative child labor.
D. Early unions were formed by federal courts to ban strikes and require employees to purchase their own heavy factory machinery.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Workers joined together to bargain collectively for safer working conditions, an eight-hour workday, fair living wages, and laws ending exploitative child labor.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The American labor movement arose so workers could use collective bargaining to address workplace hazards, excessive hours, low pay, and child labor.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What contributed to the uneven, 'fits and starts' growth of trade unionism in American history?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What contributed to the uneven, 'fits and starts' growth of trade unionism in American history?
options: A. A constitutional ban on all worker associations prior to 1950
B. Complete agreement between corporate boards and union organizers
C. The success or failure of strikes, boom-and-bust business cycles, and union militancy
D. Mandatory federal conscription of all factory workers into craft guilds
choices: A. A constitutional ban on all worker associations prior to 1950
B. Complete agreement between corporate boards and union organizers
C. The success or failure of strikes, boom-and-bust business cycles, and union militancy
D. Mandatory federal conscription of all factory workers into craft guilds
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. The success or failure of strikes, boom-and-bust business cycles, and union militancy
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Trade unionism expanded and contracted in response to strike outcomes, boom-and-bust business cycles, and intense employer opposition (p. 16).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In a craft union training program, what title does an apprentice earn after successfully completing four or more years of instruction and on-the-job training?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In a craft union training program, what title does an apprentice earn after successfully completing four or more years of instruction and on-the-job training?
options: A. Shop steward
B. Federal mediator
C. Corporate trustee
D. Journey worker
choices: A. Shop steward
B. Federal mediator
C. Corporate trustee
D. Journey worker
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Journey worker
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): After finishing a training period of four or more years at a union-sponsored school and on the job, an apprentice becomes a fully qualified skilled worker known as a journey worker (p. 19).

choices: A. To show how quickly a simple work agreement can become complicated by disputes over duties and profits
B. To prove that youth businesses are exempt from all equipment maintenance costs

D. To illustrate how federal mediators set neighborhood lawn-mowing prices
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. To show how quickly a simple work agreement can become complicated by disputes over duties and profits
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The lawn-care scenario shows how quickly a simple plan becomes complicated when real-world disagreements arise over equipment upkeep, expenses, and splitting profits (p. 49).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which methods did management historically use to suppress early union organizing and strikes?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which methods did management historically use to suppress early union organizing and strikes?
options: A. Offering immediate profit-sharing bonuses and four-day workweeks
B. Using court injunctions, private armies, federal troops, and convict strikebreakers
C. Turning factory ownership over to local municipal governments
D. Petitioning Congress to make union membership mandatory for all trades
choices: A. Offering immediate profit-sharing bonuses and four-day workweeks
B. Using court injunctions, private armies, federal troops, and convict strikebreakers
C. Turning factory ownership over to local municipal governments
D. Petitioning Congress to make union membership mandatory for all trades
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Using court injunctions, private armies, federal troops, and convict strikebreakers
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): To block union influence in the workplace, management used the courts, private armies, federal troops, and prison convict contracts to break strikes (p. 16).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does the 21st-century global economy differ from the international economy of the previous 200 years?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does the 21st-century global economy differ from the international economy of the previous 200 years?
options: A. National governments now control every aspect of cross-border commerce without corporate input
B. International shipping of manufactured goods has been completely replaced by local barter
C. Corporations, investment bankers, and traders treat the world as one big market, outpacing government regulation
D. Tariffs have eliminated all foreign competition for American manufacturing workers
choices: A. National governments now control every aspect of cross-border commerce without corporate input
B. International shipping of manufactured goods has been completely replaced by local barter
C. Corporations, investment bankers, and traders treat the world as one big market, outpacing government regulation
D. Tariffs have eliminated all foreign competition for American manufacturing workers
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Corporations, investment bankers, and traders treat the world as one big market, outpacing government regulation
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Previously, trade occurred between nations under government-set rules, whereas today corporations and investors treat the world as one big market changing faster than governments can regulate (p. 12).

options: A. Holsteins and Jerseys are dairy breeds selected for high milk volume and butterfat production, whereas Angus and Herefords are beef breeds selected for muscle marbling and meat yield.
B. Holsteins and Jerseys are draft breeds raised to pull heavy farm implements, whereas Angus and Herefords are raised exclusively for fine wool and mohair.
C. Holsteins and Jerseys are arid-climate beef cattle from Texas, whereas Angus and Herefords are tropical dairy breeds imported from India.
D. All four breeds are dual-purpose poultry and swine hybrids developed for small urban backyard farms.
choices: A. Holsteins and Jerseys are dairy breeds selected for high milk volume and butterfat production, whereas Angus and Herefords are beef breeds selected for muscle marbling and meat yield.

quiz_item.question: In cattle breeding and herd management terminology, what is a freemartin?
options: A. A heifer or cow that is nearly ready to calve and begin lactating
B. A young cow that has had only one calf before being placed in a feedlot
C. A sterile female calf born as a twin alongside a male calf
D. A male bovine castrated prior to reaching sexual maturity
choices: A. A heifer or cow that is nearly ready to calve and begin lactating
B. A young cow that has had only one calf before being placed in a feedlot
C. A sterile female calf born as a twin alongside a male calf
D. A male bovine castrated prior to reaching sexual maturity
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. A sterile female calf born as a twin alongside a male calf
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A freemartin is a female calf born as a twin with a male calf; shared hormones in the uterus almost always render the female twin sterile and unsuitable for breeding (p. 15).

requirements.lead_text: Complete ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Complete ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Beef Cattle. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit a farm or ranch where beef cattle are produced under any of these systems: feeding market cattle for harvest, cow/calf operation (producing cattle for sale to commercial feeders), or producing purebred cattle for sale as breeding stock to others. Talk with the operator to learn how the cattle were handled, fed, weighed, and shipped. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a cattle ranch or farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on beef cattle production. Tell about your findings. (2) Sketch a plan of a feedlot to include its forage and grain storage facilities, and loading chute for 30 or more fattening steers; or sketch a corral plan with cutting and loading chutes for handling 50 or more beef cows and their calves at one time. (3) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of beef. Tell about the U. S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) dual grading system of beef. Tell the basis of each grade in each system. (4) Define the following terms: bull, steer, bullock, cow, heifer, freemartin, heiferette, and calf. (b) Option B, Dairy. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell how a cow or a goat converts forage and grain into milk. Explain the differences in feeds typically used for dairy cows versus those fed to beef cows. (2) Make a chart showing the components in cow's milk or goat's milk. Chart the amount of each component. (3) Explain the requirements for producing grade A milk. Tell how and why milk is pasteurized. (4) Tell about the kinds of equipment used for milking and the sanitation standards that must be met on dairy farms. (5) Define the following terms: bull, cow, steer, heifer, springer, buck, doe, and kid. (6) Visit a dairy farm or a milk processing plant. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a dairy farm or processing plant, view a video from a breed or dairy association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on dairying. Tell about your findings. (c) Option C, Horse. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a useful saddle horse barn and exercise yard. (2) Tell about the history of the horse and the benefits it has brought to people. Using the four breeds of horses you chose in requirement 1, discuss the different special uses of each breed. (3) Define the following terms: mare, stallion, gelding, foal, colt, filly; mustang, quarter horse, draft horse, pacer, trotter; pinto, calico, palomino, roan, overo, and tobiano. (4) Visit a horse farm. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a horse farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on horses. Tell about your findings. (5) Outline the proper feeding of a horse doing light work. Explain why the amount and kind of feed will change according to the kind of horse and the work it does. Describe what colic is, what can cause it, and its symptoms. (d) Option D, Sheep or Goat. Choose one and do ALL of the following based upon the choice: (1) Make a sketch of a live lamb or goat. Show the location of the various wholesale and retail cuts. (2) Discuss how wools are sorted and graded. (3) List products that can be made from the milk. (4) Based on your choice, do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a lamb or goat from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm or ranch where sheep or goats are raised. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a sheep or goat farm or ranch, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on sheep or goats. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms for a sheep (wether, ewe, ram, and lamb) OR a goat (doe, nanny, kid, buck, and billy). (e) Option E, Hog. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of pork. Tell about the recommended USDA grades of pork. Tell the basis for each grade. (2) Outline in writing the proper feeding programs used from the breeding of a gilt or sow through the weaning of the litter. Discuss the feeding programs for the growth and finishing periods. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a feeder pig from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm where hogs are produced, or visit a packing plant handling hogs. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a hog production unit or packing plant, view a video from a packer or processor, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on hogs. Tell about your findings. (4) Define the following terms: gilt, sow, barrow, and boar. (f) Option F, Avian. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a layer house or broiler house showing nests, roosts, feeders, waterers, and means of ventilation. Explain how insulation, ventilation, temperature controls, automatic lights, and other environmental controls are used to protect birds from heat, cold, and bad weather. Explain the importance of light for egg production. (2) Explain why overcrowding is dangerous for poultry flocks. (3) Tell about the grading of eggs. Describe the classes of chicken meat. (4) Do ONE of the following: (a) Manage an egg-producing flock for five months. Keep records of feed purchased, eggs sold, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Raise five chickens from hatching. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (c) Visit a commercial avian production facility. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a commercial facility, view a video from a poultry association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on poultry production. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms: chick, pullet, hen, cockerel, cock, and capon.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Beef Cattle. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit a farm or ranch where beef cattle are produced under any of these systems: feeding market cattle for harvest, cow/calf operation (producing cattle for sale to commercial feeders), or producing purebred cattle for sale as breeding stock to others. Talk with the operator to learn how the cattle were handled, fed, weighed, and shipped. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a cattle ranch or farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on beef cattle production. Tell about your findings. (2) Sketch a plan of a feedlot to include its forage and grain storage facilities, and loading chute for 30 or more fattening steers; or sketch a corral plan with cutting and loading chutes for handling 50 or more beef cows and their calves at one time. (3) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of beef. Tell about the U. S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) dual grading system of beef. Tell the basis of each grade in each system. (4) Define the following terms: bull, steer, bullock, cow, heifer, freemartin, heiferette, and calf.

sub_requirements.text: Option B, Dairy. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell how a cow or a goat converts forage and grain into milk. Explain the differences in feeds typically used for dairy cows versus those fed to beef cows. (2) Make a chart showing the components in cow's milk or goat's milk. Chart the amount of each component. (3) Explain the requirements for producing grade A milk. Tell how and why milk is pasteurized. (4) Tell about the kinds of equipment used for milking and the sanitation standards that must be met on dairy farms. (5) Define the following terms: bull, cow, steer, heifer, springer, buck, doe, and kid. (6) Visit a dairy farm or a milk processing plant. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a dairy farm or processing plant, view a video from a breed or dairy association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on dairying. Tell about your findings.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Dairy. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell how a cow or a goat converts forage and grain into milk. Explain the differences in feeds typically used for dairy cows versus those fed to beef cows. (2) Make a chart showing the components in cow's milk or goat's milk. Chart the amount of each component. (3) Explain the requirements for producing grade A milk. Tell how and why milk is pasteurized. (4) Tell about the kinds of equipment used for milking and the sanitation standards that must be met on dairy farms. (5) Define the following terms: bull, cow, steer, heifer, springer, buck, doe, and kid. (6) Visit a dairy farm or a milk processing plant. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a dairy farm or processing plant, view a video from a breed or dairy association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on dairying. Tell about your findings.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option E, Hog. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of pork. Tell about the recommended USDA grades of pork. Tell the basis for each grade. (2) Outline in writing the proper feeding programs used from the breeding of a gilt or sow through the weaning of the litter. Discuss the feeding programs for the growth and finishing periods. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a feeder pig from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm where hogs are produced, or visit a packing plant handling hogs. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a hog production unit or packing plant, view a video from a packer or processor, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on hogs. Tell about your findings. (4) Define the following terms: gilt, sow, barrow, and boar.

sub_requirements.text: Option F, Avian. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a layer house or broiler house showing nests, roosts, feeders, waterers, and means of ventilation. Explain how insulation, ventilation, temperature controls, automatic lights, and other environmental controls are used to protect birds from heat, cold, and bad weather. Explain the importance of light for egg production. (2) Explain why overcrowding is dangerous for poultry flocks. (3) Tell about the grading of eggs. Describe the classes of chicken meat. (4) Do ONE of the following: (a) Manage an egg-producing flock for five months. Keep records of feed purchased, eggs sold, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Raise five chickens from hatching. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (c) Visit a commercial avian production facility. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a commercial facility, view a video from a poultry association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on poultry production. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms: chick, pullet, hen, cockerel, cock, and capon.

requirements.description: Complete ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Beef Cattle. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit a farm or ranch where beef cattle are produced under any of these systems: feeding market cattle for harvest, cow/calf operation (producing cattle for sale to commercial feeders), or producing purebred cattle for sale as breeding stock to others. Talk with the operator to learn how the cattle were handled, fed, weighed, and shipped. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a cattle ranch or farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on beef cattle production. Tell about your findings. (2) Sketch a plan of a feedlot to include its forage and grain storage facilities, and loading chute for 30 or more fattening steers; or sketch a corral plan with cutting and loading chutes for handling 50 or more beef cows and their calves at one time. (3) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of beef. Tell about the U. S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) dual grading system of beef. Tell the basis of each grade in each system. (4) Define the following terms: bull, steer, bullock, cow, heifer, freemartin, heiferette, and calf. (b) Option B, Dairy. Do ALL of the following: (1) Tell how a cow or a goat converts forage and grain into milk. Explain the differences in feeds typically used for dairy cows versus those fed to beef cows. (2) Make a chart showing the components in cow's milk or goat's milk. Chart the amount of each component. (3) Explain the requirements for producing grade A milk. Tell how and why milk is pasteurized. (4) Tell about the kinds of equipment used for milking and the sanitation standards that must be met on dairy farms. (5) Define the following terms: bull, cow, steer, heifer, springer, buck, doe, and kid. (6) Visit a dairy farm or a milk processing plant. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a dairy farm or processing plant, view a video from a breed or dairy association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on dairying. Tell about your findings. (c) Option C, Horse. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a useful saddle horse barn and exercise yard. (2) Tell about the history of the horse and the benefits it has brought to people. Using the four breeds of horses you chose in requirement 1, discuss the different special uses of each breed. (3) Define the following terms: mare, stallion, gelding, foal, colt, filly; mustang, quarter horse, draft horse, pacer, trotter; pinto, calico, palomino, roan, overo, and tobiano. (4) Visit a horse farm. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a horse farm, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on horses. Tell about your findings. (5) Outline the proper feeding of a horse doing light work. Explain why the amount and kind of feed will change according to the kind of horse and the work it does. Describe what colic is, what can cause it, and its symptoms. (d) Option D, Sheep or Goat. Choose one and do ALL of the following based upon the choice: (1) Make a sketch of a live lamb or goat. Show the location of the various wholesale and retail cuts. (2) Discuss how wools are sorted and graded. (3) List products that can be made from the milk. (4) Based on your choice, do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a lamb or goat from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm or ranch where sheep or goats are raised. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a sheep or goat farm or ranch, view a video from a breed association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on sheep or goats. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms for a sheep (wether, ewe, ram, and lamb) OR a goat (doe, nanny, kid, buck, and billy). (e) Option E, Hog. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch showing the principal wholesale and retail cuts of pork. Tell about the recommended USDA grades of pork. Tell the basis for each grade. (2) Outline in writing the proper feeding programs used from the breeding of a gilt or sow through the weaning of the litter. Discuss the feeding programs for the growth and finishing periods. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Raise a feeder pig from weaning to market weight. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Visit a farm where hogs are produced, or visit a packing plant handling hogs. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a hog production unit or packing plant, view a video from a packer or processor, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on hogs. Tell about your findings. (4) Define the following terms: gilt, sow, barrow, and boar. (f) Option F, Avian. Do ALL of the following: (1) Make a sketch of a layer house or broiler house showing nests, roosts, feeders, waterers, and means of ventilation. Explain how insulation, ventilation, temperature controls, automatic lights, and other environmental controls are used to protect birds from heat, cold, and bad weather. Explain the importance of light for egg production. (2) Explain why overcrowding is dangerous for poultry flocks. (3) Tell about the grading of eggs. Describe the classes of chicken meat. (4) Do ONE of the following: (a) Manage an egg-producing flock for five months. Keep records of feed purchased, eggs sold, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (b) Raise five chickens from hatching. Keep records of feed intake, weight gains, medication, vaccination, and mortality. Present your records to your counselor for review. (c) Visit a commercial avian production facility. Describe what you saw and explain what you learned. If you cannot visit a commercial facility, view a video from a poultry association, or research the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission) for information on poultry production. Tell about your findings. (5) Define the following terms: chick, pullet, hen, cockerel, cock, and capon.

choices: A. Holsteins and Jerseys are dairy breeds selected for high milk volume and butterfat production, whereas Angus and Herefords are beef breeds selected for muscle marbling and meat yield.

D. Fresh, clean water available at all times

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): While protein, energy, mineral, and fiber requirements differ across digestive systems, fresh, clean water must be available at all times for every livestock species (p. 44).

B. Regular manure removal, clean dry bedding, and controlling visitor and equipment traffic
C. Sealing barn windows tightly in summer to trap heat and humidity inside

choices: A. Allowing visitors from other farms to walk freely through feed alleys without washing boots

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Regular manure removal, clean dry bedding, and controlling visitor and equipment traffic
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Effective waste management and biosecurity reduce fly breeding, prevent parasite transmission, protect water quality, and keep external pathogens from entering the herd or flock (p. 44).

C. A sterile female calf born as a twin alongside a male calf

choices: A. A heifer or cow that is nearly ready to calve and begin lactating

pamphlet_excerpts: Ancient Storytelling and Motion: The history of animation is as old as the history of story telling (p. 21).
Prehistoric Painted Cave Art: The word animate means "alive." When early humans first painted animals and hunting scenes on cave walls, they lit fires to show off their work (p. 21).
Flickering Firelight Motion Illusions: The dancing flames cast irregular light in the caves, making the images of prehistoric animals appear to be alive and moving (p. 21).
Projected Hand Shadow Animals: Also, from the earliest times, children worldwide have used a light source to project hand shadows onto a wall to create the shapes of animals (p. 21).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Observe Flickering Light Illusions: The dancing flames cast irregular light in the caves, making the images of prehistoric animals appear to be alive and moving (p. 21).
Step 2 - Project Hand Shadow Shapes: Also, from the earliest times, children worldwide have used a light source to project hand shadows onto a wall to create the shapes of animals (p. 21).
Step 3 - Share Visual Storytelling Experiences: This kind of entertainment can be enjoyed by a group of friends (p. 21).
Step 4 - Create Lifelike Moving Imitations: The shared experience of creating lifelike imitation is a key part of the attraction of animation (p. 21).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Animation Requirement 1, what optical and neurological phenomenon allows a viewer to perceive a sequence of 24 still images per second as continuous fluid motion, and what is the role of keyframes?
quiz_item.question: In Animation Requirement 1, what optical and neurological phenomenon allows a viewer to perceive a sequence of 24 still images per second as continuous fluid motion, and what is the role of keyframes?
options: A. Chromatic aberration blends primary colors on the screen, while keyframes are the final audio tracks mixed after rendering.
B. Binocular parallax shifts depth perception between the left and right eyes, while keyframes are discarded background sketches.
C. Refractive dispersion slows light entering the cornea, while keyframes are every single in-between drawing made by assistant animators.
D. Persistence of vision and beta movement cause the brain to bridge rapid sequential frames into smooth motion, while keyframes define the primary start and end poses of an action.
choices: A. Chromatic aberration blends primary colors on the screen, while keyframes are the final audio tracks mixed after rendering.
B. Binocular parallax shifts depth perception between the left and right eyes, while keyframes are discarded background sketches.
C. Refractive dispersion slows light entering the cornea, while keyframes are every single in-between drawing made by assistant animators.
D. Persistence of vision and beta movement cause the brain to bridge rapid sequential frames into smooth motion, while keyframes define the primary start and end poses of an action.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Persistence of vision and beta movement cause the brain to bridge rapid sequential frames into smooth motion, while keyframes define the primary start and end poses of an action.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Animation relies on persistence of vision and perceptual motion processing across sequential frames, with lead animators setting extreme poses (keyframes) and in-between frames completing the transition.
