patrol_quiz_bank.question: In geocaching terminology, what are attributes on a cache listing page?
options: A. Icons on a cache detail page that show specific characteristics like kid-friendly access or 24-hour availability
B. Satellite correction codes entered into a GPS receiver to boost signal strength
C. Coordinates that mark where you parked your vehicle at the trailhead
D. Serial numbers engraved on metal tags that travel from cache to cache
choices: A. Icons on a cache detail page that show specific characteristics like kid-friendly access or 24-hour availability
B. Satellite correction codes entered into a GPS receiver to boost signal strength
C. Coordinates that mark where you parked your vehicle at the trailhead
D. Serial numbers engraved on metal tags that travel from cache to cache
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Icons on a cache detail page that show specific characteristics like kid-friendly access or 24-hour availability
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Attribute icons on a cache listing communicate specific characteristics, such as whether the cache is kid-friendly, available 24 hours a day, or requires special equipment (p. 69).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does a GPS receiver calculate its position on Earth?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does a GPS receiver calculate its position on Earth?
options: A. By measuring variations in Earth's magnetic field and local barometric air pressure
B. By bouncing a laser beam off cell phone towers within five miles of the trailhead
C. By taking high-resolution photographs of the ground from orbit and matching landmarks
D. By timing the slight differences in arrival times of radio signals sent by multiple orbiting satellites
choices: A. By measuring variations in Earth's magnetic field and local barometric air pressure
B. By bouncing a laser beam off cell phone towers within five miles of the trailhead
C. By taking high-resolution photographs of the ground from orbit and matching landmarks
D. By timing the slight differences in arrival times of radio signals sent by multiple orbiting satellites
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. By timing the slight differences in arrival times of radio signals sent by multiple orbiting satellites
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): All GPS satellites transmit their location and current time simultaneously, and the receiver calculates its position by measuring the slight differences in arrival times from 24 to 30 orbiting satellites (p. 11).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why must a geocacher carry and know how to use a map and compass even when carrying a modern GPS receiver?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why must a geocacher carry and know how to use a map and compass even when carrying a modern GPS receiver?
options: A. Because geocaching rules prohibit turning on a GPS unit until you are within 100 feet of the cache
B. Because heavy tree cover, narrow canyons, or tall buildings can block satellite reception and GPS units fail without showing terrain obstacles
C. Because GPS satellites are turned off over wilderness areas during the winter months
D. Because a magnetic compass automatically points directly toward plastic geocache containers
choices: A. Because geocaching rules prohibit turning on a GPS unit until you are within 100 feet of the cache
B. Because heavy tree cover, narrow canyons, or tall buildings can block satellite reception and GPS units fail without showing terrain obstacles
C. Because GPS satellites are turned off over wilderness areas during the winter months
D. Because a magnetic compass automatically points directly toward plastic geocache containers
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Because heavy tree cover, narrow canyons, or tall buildings can block satellite reception and GPS units fail without showing terrain obstacles
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Heavy tree cover, nearby power lines, tall buildings, and narrow canyons can block or degrade satellite reception, and batteries or electronics can fail, making a map and compass essential (p. 27).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What rule applies to placing a public geocache on Scout camp property?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What rule applies to placing a public geocache on Scout camp property?
options: A. Caches can be hidden inside any restricted staff cabin as long as the camp ranger knows the coordinates
B. Scout camps are completely banned from hosting any geocaches under all circumstances
C. A public geocache can only be placed on a portion of the Scout camp property that is available to the general public to seek
D. Caches placed at Scout camps do not need permission or coordinate reviews before posting online
choices: A. Caches can be hidden inside any restricted staff cabin as long as the camp ranger knows the coordinates
B. Scout camps are completely banned from hosting any geocaches under all circumstances
C. A public geocache can only be placed on a portion of the Scout camp property that is available to the general public to seek
D. Caches placed at Scout camps do not need permission or coordinate reviews before posting online
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. A public geocache can only be placed on a portion of the Scout camp property that is available to the general public to seek
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Geocaches can only be placed at Scout camps if the chosen spot is on a portion of the property that is open and available to the general public to seek (p. 42).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the first basic step to finding your first public geocache?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the first basic step to finding your first public geocache?
options: A. Researching local caches online at geocaching.com and selecting an appropriate cache listing
B. Purchasing a metal detector and shovel before leaving home
C. Mailing a paper registration postcard to the national geocaching headquarters
D. Hiding three containers of your own before unlocking access to public cache coordinates
choices: A. Researching local caches online at geocaching.com and selecting an appropriate cache listing
B. Purchasing a metal detector and shovel before leaving home
C. Mailing a paper registration postcard to the national geocaching headquarters
D. Hiding three containers of your own before unlocking access to public cache coordinates
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Researching local caches online at geocaching.com and selecting an appropriate cache listing
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Step 1 of finding your first public geocache is Research: registering for a free basic membership at geocaching.com, searching your area, and clicking a cache name to review its details and coordinates (p. 37).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What long-term responsibility do you take on once your public geocache passes volunteer review and is published?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What long-term responsibility do you take on once your public geocache passes volunteer review and is published?
options: A. Leave the cache permanently in the woods without ever checking on it again
B. Expect the local park rangers to replace wet logbooks and broken containers for you
C. Move the container to a new set of coordinates every week without updating the listing
D. Maintain the cache container and surrounding area and act on online maintenance logs for as long as it is active
choices: A. Leave the cache permanently in the woods without ever checking on it again
B. Expect the local park rangers to replace wet logbooks and broken containers for you
C. Move the container to a new set of coordinates every week without updating the listing
D. Maintain the cache container and surrounding area and act on online maintenance logs for as long as it is active
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Maintain the cache container and surrounding area and act on online maintenance logs for as long as it is active
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Once you place a public geocache, you have an ongoing obligation to monitor the online logs and maintain both the container and the surrounding area for as long as the cache remains active (p. 42).

quiz_item.question: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
options: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
choices: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.

pamphlet_excerpts: Grain Size Cooling Depth: Rock texture, or grain size, provides information about the depth at which the minerals in the magma began to cool, forming igneous rocks (p. 66).
Fine Grained Extrusive Rocks: As an example, if you find a fine-grained igneous rock, you interpret the rock to be an extrusive rock that cooled at or near the surface (p. 66).
Coarse Grained Intrusive Rocks: Coarse-grained igneous rocks are intrusive rocks that cooled over very long periods of time (p. 66).
Tectonic Uplift and Erosion: These deep rocks get to the surface when tectonic (mountain-building) forces uplift the area and the material covering the intrusive rock is eroded away by wind (p. 66).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Identify Slow Cooling Intrusive Rocks: Coarse-grained igneous rocks are intrusive rocks that cooled over very long periods of time (p. 66).

Step 2 - Trace Uplift and Weathering Exposure: These deep rocks get to the surface when tectonic (mountain-building) forces uplift the area and the material covering the intrusive rock is eroded away by wind (p. 66).
Step 3 - Inspect Rock Color for Minerals: Another important characteristic of igneous rocks is color, which indicates the kinds of rock minerals (p. 66).
Step 4 - Recognize Quartz Rich Silicic Granite: Lighter colored igneous rocks such as granite are usually formed fromsialic or silicic magmas, rich in quartz and feldspar (p. 66).

C. Ocean tides wash deep magma chambers onto beaches every spring
D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Surface and Sedimentary Processes. Do ALL of the following: (1) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that demonstrates how sediments settle from suspension in water. Explain to your counselor what the exercise shows and why it is important. (2) Using topographical maps provided by your counselor, plot the stream gradients (different elevations divided by distance) for four different stream types (straight, meandering, dendritic, trellis). Explain which ones flow fastest and why, and which ones will carry larger grains of sediment and why. (3) On a stream diagram, show areas where you will find the following features: cut bank, fill bank, point bar, medial channel bars, and lake delta. Describe the relative sediment grain size found in each feature. (4) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that shows how some sedimentary material carried by water may be too small for you to see without a magnifier. (5) Visit a nearby stream. Find clues that show the direction of water flow, even if the water is missing. Record your observations in a notebook, and sketch those clues you observe. Discuss your observations with your counselor. (b) Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site. (c) Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor. (d) Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Surface and Sedimentary Processes. Do ALL of the following: (1) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that demonstrates how sediments settle from suspension in water. Explain to your counselor what the exercise shows and why it is important. (2) Using topographical maps provided by your counselor, plot the stream gradients (different elevations divided by distance) for four different stream types (straight, meandering, dendritic, trellis). Explain which ones flow fastest and why, and which ones will carry larger grains of sediment and why. (3) On a stream diagram, show areas where you will find the following features: cut bank, fill bank, point bar, medial channel bars, and lake delta. Describe the relative sediment grain size found in each feature. (4) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that shows how some sedimentary material carried by water may be too small for you to see without a magnifier. (5) Visit a nearby stream. Find clues that show the direction of water flow, even if the water is missing. Record your observations in a notebook, and sketch those clues you observe. Discuss your observations with your counselor.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site.

sub_requirements.label: (c)
sub_requirements.text: Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor.

sub_requirements.text: Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

(c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

requirements.description: Do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Surface and Sedimentary Processes. Do ALL of the following: (1) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that demonstrates how sediments settle from suspension in water. Explain to your counselor what the exercise shows and why it is important. (2) Using topographical maps provided by your counselor, plot the stream gradients (different elevations divided by distance) for four different stream types (straight, meandering, dendritic, trellis). Explain which ones flow fastest and why, and which ones will carry larger grains of sediment and why. (3) On a stream diagram, show areas where you will find the following features: cut bank, fill bank, point bar, medial channel bars, and lake delta. Describe the relative sediment grain size found in each feature. (4) Conduct an experiment approved by your counselor that shows how some sedimentary material carried by water may be too small for you to see without a magnifier. (5) Visit a nearby stream. Find clues that show the direction of water flow, even if the water is missing. Record your observations in a notebook, and sketch those clues you observe. Discuss your observations with your counselor. (b) Option B, Energy Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) List the top five Earth resources used to generate electricity in the United States. (2) Discuss source rock, trap, and reservoir rock, the three components necessary for the occurrence of oil and gas underground. (3) Explain how each of the following items is used in subsurface exploration to locate oil or gas: reflection seismic, electric well logs, stratigraphic correlation, offshore platform, geologic map, subsurface structure map, subsurface isopach map, and core samples and cutting samples. (4) Using at least 20 data points provided by your counselor, create a subsurface structure map and use it to explain how subsurface geology maps are used to find oil, gas, or coal resources. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a display or presentation showing how oil and gas or coal is found, extracted, and processed. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school) in a five-minute presentation. (b) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's permission and assistance, arrange for a visit to an operating drilling rig. While there, talk with a geologist and ask to see what the geologist does onsite. Ask to see cutting samples taken at the site. (c) Option C, Mineral Resources. Do ALL of the following: (1) Define rock. Discuss the three classes of rocks including their origin and characteristics. (2) Define mineral. Discuss the origin of minerals and their chemical composition and identification properties, including hardness, specific gravity, color, streak, cleavage, luster, and crystal form. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect 10 different rocks or minerals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Label each specimen, identify its class and origin, determine its chemical composition, and list its physical properties. Share your collection with your counselor. (b) With your counselor's assistance, identify 15 different rocks and minerals. List the name of each specimen, tell whether it is a rock or mineral, and give the name of its class (if it is a rock) or list its identifying physical properties (if it is a mineral). (4) List three of the most common road-building materials used in your area. Explain how each material is produced and how each is used in road building. (5) Do ONE of the following: (a) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit an active mining site, quarry, or sand and gravel pit. Tell your counselor what you learned about the resources extracted from this location and how these resources are used by society. (b) With your counselor, choose two examples of rocks and two examples of minerals. Discuss the mining of these materials and describe how each is used by society. (c) With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, visit the office of a civil engineer and learn how geology is used in construction. Discuss what you learned with your counselor. (d) Option D, Earth History. Do ALL of the following: (1) Create a chart showing suggested geological eras and periods. Determine which period the rocks in your region might have been formed. (2) Explain the theory of plate tectonics. Make a chart explaining, or discuss with your counselor, how the processes of plate tectonics work. Discuss how plate tectonics determines the distribution of most of the Earth's volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountain belts. (3) Explain to your counselor the processes of burial and fossilization, and discuss the concept of extinction. (4) Explain to your counselor how fossils provide information about ancient life, environment, climate, and geography. Discuss the following terms and explain how animals from each habitat obtain food: benthonic, pelagic, littoral, lacustrine, open marine, brackish, fluvial, eolian, and protected reef. (5) Collect 10 different fossil plants or animals OR (with your counselor's assistance) identify 15 different fossil plants or animals. Record in a notebook where you obtained (found, bought, traded) each one. Classify each specimen to the best of your ability, and explain how each one might have survived and obtained food. Tell what else you can learn from these fossils. (6) Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit a science museum or the geology department of a local university that has fossils on display. With your parent or guardian's and counselor's approval, before you go, make an appointment with a curator or guide who can show you how the fossils are preserved and prepared for display. (b) Visit a structure in your area that was built using fossiliferous rocks. Determine what kind of rock was used and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found there. (c) Visit a rock outcrop that contains fossils. Determine what kind of rock contains the fossils, and tell your counselor the kinds of fossil evidence you found at the outcrop. (d) Prepare a display or presentation on your state fossil. Include an image of the fossil, the age of the fossil, and its classification. You may use maps, books, articles from periodicals, and research found on the internet (with your parent or guardian's permission). Share the display with your counselor or a small group (such as your class at school). If your state does not have a state fossil, you may select a state fossil from a neighboring state.

pamphlet_excerpts: Hot Steam Altering Rock Minerals: Earth's Treasures. elements are brought by very hot steam moving through existing rock, which can alter the minerals in the rock to form new minerals (p. 68).
Hydrothermal Ore Deposit Formation: Hydrothermal solutions often associated with metamorphic processes penetrate surrounding rocks forming many of the ore deposits found in the world (p. 68).
Magma Heat and Burial Pressure: Metamorphic rocks can be formed by contact with magma, by heat and pressure associated with burial of sediments, or by squeezing forces (p. 68).
Foliated Metamorphic Mineral Layers: Foliated, or layered, metamorphic rocks generally form from existing rocks that have many different mineral grains (p. 68).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Identify Heat and Pressure Sources: Metamorphic rocks can be formed by contact with magma, by heat and pressure associated with burial of sediments, or by squeezing forces (p. 68).
Step 2 - Check Multi Mineral Foliated Layers: Foliated, or layered, metamorphic rocks generally form from existing rocks that have many different mineral grains (p. 68).

Step 3 - Trace Shale to Gneiss Progression: Depending on the degree of metamorphism, shale may be altered to form slate, schist, or gneiss, all of which exhibit foliation but varying grain sizes (p. 68).
Step 4 - Recognize Metamorphosed Igneous Rocks: Even igneous rocks can be altered by metamorphic conditions (p. 68).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Geology Requirement 1, how does James Hutton's principle of uniformitarianism ('the present is the key to the past') help geologists interpret the rock cycle?
options: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
choices: A. It states that all rocks on Earth formed simultaneously during a single afternoon and have never changed since.

B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
C. It proves that sedimentary sandstone only forms deep inside the molten outer core of the planet.
D. It states that fossils found in upper rock layers are always millions of years older than undisturbed rock layers buried far beneath them.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It explains that the physical, chemical, and biological geological processes observable today (such as volcanic cooling forming igneous rock, weathering and deposition forming sedimentary rock, and heat and pressure forming metamorphic rock) operated by the same natural laws throughout Earth's history.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Uniformitarianism holds that ongoing geologic processes (magma crystallization, erosion, sedimentation, lithification, and metamorphism) explain the rock structures and stratigraphic record formed over geologic time.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What three stages must all Earth natural resources go through before people can use them in daily life?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What three stages must all Earth natural resources go through before people can use them in daily life?
options: A. They must be found, extracted, and processed before they can be used
B. They must be synthesized in laboratories before being buried in mines
C. They can be pumped or dug directly into finished consumer products without refinement
D. They are gathered exclusively from surface riverbeds without geological exploration
choices: A. They must be found, extracted, and processed before they can be used
B. They must be synthesized in laboratories before being buried in mines
C. They can be pumped or dug directly into finished consumer products without refinement
D. They are gathered exclusively from surface riverbeds without geological exploration
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. They must be found, extracted, and processed before they can be used
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): All natural resources must follow a three-stage sequence: they must be found (discovered), extracted (removed from Earth), and processed before they can be used (p. 37).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do coarse-grained intrusive igneous rocks that formed deep underground eventually become exposed at Earth's surface?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do coarse-grained intrusive igneous rocks that formed deep underground eventually become exposed at Earth's surface?
options: A. They float upward through solid crust like bubbles in water without any erosion
B. Burrowing animals dig them up from several miles beneath the crust
C. Ocean tides wash deep magma chambers onto beaches every spring
D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers
choices: A. They float upward through solid crust like bubbles in water without any erosion
B. Burrowing animals dig them up from several miles beneath the crust
C. Ocean tides wash deep magma chambers onto beaches every spring
D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Tectonic forces uplift the region and erosion strips away the overlying rock layers
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Deep intrusive rocks reach Earth's surface when mountain-building tectonic forces uplift the area and wind and water erode away the overlying material (p. 66).

pamphlet_excerpts: Licking Golf Balls: You may have seen golfers lick the dirt off their golf ball so the ball will roll true or to hold a used tee in their mouth (p. 53).
Course Chemical Residue: Toxic substances on the courses may cling to the ball and tee (p. 53).
Common Turf Contaminants: These include fertilizers, pesticides, weed killers, and animal excrement (p. 53).
Hepatitis Infection Risk: Some golfers who have a habit of cleaning their golf balls by licking them develop hepatitis, an inflammation of the liver (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Identify Turf Contaminants: These include fertilizers, pesticides, weed killers, and animal excrement (p. 53).
Step 2 - Avoid Mouth Contact: Some golfers who have a habit of cleaning their golf balls by licking them develop hepatitis, an inflammation of the liver (p. 53).
Step 3 - Use Damp Towel: It is best to always carry a towel in your golf bag and dampen it to wipe your ball clean (p. 53).
Step 4 - Practice Course First Aid: There are a few first-aid issues that apply especially to golfers and golfing (p. 53).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Your patrol is on the 6th fairway when dark thunderclouds build and you hear thunder 20 seconds after seeing a lightning flash. What must your group do immediately?
quiz_item.question: Your patrol is on the 6th fairway when dark thunderclouds build and you hear thunder 20 seconds after seeing a lightning flash. What must your group do immediately?
options: A. Finish playing the current hole quickly while holding metal golf umbrellas overhead.
B. Take shelter together under the tallest oak tree along the fairway edge until the rain passes.

C. Suspend play immediately under the 30/30 lightning rule, leave golf bags/metal clubs behind if needed, and move to the clubhouse or a designated lightning-safe building, waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
D. Sit inside an open-sided golf cart parked on the elevated 7th tee box while holding a 1-iron.

requirements.lead_text: Complete ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Complete ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Traditional Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the USGA Rules of Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the three categories of golf etiquette. (b) Demonstrate that you understand the definitions of golf terms. (c) Show that you understand the Rules of Amateur Status. (2) Tell about your understanding of the World Handicap System. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the early history of golf. (b) Describe golf's early years in the United States. (c) Tell about the accomplishments of a top golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) The proper grip, stance, posture, and key fundamentals of a good swing (b) Driver played from a tee (c) The fairway wood shot (d) The long iron shot (e) The short iron shot (f) The approach, chip-and-run, and pitch shots (g) A recovery shot from a bunker or heavy rough (h) A sound putting stroke (6) Play a minimum of two nine-hole rounds or one 18-hole round of golf with another golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the Rules of Golf. (b) Practice good golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow golfers, committee, sponsor, and gallery. (7) Find out about three careers related to traditional golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests you. (b) Option B, Disc Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the six areas of Courtesy (812). (b) Describe the seven areas of Scoring (808). (2) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (b) Discuss with your counselor the contributions Ed Headrick made to the sport of disc golf. (c) Describe the evolution of disc design. (d) Tell about the accomplishments of a top disc golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how disc golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a disc golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) A good throwing grip (b) A good runup (X-step) when throwing a disc (c) Backhand shot (d) Forehand shot (e) Overhand shot (f) Rolling shot (g) A good (in-line) putting stance (h) A good straddle putting stance (i) A good putting grip (j) A good putting motion and follow through (k) The proper use of a mini-marking disc (6) Play a minimum of 18-holes of disc golf with another disc golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf. (b) Practice good disc golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow disc golfers and other people in the park along with any wildlife, trees, and plants on the property. (7) Find out about three careers related to disc golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests you.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Traditional Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the USGA Rules of Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the three categories of golf etiquette. (b) Demonstrate that you understand the definitions of golf terms. (c) Show that you understand the Rules of Amateur Status. (2) Tell about your understanding of the World Handicap System. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the early history of golf. (b) Describe golf's early years in the United States. (c) Tell about the accomplishments of a top golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) The proper grip, stance, posture, and key fundamentals of a good swing (b) Driver played from a tee (c) The fairway wood shot (d) The long iron shot (e) The short iron shot (f) The approach, chip-and-run, and pitch shots (g) A recovery shot from a bunker or heavy rough (h) A sound putting stroke (6) Play a minimum of two nine-hole rounds or one 18-hole round of golf with another golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the Rules of Golf. (b) Practice good golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow golfers, committee, sponsor, and gallery. (7) Find out about three careers related to traditional golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Disc Golf. Do ALL of the following: (1) Study the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf now in use. (a) Tell about the six areas of Courtesy (812). (b) Describe the seven areas of Scoring (808). (2) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (3) Do the following: (a) Tell about the history of disc golf and why it is an inclusive game. (b) Discuss with your counselor the contributions Ed Headrick made to the sport of disc golf. (c) Describe the evolution of disc design. (d) Tell about the accomplishments of a top disc golfer of your choice. (4) Do the following: (a) Tell how disc golf can contribute to a healthy lifestyle, mentally and physically. (b) Tell how a disc golf exercise plan can help you play better. Show two exercises that would help improve your game. (5) Show the following: (a) A good throwing grip (b) A good runup (X-step) when throwing a disc (c) Backhand shot (d) Forehand shot (e) Overhand shot (f) Rolling shot (g) A good (in-line) putting stance (h) A good straddle putting stance (i) A good putting grip (j) A good putting motion and follow through (k) The proper use of a mini-marking disc (6) Play a minimum of 18-holes of disc golf with another disc golfer about your age and with your counselor, or an adult approved by your counselor. Do the following: (a) Follow the PDGA Official Rules of Disc Golf. (b) Practice good disc golf etiquette. (c) Show respect to fellow disc golfers and other people in the park along with any wildlife, trees, and plants on the property. (7) Find out about three careers related to disc golf. Pick one and identify the education, training, and experience required for this profession. Discuss this with your counselor, and explain why this interests.

pamphlet_excerpts: Professional Disc Golfers: Introduction to Disc Golf. are professional players (p. 50).
PDGA Tour Oversight: The Professional Disc Golf Association (PDGA) oversees both amateur events and a professional tour (p. 50).
Global Tournament Sanctioning: The PDGA sanctions more than 9,000 events each year and has an active membership of more than 129,000 competitive disc golfers from 70+ countries (p. 50).
Early Frisbee Origins: The roots of disc golf are firmly grounded with the Frisbee® and date to early disc golf promoters like "Steady" Ed Head rick and George Sappenfield (p. 50).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Explore Sanctioned Events: The PDGA sanctions more than 9,000 events each year and has an active membership of more than 129,000 competitive disc golfers from 70+ countries (p. 50).
Step 2 - Trace Sport History: The roots of disc golf are firmly grounded with the Frisbee® and date to early disc golf promoters like "Steady" Ed Head rick and George Sappenfield (p. 50).
Step 3 - Examine Beveled-Edge Discs: Soon the days of using a simple Frisbee® graduated to the modern golf disc, with the triangular beveled-edge disc patented by Dave Dunipace in 1983 (p. 50).
Step 4 - Select Specialized Discs: This disc provides the player a next-level experience (p. 50).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Your patrol is on the 6th fairway when dark thunderclouds build and you hear thunder 20 seconds after seeing a lightning flash. What must your group do immediately?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Your patrol is on the 6th fairway when dark thunderclouds build and you hear thunder 20 seconds after seeing a lightning flash. What must your group do immediately?
options: A. Finish playing the current hole quickly while holding metal golf umbrellas overhead.
B. Take shelter together under the tallest oak tree along the fairway edge until the rain passes.

C. Suspend play immediately under the 30/30 lightning rule, leave golf bags/metal clubs behind if needed, and move to the clubhouse or a designated lightning-safe building, waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
D. Sit inside an open-sided golf cart parked on the elevated 7th tee box while holding a 1-iron.
choices: A. Finish playing the current hole quickly while holding metal golf umbrellas overhead.
B. Take shelter together under the tallest oak tree along the fairway edge until the rain passes.

C. Suspend play immediately under the 30/30 lightning rule, leave golf bags/metal clubs behind if needed, and move to the clubhouse or a designated lightning-safe building, waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
D. Sit inside an open-sided golf cart parked on the elevated 7th tee box while holding a 1-iron.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Suspend play immediately under the 30/30 lightning rule, leave golf bags/metal clubs behind if needed, and move to the clubhouse or a designated lightning-safe building, waiting 30 minutes after the last thunder before resuming.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A 20-second flash-to-bang count means lightning is 4 miles away (within the 6-mile / 30-second strike zone); isolated trees and metal clubs/umbrellas are acute lightning hazards.

pamphlet_excerpts: Raised Ink Surfaces: Relief printing uses a raised surface to press ink onto paper (p. 17).
Letterpress and Flexography: The most common forms of relief printing are letterpress and flexography (p. 17).
Movable Type Origins: Letter press is one of the oldest printing methods, with its origins in the movable type invented in China in the 11th century and in Germany (p. 17).
Reusable Metal Type: The significance of Johann Gutenberg's invention was that his movable metal type was reusable (p. 17).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Trace Letterpress Origins: Letter press is one of the oldest printing methods, with its origins in the movable type invented in China in the 11th century and in Germany (p. 17).
Step 2 - Examine Metal Type: The significance of Johann Gutenberg's invention was that his movable metal type was reusable (p. 17).
Step 3 - Set Reusable Type: Individual letters could be set by hand for a printing job, printed, and then taken apart and used in another project (p. 17).
Step 4 - Compare Modern Methods: Letter press printing was the dominant process for 500 years, but new technologies in the last 50 years have offered better and more efficient ways (p. 17).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In Graphic Arts Requirement 1, how do the four traditional printing processes (relief, intaglio, planographic, and porous) transfer ink to a substrate?
quiz_item.question: In Graphic Arts Requirement 1, how do the four traditional printing processes (relief, intaglio, planographic, and porous) transfer ink to a substrate?
options: A. All four processes carve deep grooves into wooden blocks and melt solid wax crayons onto the paper using laser beams.
B. Offset lithography forces ink through a woven silk mesh, while screen printing etches microscopic wells into a heavy copper cylinder.

C. Relief prints from raised surfaces, gravure/intaglio prints from recessed ink-filled cells etched into a cylinder, offset lithography prints from a flat plate using the mutual repulsion of oil-based ink and water, and screen printing squeegees ink through open mesh areas of a stencil.
D. Gravure uses raised rubber stamps for corrugated cardboard, while flexography uses only home inkjet cartridges.
choices: A. All four processes carve deep grooves into wooden blocks and melt solid wax crayons onto the paper using laser beams.
B. Offset lithography forces ink through a woven silk mesh, while screen printing etches microscopic wells into a heavy copper cylinder.

C. Relief prints from raised surfaces, gravure/intaglio prints from recessed ink-filled cells etched into a cylinder, offset lithography prints from a flat plate using the mutual repulsion of oil-based ink and water, and screen printing squeegees ink through open mesh areas of a stencil.
D. Gravure uses raised rubber stamps for corrugated cardboard, while flexography uses only home inkjet cartridges.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Relief prints from raised surfaces, gravure/intaglio prints from recessed ink-filled cells etched into a cylinder, offset lithography prints from a flat plate using the mutual repulsion of oil-based ink and water, and screen printing squeegees ink through open mesh areas of a stencil.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Graphic Arts Requirement 1 differentiates printing methods by image carrier geometry: raised image areas (relief/flexography), recessed wells (intaglio/gravure), flat chemically treated plates (offset lithography), and stencil mesh openings (screen printing), alongside modern digital printing.

common_misconception_pair.fact: Presses print solid ink in tiny halftone dots of varying sizes, where large dots create dark shadows and small dots create light highlights (p. 44).

pamphlet_excerpts: Microscopic Halftone Dots: The half tone dots are so small, the human eye cannot see the individual dots unless they are magnified, but the eye does see an overall effect (p. 44).
Optical Tone Illusion: The arrangement of the half tone dots creates this effect (p. 44).
Shadow Dot Density: The half tone dots in the part of an image that is supposed to look dark are big and fill most of the half tone dot area (p. 44).
Highlight Dot Spacing: The half tone dots in the part of an image that is supposed to look light are small and fill very little of the halftone dot area (p. 44).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Inspect Shadow Dots: The half tone dots in the part of an image that is supposed to look dark are big and fill most of the half tone dot area (p. 44).
Step 2 - Inspect Highlight Dots: The half tone dots in the part of an image that is supposed to look light are small and fill very little of the halftone dot area (p. 44).
Step 3 - Select Continuous-Tone Photo: Generally, half tones are made from a continuous-tone image, such as a traditional photograph (p. 44).
Step 4 - Convert Image to Halftone: In the past, the continuous-tone image was photographed through a special screen that created a half tone version of the original (p. 44).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How does a single color of black ink on a printing press create the appearance of dark shadows and bright highlights in a halftone photograph?
quiz_item.question: How does a single color of black ink on a printing press create the appearance of dark shadows and bright highlights in a halftone photograph?
options: A. The press applies thicker layers of wet ink in dark areas and thinner layers in light areas
B. Dark areas use large dots that fill most of the grid while light areas use tiny dots
C. White ink is mixed into the fountain rollers to lighten the highlight regions
D. The paper is chemically bleached after printing to fade the highlight sections
choices: A. The press applies thicker layers of wet ink in dark areas and thinner layers in light areas
B. Dark areas use large dots that fill most of the grid while light areas use tiny dots
C. White ink is mixed into the fountain rollers to lighten the highlight regions
D. The paper is chemically bleached after printing to fade the highlight sections
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Dark areas use large dots that fill most of the grid while light areas use tiny dots
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Halftones simulate continuous shading by varying dot size: large dots fill dark shadow areas while small dots leave mostly white paper showing in light areas (p. 44).

pamphlet_excerpts: Thick Brilliant Ink: Screen printing is used wherever a thick, brilliant film of ink is required (p. 29).
Durable Outdoor Sign age: Outdoor signs, bumper stickers, and decals rely on screen printing for their rich color and durability (p. 29).
Versatile Screen Inks: The versatility of today's screen printing owes a great deal to the variety of inks that can be printed through a screen (p. 29).
Diverse Substrate Options: Screen printers can print successfully on paper, metal, wood, many kinds of plastics, glass, ceramics, cloth, and card stock, almost any material (p. 29).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Choose Specialty Inks: The versatility of today's screen printing owes a great deal to the variety of inks that can be printed through a screen (p. 29).
Step 2 - Select Target Substrate: Screen printers can print successfully on paper, metal, wood, many kinds of plastics, glass, ceramics, cloth, and card stock, almost any material (p. 29).
Step 3 - Adapt to Surface Shape: The process make sprinting possible on substrates of different shapes and sizes (p. 29).
Step 4 - Print Contoured Containers: Screen printing is the primary method used to print on oddly shaped bottles, jars, and other product containers (p. 29).

Make a layout, and produce a plate using a process approved by your counselor. Run the plate and print at least 50 copies. (b) Screen printing. B. A master is created and a single sample test print is produced for inspection
C. The operator must hand-cut a rubylith film stencil and tape it to the drum
D. The duplicator folds and saddle-stitches blank paper before applying liquid ink
choices: A. The machine etches a copper gravure cylinder and prints the entire run nonstop
B. A master is created and a single sample test print is produced for inspection
C. The operator must hand-cut a rubylith film stencil and tape it to the drum
D. The duplicator folds and saddle-stitches blank paper before applying liquid ink
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. A master is created and a single sample test print is produced for inspection
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): When a layout is sent to a digital duplicator, the machine makes a master and prints a sample test sheet so the operator can approve it before entering the final run quantity (p. 29).

pamphlet_excerpts: Bindery Supervisor Duties: A bindery supervisor coordinates operations in the bindery, schedules jobs, and supervises and trains workers (p. 81).
Automated Bindery Machinery: A bindery worker may prepare and tend one or more automated machines that do cutting, scoring, folding, stitching, taping, and gluing (p. 81).
Assembly Line Finishing: In large binderies, the work is done on an assembly line, with workers performing one or two types of tasks (p. 81).
Perfect-Binder Machine Setup: A perfect-binder setter sets up and controls a binding machine that gathers magazine or book signatures, glues them, and adds the cover to magazines (p. 81).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Specialize Finishing Tasks: In large binderies, the work is done on an assembly line, with workers performing one or two types of tasks (p. 81).
Step 2 - Operate Perfect-Binder Line: A perfect-binder setter sets up and controls a binding machine that gathers magazine or book signatures, glues them, and adds the cover to magazines (p. 81).
Step 3 - Craft Custom Bindings: A book binder hand binds books, usually working on special editions and custom binding, and repairs old and rare books (p. 81).
Step 4 - Apprentice With Experts: Book binders learn by training with the relatively few experts in the field (p. 81).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In Graphic Arts Requirement 1, how do the four traditional printing processes (relief, intaglio, planographic, and porous) transfer ink to a substrate?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In Graphic Arts Requirement 1, how do the four traditional printing processes (relief, intaglio, planographic, and porous) transfer ink to a substrate?
options: A. All four processes carve deep grooves into wooden blocks and melt solid wax crayons onto the paper using laser beams.
B. Offset lithography forces ink through a woven silk mesh, while screen printing etches microscopic wells into a heavy copper cylinder.

C. Relief prints from raised surfaces, gravure/intaglio prints from recessed ink-filled cells etched into a cylinder, offset lithography prints from a flat plate using the mutual repulsion of oil-based ink and water, and screen printing squeegees ink through open mesh areas of a stencil.
D. Gravure uses raised rubber stamps for corrugated cardboard, while flexography uses only home inkjet cartridges.
choices: A. All four processes carve deep grooves into wooden blocks and melt solid wax crayons onto the paper using laser beams.
B. Offset lithography forces ink through a woven silk mesh, while screen printing etches microscopic wells into a heavy copper cylinder.

C. Relief prints from raised surfaces, gravure/intaglio prints from recessed ink-filled cells etched into a cylinder, offset lithography prints from a flat plate using the mutual repulsion of oil-based ink and water, and screen printing squeegees ink through open mesh areas of a stencil.
D. Gravure uses raised rubber stamps for corrugated cardboard, while flexography uses only home inkjet cartridges.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Relief prints from raised surfaces, gravure/intaglio prints from recessed ink-filled cells etched into a cylinder, offset lithography prints from a flat plate using the mutual repulsion of oil-based ink and water, and screen printing squeegees ink through open mesh areas of a stencil.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Graphic Arts Requirement 1 differentiates printing methods by image carrier geometry: raised image areas (relief/flexography), recessed wells (intaglio/gravure), flat chemically treated plates (offset lithography), and stencil mesh openings (screen printing), alongside modern digital printing.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does a single color of black ink on a printing press create the appearance of dark shadows and bright highlights in a halftone photograph?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does a single color of black ink on a printing press create the appearance of dark shadows and bright highlights in a halftone photograph?
options: A. The press applies thicker layers of wet ink in dark areas and thinner layers in light areas
B. Dark areas use large dots that fill most of the grid while light areas use tiny dots
C. White ink is mixed into the fountain rollers to lighten the highlight regions
D. The paper is chemically bleached after printing to fade the highlight sections
choices: A. The press applies thicker layers of wet ink in dark areas and thinner layers in light areas
B. Dark areas use large dots that fill most of the grid while light areas use tiny dots
C. White ink is mixed into the fountain rollers to lighten the highlight regions
D. The paper is chemically bleached after printing to fade the highlight sections
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Dark areas use large dots that fill most of the grid while light areas use tiny dots
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Halftones simulate continuous shading by varying dot size: large dots fill dark shadow areas while small dots leave mostly white paper showing in light areas (p. 44).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which printing process is best suited for applying a thick, vibrant layer of ink onto T-shirts, outdoor bumper stickers, or curved bottles?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which printing process is best suited for applying a thick, vibrant layer of ink onto T-shirts, outdoor bumper stickers, or curved bottles?
options: A. Sheet-fed offset lithography
B. Rotogravure cylinder printing
C. Screen printing
D. Hand-set metal letterpress
choices: A. Sheet-fed offset lithography
B. Rotogravure cylinder printing
C. Screen printing
D. Hand-set metal letterpress
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Screen printing
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Screen printing deposits a thick, durable film of ink on almost any material or shape, including cloth, vinyl decals, wood, glass, and curved containers (p. 29).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What do letterpress and flexography have in common when producing a print run?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What do letterpress and flexography have in common when producing a print run?
options: A. Both transfer ink to paper from a raised image surface
B. Both push ink through a fine woven fabric mesh using a squeegee
C. Both fuse dry toner powder onto paper using an electrostatic drum
D. Both use water rollers to repel oil-based ink on a flat aluminum sheet
choices: A. Both transfer ink to paper from a raised image surface
B. Both push ink through a fine woven fabric mesh using a squeegee
C. Both fuse dry toner powder onto paper using an electrostatic drum
D. Both use water rollers to repel oil-based ink on a flat aluminum sheet
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Both transfer ink to paper from a raised image surface
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Letterpress and flexography are the two most common forms of relief printing, which uses a raised surface to press ink onto the substrate (p. 17).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does saddle stitching fasten the pages of a merit badge pamphlet or small magazine together?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does saddle stitching fasten the pages of a merit badge pamphlet or small magazine together?
options: A. By grinding the folded spine edges and applying hot-melt glue to a wraparound cover
B. By driving wire staples directly through the center fold of nested multi-page sheets
C. By punching rectangular slots along the margin and inserting a curled plastic comb
D. By sewing folded signatures together with thread and gluing them into rigid cardboard boards
choices: A. By grinding the folded spine edges and applying hot-melt glue to a wraparound cover
B. By driving wire staples directly through the center fold of nested multi-page sheets
C. By punching rectangular slots along the margin and inserting a curled plastic comb
D. By sewing folded signatures together with thread and gluing them into rigid cardboard boards
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. By driving wire staples directly through the center fold of nested multi-page sheets
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Saddle stitching binds smaller publications and booklets by stapling wire through the center fold of gathered multi-page sheets (p. 73).

options: A. Each professional operates within a defined education, state licensure, and legal scope of practice: physicians and PAs diagnosing and prescribing, pharmacists verifying medication safety and interactions, RNs delivering and coordinating bedside patient care, and allied health specialists performing diagnostic imaging, lab analysis, and physical rehabilitation.
B. Every member of a hospital team performs open-heart surgery interchangeably without specialized board certification or state licensing.
C. Pharmacists only work at retail cash registers and have no clinical training in drug dosing, pharmacology, or adverse chemical interactions.
D. Registered nurses and respiratory therapists work only in administrative billing offices and never assess patients directly.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How do Medical Appliance Technicians typically acquire their skills, and how do they interact with orthotists or prosthetists?
quiz_item.question: How do Medical Appliance Technicians typically acquire their skills, and how do they interact with orthotists or prosthetists?
options: A. They typically learn through on-the-job training while working under the supervision of an orthotist or prosthetist who designs the device.
B. They must complete a four-year Doctor of Medicine degree followed by a surgical residency before touching prosthetic materials.
C. They independently diagnose neuromuscular diseases and prescribe physical therapy regimens without clinical oversight.
D. They are required by federal law to hold a doctorate in physical therapy before fabricating removable splints.
choices: A. They typically learn through on-the-job training while working under the supervision of an orthotist or prosthetist who designs the device.
B. They must complete a four-year Doctor of Medicine degree followed by a surgical residency before touching prosthetic materials.
C. They independently diagnose neuromuscular diseases and prescribe physical therapy regimens without clinical oversight.
D. They are required by federal law to hold a doctorate in physical therapy before fabricating removable splints.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. They typically learn through on-the-job training while working under the supervision of an orthotist or prosthetist who designs the device.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Medical appliance technicians typically learn to construct and repair braces and artificial limbs through on-the-job training under the supervision of an orthotist or prosthetist (p. 47).

D. A reduction in the number of allied health specialties to only physicians and registered nurses.

C. It establishes an ethical commitment to prioritize patient welfare, practice with integrity, avoid harm, and respect patient confidences.
D. It restricts medical school graduates from collaborating with nurses, therapists, or physician assistants.

B. It replaces the need to apply to a state professional licensing board before practicing medicine.
C. It establishes an ethical commitment to prioritize patient welfare, practice with integrity, avoid harm, and respect patient confidences.

quiz_item.correct_answer: C. It establishes an ethical commitment to prioritize patient welfare, practice with integrity, avoid harm, and respect patient confidences.

pamphlet_excerpts: Water and Bodily Functions: Water is essential for nearly every bodily function (p. 48).
Causes of Trail Dehydration: People who lose more water than they take in risk becoming dehydrated (p. 48).
Early Signs of Dehydration: The first sign of dehydration usually is dark urine (p. 48).
Systemic Symptoms of Fluid Loss: Other signs can include weariness, headache, body aches, and confusion (p. 48).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Monitor Urine Color Regularly: The first sign of dehydration usually is dark urine (p. 48).
Step 2 - Recognize Dehydration Warning Signs: Other signs can include weariness, headache, body aches, and confusion (p. 48).
Step 3 - Assess Temperature Related Illnesses: Heat exhaustion, heatstroke, and hypothermia might all be caused in part by dehydration (p. 48).
Step 4 - Drink Fluids Before Thirst: Prevent dehydration and heat reactions by drinking plenty of fluids (p. 48).

pamphlet_excerpts: Environmental Stewardship on Trails: Caring for the environment is an important responsibility of every hiker (p. 28).
Leave No Trace Foundations: Leave No Trace is just one set of principles that can help you live up to that responsibility and enjoy the outdoors fully by knowing (p. 28).
Group Trip Planning Ethics: As you and your group plan a hike, ask yourselves how you can follow each of the principles of Leave No Trace (p. 28).
Respecting Nature and Others: Leave No Trace and The Outdoor Code are principles that help you respect the environment and be considerate to others who are enjoying the outdoors (p. 28).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Plan Low Impact Routes: As you and your group plan a hike, ask yourselves how you can follow each of the principles of Leave No Trace (p. 28).
Step 2 - Practice Trail Courtesy Daily: Leave No Trace and The Outdoor Code are principles that help you respect the environment and be considerate to others who are enjoying the outdoors (p. 28).
Step 3 - Review Route With Leaders: Explain your desired route and ask how you can best implement Leave No Trace (p. 28).
Step 4 - Follow Backcountry Stewardship Guidelines: Here are some additional guidelines to remember (p. 28).

pamphlet_excerpts: Risks of Unprepared Hiking: Setting off on a hike without properly preparing can have disastrous results (p. 33).
Physical Readiness and Gear: Make sure you are ready, from your physical condition to the best gear for the trip (p. 33).
Fitness for Trail Enjoyment: To enjoy hiking to the fullest, you will want to be in good shape (p. 33).
Structured Personal Conditioning Plans: That is why requirement 3 calls for developing a plan for conditioning yourself (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Build Baseline Aerobic Fitness: To enjoy hiking to the fullest, you will want to be in good shape (p. 33).
Step 2 - Design a Conditioning Schedule: That is why requirement 3 calls for developing a plan for conditioning yourself (p. 33).
Step 3 - Increase Trail Mileage Gradually: Begin with short trips, increasing the length of your journeys as you become more fit (p. 33).
Step 4 - Walk Daily for Endurance: A good way to prepare for Scout hikes is to walk whenever you can rather than riding in a car or relying on public transit (p. 33).
