requirements.lead_text: Do ALL the requirements in FIVE of the following fields:
requirements.req_text: Do ALL the requirements in FIVE of the following fields: (a) Birds. Do ALL of the following: (1) In the field, identify eight species of birds. (2) Make and set out a birdhouse OR a feeding station OR a birdbath. List what birds used it during a period of one month. (b) Mammals. Do ALL of the following: (1) In the field, identify three species of wild mammals. (2) Make plaster casts of the tracks of a wild mammal. (c) Reptiles and Amphibians. Do ALL of the following: (1) Show that you can recognize the venomous snakes in your area. (2) In the field, identify three species of reptiles or amphibians. (3) Recognize one species of toad or frog by voice; OR identify one reptile or amphibian by eggs, den, burrow, or other signs. (d) Insects and Spiders. Do ALL of the following: (1) Collect and identify either in the field or through photographs 10 species of insects or spiders. Photos may be taken with your own equipment or gathered from other sources. (2) Hatch an insect from the pupa or cocoon; OR hatch adults from nymphs; OR keep larvae until they form pupae or cocoons; OR keep a colony of ants or bees through one season. (e) Fish. Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify two species of fish native to your area. (2) Collect four kinds of animal food eaten by fish in the wild. (f) Mollusks and Crustaceans. Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify five species of mollusks and crustaceans. (2) Collect, mount, and label six shells. (g) Plants. requirements.description: Do ALL the requirements in FIVE of the following fields: (a) Birds. Do ALL of the following: (1) In the field, identify eight species of birds. (2) Make and set out a birdhouse OR a feeding station OR a birdbath. List what birds used it during a period of one month. (b) Mammals. Do ALL of the following: (1) In the field, identify three species of wild mammals. (2) Make plaster casts of the tracks of a wild mammal. (c) Reptiles and Amphibians. Do ALL of the following: (1) Show that you can recognize the venomous snakes in your area. (2) In the field, identify three species of reptiles or amphibians. (3) Recognize one species of toad or frog by voice; OR identify one reptile or amphibian by eggs, den, burrow, or other signs. (d) Insects and Spiders. Do ALL of the following: (1) Collect and identify either in the field or through photographs 10 species of insects or spiders. Photos may be taken with your own equipment or gathered from other sources. (2) Hatch an insect from the pupa or cocoon; OR hatch adults from nymphs; OR keep larvae until they form pupae or cocoons; OR keep a colony of ants or bees through one season. (e) Fish. Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify two species of fish native to your area. (2) Collect four kinds of animal food eaten by fish in the wild. (f) Mollusks and Crustaceans. Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify five species of mollusks and crustaceans. (2) Collect, mount, and label six shells. (g) Plants. Do ALL of the following: (1) In the field, identify 15 species of wild plants. (2) Do ONE of the following: (a) Collect and label the seeds of six plants OR the leaves of 12 plants. (b) Photograph the seeds of six plants OR the leaves of 12 plants and create a catalog of your photos. (h) Soils and Rocks. Do ALL of the following: (1) Collect and identify three different types of soil that represent soils high in sand, clay and humus. (2) Collect and identify five different types of rocks from your area.

pamphlet_excerpts: Clean Outdoor Manners: As an American, I will do my best to, Be clean in my outdoor manners (p. 9).
Keeping Nature Natural: Do your part to keep nature natural by following these principles (p. 9).
Planning and Preparation: Proper planning and preparation increases safety, reduces the impact of your visit on the environment, and helps make your outdoor experience (p. 9).
Foot Traffic Damage: Natural environments are easily damaged by foot traffic (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Plan Before Field Trips: Proper planning and preparation increases safety, reduces the impact of your visit on the environment, and helps make your outdoor experience (p. 9).
Step 2 - Protect Fragile Ground: Natural environments are easily damaged by foot traffic (p. 9).
Step 3 - Walk on Durable Surfaces: Use existing trails or travel on durable surfaces such as rock, gravel, sand, compacted soil, dry grasses, or snow (p. 9).
Step 4 - Spread Out Off Trail: Large groups should spread out to avoid creating new trails (p. 9).

pamphlet_excerpts: Deep Water Fish Zones: There might be fish such as bass, and down deep there might be lake trout (p. 19).
Diving Duck Foraging: A few diving ducks, such as mergansers, might find food (p. 19).
Surface Hunting Ospreys: An osprey might catch a fish near the surface of the water (p. 19).
Bottom Dwelling Mussels: Animals such as clams or mussels might be found on the bottom (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Spot Surface Predators: An osprey might catch a fish near the surface of the water (p. 19).
Step 2 - Check Bottom Habitats: Animals such as clams or mussels might be found on the bottom (p. 19).
Step 3 - Inspect Shallow Water Plants: In shallower water, plants such as algae and pond weed will live and provide food for more animals (p. 19).
Step 4 - Find Larvae and Sunfish: Insect larvae live on these plants and provide food for fish such as sunfish or crappie (p. 19).

pamphlet_excerpts: Plant Temperature Ranges: In the same way that plants have soil requirements, they have requirements of temperature range, from hot to cold (p. 11).
High Elevation Climate: The higher you go, generally the colder the temperature and the higher the rainfall (p. 11).
Mountain Slope Ecology: As far as plants are concerned, going up the side of a mountain is much the same as going north (p. 11).
Altitude and Latitude Ratios: Going up 300 to 500 feet of altitude is roughly equivalent to moving northward one degree of latitude (68 miles) (p. 11).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Relate Slope to Latitude: As far as plants are concerned, going up the side of a mountain is much the same as going north (p. 11).
Step 2 - Measure Elevation Shifts: Going up 300 to 500 feet of altitude is roughly equivalent to moving northward one degree of latitude (68 miles) (p. 11).
Step 3 - Compare Regional Growth: So, the same plants will grow at a higher elevation in the South than in the North (p. 11).
Step 4 - Map Timberline Differences: Trees that will not grow at 4,000 feet in one place might grow at 6,000 feet farther south (p. 11).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why do terrestrial food webs and animals depend directly on green plants and other photosynthetic organisms for survival?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why do terrestrial food webs and animals depend directly on green plants and other photosynthetic organisms for survival?
options: A. Plants convert solar energy, water, and carbon dioxide into chemical energy (sugars) and release oxygen, forming the primary producer base of the food web and providing habitat shelter.
B. Plants absorb nitrogen gas directly through their leaves and convert animal predators into decomposers.
C. Photosynthesis consumes excess oxygen from the atmosphere and releases carbon monoxide to warm forest soil.
D. Green plants rely on herbivorous insects to manufacture chlorophyll before roots can absorb soil minerals.
choices: A. Plants convert solar energy, water, and carbon dioxide into chemical energy (sugars) and release oxygen, forming the primary producer base of the food web and providing habitat shelter.
B. Plants absorb nitrogen gas directly through their leaves and convert animal predators into decomposers.
C. Photosynthesis consumes excess oxygen from the atmosphere and releases carbon monoxide to warm forest soil.
D. Green plants rely on herbivorous insects to manufacture chlorophyll before roots can absorb soil minerals.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Plants convert solar energy, water, and carbon dioxide into chemical energy (sugars) and release oxygen, forming the primary producer base of the food web and providing habitat shelter.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Through photosynthesis, plants act as primary producers that capture solar energy to build organic nutrients and release oxygen, supporting herbivores, carnivores, and shelter needs across the ecosystem.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which group of three activities best describes how wild animals help plants survive and spread?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which group of three activities best describes how wild animals help plants survive and spread?
options: A. Decreasing soil moisture, blocking sunlight, and eating tree bark
B. Pollinating blossoms, dispersing seeds, and aerating or fertilizing soil
C. Converting oxygen into nitrogen, cooling the air, and shading roots
D. Stripping lower branches, compacting mud, and filtering rainwater
choices: A. Decreasing soil moisture, blocking sunlight, and eating tree bark
B. Pollinating blossoms, dispersing seeds, and aerating or fertilizing soil
C. Converting oxygen into nitrogen, cooling the air, and shading roots
D. Stripping lower branches, compacting mud, and filtering rainwater
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Pollinating blossoms, dispersing seeds, and aerating or fertilizing soil
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Animals assist plants by transferring pollen between flowers, carrying seeds on their fur or in their digestive systems, and enriching and loosening the soil (p. 17).

options: A. Floating mats of dead driftwood washed out from rivers
B. Bottom-dwelling clams and mussels filtering mineral silt
C. Microscopic plant-like phytoplankton and tiny animal zooplankton
D. Schools of small minnows feeding on dissolved salt crystals
choices: A. Floating mats of dead driftwood washed out from rivers
B. Bottom-dwelling clams and mussels filtering mineral silt
C. Microscopic plant-like phytoplankton and tiny animal zooplankton
D. Schools of small minnows feeding on dissolved salt crystals
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Microscopic plant-like phytoplankton and tiny animal zooplankton
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Where water is too deep for rooted plants, thousands of microscopic phytoplankton per drop capture energy and feed zooplankton, forming the base of the ocean food chain (p. 10).

pamphlet_excerpts: Radiation Effects on Wildlife: Although we know much about the dangers of radiation to humans, its effects on wildlife are less understood (p. 67).
Past Protection Assumptions: Scientists have tended to assume that as long as people were protected, animals and plants would be, too (p. 67).
Safeguarding Plants and Animals: But that idea is changing, and more research is now being done to learn how best to safeguard wildlife (p. 67).
Reactor Release Field Studies: Many researchers are focusing on how wild plants and animals have been affected by the radioactivity released from the exploded nuclear reactor (p. 67).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Study Wildlife Protection: But that idea is changing, and more research is now being done to learn how best to safeguard wildlife (p. 67).
Step 2 - Examine Reactor Fallout Effects: Many researchers are focusing on how wild plants and animals have been affected by the radioactivity released from the exploded nuclear reactor (p. 67).
Step 3 - Distinguish Exposure From Contamination: A person exposed to radiation does not become radioactive (p. 67).
Step 4 - Understand Medical X-Ray Safety: When you get an X-ray at the doctor's office, it does not make you radioactive (p. 67).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Under the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) radiation safety principle, what are the three primary methods used to minimize exposure to ionizing radiation?
quiz_item.question: Under the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) radiation safety principle, what are the three primary methods used to minimize exposure to ionizing radiation?
options: A. Ventilation, grounding, and magnetic deflection.
B. Filtration, chemical neutralization, and thermal cooling.
C. Compression, humidification, and ultraviolet sterilization.
D. Minimizing time spent near the source, maximizing distance from the source, and placing appropriate shielding between yourself and the source.
choices: A. Ventilation, grounding, and magnetic deflection.
B. Filtration, chemical neutralization, and thermal cooling.
C. Compression, humidification, and ultraviolet sterilization.
D. Minimizing time spent near the source, maximizing distance from the source, and placing appropriate shielding between yourself and the source.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Minimizing time spent near the source, maximizing distance from the source, and placing appropriate shielding between yourself and the source.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Radiation protection relies on Time, Distance, and Shielding: reducing exposure duration, increasing distance (which follows the inverse-square law), and using proper absorber materials.

pamphlet_excerpts: Charged Particle Beams: Particle accelerators, sometimes called atom smashers, are machines that can create beams of electrically charged particles and accelerate them (p. 23).
Increasing Kinetic Energy: This acceleration increases the particles' energy of motion (p. 23).
Fastball Energy Analogy: Think of the difference between catching a baseball that is gently underhanded to you and catching a fast ball fired at you by a major-league pitcher (p. 23).
Energy Binding Matter: Energy is the universal container that holds things together (p. 23).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Compare Low and High Energy: Think of the difference between catching a baseball that is gently underhanded to you and catching a fast ball fired at you by a major-league pitcher (p. 23).
Step 2 - Recognize Nuclear Binding Energy: Energy is the universal container that holds things together (p. 23).
Step 3 - Overcome Atomic Container Energy: If you want to break open a container such as an atom or a proton to see what's inside, you must overcome that container'senergy (p. 23).
Step 4 - Probe Subatomic Particle Makeup: From accelerators, scientists get the energy they need to break open and explore the makeup of atomic and subatomic particles (p. 23).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why do physicists need particle accelerators to study the internal makeup of atomic nuclei and nucleons?
quiz_item.question: Why do physicists need particle accelerators to study the internal makeup of atomic nuclei and nucleons?
options: A. Accelerators freeze atoms to absolute zero so their electrons stop moving
B. Accelerators magnify visible light waves enough to photograph individual quarks directly
C. High-energy particle beams are needed to overcome the strong binding energy holding nuclei and nucleons together
D. Only uncharged neutrons can be pushed by static electricity in a vacuum tube
choices: A. Accelerators freeze atoms to absolute zero so their electrons stop moving
B. Accelerators magnify visible light waves enough to photograph individual quarks directly
C. High-energy particle beams are needed to overcome the strong binding energy holding nuclei and nucleons together
D. Only uncharged neutrons can be pushed by static electricity in a vacuum tube
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. High-energy particle beams are needed to overcome the strong binding energy holding nuclei and nucleons together
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Energy holds atoms and nucleons together like a container, and particle accelerators give charged particles enough kinetic energy to break open and probe those subatomic structures (p. 23).

pamphlet_excerpts: Seeing Invisible Particle Tracks: Although ionizing particles are invisible, you can use a cloud chamber tosee the tracks the particles leave (p. 33).
Minimizing Dry Ice Sublimation: Buy dry ice the morning of the demonstration in order to minimize the sublimation losses of the dry ice (p. 33).
Venting Carbon Dioxide Safely: If you must buy the evening before, store in a sealed cooler that allows the CO2 gas to vent as it sublimes from the solid form (p. 33).
Preparing the Felt Rim: Place as trip of felt on the inside of the bottom rim (p. 33).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Store Dry Ice Safely: If you must buy the evening before, store in a sealed cooler that allows the CO2 gas to vent as it sublimes from the solid form (p. 33).
Step 2 - Line Rim With Felt: Place as trip of felt on the inside of the bottom rim (p. 33).
Step 3 - Add Methanol With Dropper: With an eye dropper, carefully add about 3 ml of methanol topetri dish around felt rim. *Methanol is flammable and poisonous (p. 33).
Step 4 - Follow Ventilation and Glove Rules: Use it in a well-ventilated area, wear plastic gloves to protect your skin, and never drink (p. 33).

pamphlet_excerpts: Hahn and Meitner Discovery: Hahn and Strassmann wrote to Lise Meitner about their research (p. 53).
Splitting the Uranium Nucleus: She concluded that when uranium is hit with a neutron, it must break in half (p. 53).
Coining the Term Fission: An American biologist, William Arnold, read the paper and decided to call the splitting of atoms fission, the word biologists used for the splitting (p. 53).
Need for Chain Reactions: Fission would not be useful for producing energy if we had to shoot each nucleus with a neutron to break (p. 53).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Define Atomic Fission: An American biologist, William Arnold, read the paper and decided to call the splitting of atoms fission, the word biologists used for the splitting (p. 53).
Step 2 - Explain Self Sustaining Chains: Fission would not be useful for producing energy if we had to shoot each nucleus with a neutron to break (p. 53).
Step 3 - Slow Neutrons With Moderators: Fermi found that with the element he was using, uranium, slow neutrons hit nuclei better than fast onesdid (p. 53).
Step 4 - Study Fermi's Atomic Pile: In December 1942, Fermi and a group of other scientists completed the first atomic pile (p. 53).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Under the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) radiation safety principle, what are the three primary methods used to minimize exposure to ionizing radiation?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Under the ALARA (As Low As Reasonably Achievable) radiation safety principle, what are the three primary methods used to minimize exposure to ionizing radiation?
options: A. Ventilation, grounding, and magnetic deflection.
B. Filtration, chemical neutralization, and thermal cooling.
C. Compression, humidification, and ultraviolet sterilization.
D. Minimizing time spent near the source, maximizing distance from the source, and placing appropriate shielding between yourself and the source.
choices: A. Ventilation, grounding, and magnetic deflection.
B. Filtration, chemical neutralization, and thermal cooling.
C. Compression, humidification, and ultraviolet sterilization.
D. Minimizing time spent near the source, maximizing distance from the source, and placing appropriate shielding between yourself and the source.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Minimizing time spent near the source, maximizing distance from the source, and placing appropriate shielding between yourself and the source.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Radiation protection relies on Time, Distance, and Shielding: reducing exposure duration, increasing distance (which follows the inverse-square law), and using proper absorber materials.

options: A. It measured the carbon-14 half-life of fossilized trees growing on the Martian surface
B. It split Martian boulders in half using a miniature uranium fission chain reaction
C. It bombarded selected rocks with alpha particles and read the characteristic X-rays generated from the rocks
D. It collected rock samples in petri dishes filled with dry ice and liquid methanol
choices: A. It measured the carbon-14 half-life of fossilized trees growing on the Martian surface
B. It split Martian boulders in half using a miniature uranium fission chain reaction
C. It bombarded selected rocks with alpha particles and read the characteristic X-rays generated from the rocks
D. It collected rock samples in petri dishes filled with dry ice and liquid methanol
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. It bombarded selected rocks with alpha particles and read the characteristic X-rays generated from the rocks
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): An instrument aboard the Mars rover Sojourner bombarded Martian rocks with alpha particles and measured the resulting X-rays to identify their chemical elements (p. 42).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to the Nuclear Science merit badge pamphlet, how does the role of an experimental nuclear scientist differ from that of a nuclear theorist?
options: A. Experimental scientists only work in hospitals, while theorists only work in underground uranium mines
B. Experimental nuclear scientists create and analyze experiments, while nuclear theorists interpret experimental results and predict new phenomena
C. Theorists build particle accelerators by hand, while experimentalists write textbooks without entering labs
D. Experimentalists study only nonionizing radio waves, while theorists study only chemical bonds
choices: A. Experimental scientists only work in hospitals, while theorists only work in underground uranium mines
B. Experimental nuclear scientists create and analyze experiments, while nuclear theorists interpret experimental results and predict new phenomena
C. Theorists build particle accelerators by hand, while experimentalists write textbooks without entering labs
D. Experimentalists study only nonionizing radio waves, while theorists study only chemical bonds
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Experimental nuclear scientists create and analyze experiments, while nuclear theorists interpret experimental results and predict new phenomena
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Experimental nuclear scientists design and analyze laboratory experiments, whereas nuclear theorists interpret those findings and develop models to predict new phenomena (p. 78).

pamphlet_excerpts: Atmospheric Carbon Cycle Role: The Oceans and the Atmosphere We still have a lot to learn about the role of oceans in the atmospheric carbon cycle (p. 32).
Warm Pacific Current Flow: El Niño (ehl NEEN yoh) is a warm current in the Pacific Ocean that flows southward along South America'swest coast (p. 32).
El Niño Return Cycle: It usually lasts nine to 12 months and returns on average every four years (p. 32).
Severe Global Weather Impacts: A powerful El Niño in 1982 and 1983 caused severe drought in Australia and Indonesia and an unusually large number of storms in California (p. 32).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Track Four Year Cycles: It usually lasts nine to 12 months and returns on average every four years (p. 32).
Step 2 - Assess Regional Weather Extremes: A powerful El Niño in 1982 and 1983 caused severe drought in Australia and Indonesia and an unusually large number of storms in California (p. 32).
Step 3 - Compare Historical Event Severity: More recent El Niño events in 2003 and 2006 were not as devastating (p. 32).
Step 4 - Identify Tropical Wind Shifts: Scientists believe El Niño is related to a shift in air movements over the tropical Pacific Ocean (p. 32).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How do marine phytoplankton and the global ocean interact with Earth's atmosphere to support life and regulate climate?
quiz_item.question: How do marine phytoplankton and the global ocean interact with Earth's atmosphere to support life and regulate climate?
options: A. Deep-sea hydrothermal vents produce most atmospheric oxygen, while surface currents reflect all incoming solar heat back into space.
B. Marine phytoplankton generate at least half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen through photosynthesis, while ocean waters absorb vast amounts of solar heat and carbon dioxide.
C. Saltwater evaporation removes carbon dioxide from the ocean and locks it permanently into stratospheric clouds.
D. Ocean tides generate geothermal heat that warms polar air masses without transferring moisture to the atmosphere.
choices: A. Deep-sea hydrothermal vents produce most atmospheric oxygen, while surface currents reflect all incoming solar heat back into space.
B. Marine phytoplankton generate at least half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen through photosynthesis, while ocean waters absorb vast amounts of solar heat and carbon dioxide.
C. Saltwater evaporation removes carbon dioxide from the ocean and locks it permanently into stratospheric clouds.
D. Ocean tides generate geothermal heat that warms polar air masses without transferring moisture to the atmosphere.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Marine phytoplankton generate at least half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen through photosynthesis, while ocean waters absorb vast amounts of solar heat and carbon dioxide.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Microscopic marine phytoplankton produce over half of the world's oxygen and anchor marine food webs, while the ocean stores and redistributes solar heat and absorbs atmospheric carbon dioxide.

common_misconception_pair.fact: While surface currents are driven by wind belts like the trade winds and westerlies, deep ocean currents are driven by differences in water density caused by temperature and salinity (p. 32).

pamphlet_excerpts: Global Wind Circulation Systems: The Oceans and the Atmosphere Great wind circulation systems form (p. 32).
Equatorial East Trade Winds: Close to the equator, trade winds blow from the east (p. 32).
Temperate Zone Westerly Winds: In the temperate zone, steady winds called westerlies blow from the west (p. 32).
Wind Driven Surface Currents: Winds blowing across the ocean's surface create currents (p. 32).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Observe Temperate Westerly Winds: In the temperate zone, steady winds called westerlies blow from the west (p. 32).
Step 2 - Map Wind Driven Currents: Winds blowing across the ocean's surface create currents (p. 32).
Step 3 - Trace Circular Basin Gyres: When the trade winds and westerlies blow across the oceans, they cause the currents in each ocean basin to move in acircular pattern (p. 32).
Step 4 - Analyze Global Heat Transport: Both surface and deep water currents affect the world'sclimate by moving warm air from the tropics toward the poles, and cold air (p. 32).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How do the trade winds and westerlies work together to shape surface circulation in each ocean basin?
quiz_item.question: How do the trade winds and westerlies work together to shape surface circulation in each ocean basin?
options: A. They cancel each other out so that mid-ocean waters remain completely still
B. They push surface waters in opposite latitudinal bands, creating large circular current patterns
C. They force all ocean water to flow exclusively from the poles straight to the equator
D. They heat the ocean floor directly to generate vertical volcanic plumes
choices: A. They cancel each other out so that mid-ocean waters remain completely still
B. They push surface waters in opposite latitudinal bands, creating large circular current patterns
C. They force all ocean water to flow exclusively from the poles straight to the equator
D. They heat the ocean floor directly to generate vertical volcanic plumes
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. They push surface waters in opposite latitudinal bands, creating large circular current patterns
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Trade winds blowing from the east near the equator and westerlies blowing from the west in the temperate zone cause currents in each ocean basin to move in a circular pattern (p. 32).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What happens to a deep-water swell wave as it enters shallow water and forms a breaker?
quiz_item.question: What happens to a deep-water swell wave as it enters shallow water and forms a breaker?
options: A. The wave speeds up and stretches out until it flattens silently onto the sand
B. The bottom of the wave slows down from friction with the seafloor while the top pitches forward and collapses
C. Cold groundwater rises from the beach sand to push the wave back out to sea
D. Surface tension locks the wave crest in place so it cannot topple over
choices: A. The wave speeds up and stretches out until it flattens silently onto the sand
B. The bottom of the wave slows down from friction with the seafloor while the top pitches forward and collapses
C. Cold groundwater rises from the beach sand to push the wave back out to sea
D. Surface tension locks the wave crest in place so it cannot topple over
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. The bottom of the wave slows down from friction with the seafloor while the top pitches forward and collapses
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): When a wave reaches shallow water where depth is less than half its wavelength, friction with the bottom slows the wave base, increasing height and steepness until the crest pitches forward as surf (p. 27).

pamphlet_excerpts: Solitary Undersea Seamount Peaks: Some solitary undersea mountains called seamounts rise several thousand feet from the ocean floor (p. 14).
Submerged Cone Shaped Summits: Their cone-shaped peaks remain submerged unless the water level drops (p. 14).
Ice Age Sea Level Drop: During the last Ice Age, much of the ocean's water froze to form vast glaciers, and the ocean's level fell much lower than what it is today (p. 14).
Wave Eroded Flat Guyots: Wave action eroded and flattened the tops of exposed seamount peaks and resulted in what are called guyots (p. 14).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Note Glacial Sea Levels: During the last Ice Age, much of the ocean's water froze to form vast glaciers, and the ocean's level fell much lower than what it is today (p. 14).
Step 2 - Sketch Flat Topped Guyots: Wave action eroded and flattened the tops of exposed seamount peaks and resulted in what are called guyots (p. 14).
Step 3 - Illustrate Submerged Guyot Depth: When the glaciers melted, the ocean levels rose and covered up those guyots (p. 14).
Step 4 - Label Basal tic Basin Features: Topographic features of the ocean floor Basal tic ROCK BASIN (p. 14).

B. Submarines and dredging vessels leveled the peaks for navigation safety
C. Wave action eroded and flattened exposed volcanic seamount peaks during lower Ice Age sea levels
D. Tectonic plates pulled the mountain summits apart into wide rift valleys
choices: A. Heavy deep-sea currents scraped the tops off underwater sand dunes
B. Submarines and dredging vessels leveled the peaks for navigation safety
C. Wave action eroded and flattened exposed volcanic seamount peaks during lower Ice Age sea levels
D. Tectonic plates pulled the mountain summits apart into wide rift valleys
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Wave action eroded and flattened exposed volcanic seamount peaks during lower Ice Age sea levels
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): During the last Ice Age, lower sea levels exposed volcanic seamount peaks to surface wave action that eroded and flattened their tops before melting glaciers submerged them again as guyots (p. 14).

pamphlet_excerpts: Atmospheric Wind Circulation Patterns: The Oceans and the Atmosphere Great wind circulation systems form (p. 31).
Tropical Easterly Trade Winds: Close to the equator, trade winds blow from the east (p. 31).
Steady Temperate Westerly Winds: In the temperate zone, steady winds called westerlies blow from the west (p. 31).
Surface Current Wind Generation: Winds blowing across the ocean's surface create currents (p. 31).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Identify Temperate Wind Belts: In the temperate zone, steady winds called westerlies blow from the west (p. 31).
Step 2 - Link Winds to Currents: Winds blowing across the ocean's surface create currents (p. 31).
Step 3 - Chart Basin Gyre Circulation: When the trade winds and westerlies blow across the oceans, they cause the currents in each ocean basin to move in acircular pattern (p. 31).
Step 4 - Explain Climate Heat Exchange: Both surface and deep water currents affect the world'sclimate by moving warm air from the tropics toward the poles, and cold air (p. 31).

quiz_item.question: How do differences in evaporation and precipitation affect the salinity of surface ocean water?
options: A. High evaporation removes fresh water and raises salinity, while heavy precipitation adds fresh water and lowers salinity
B. Heavy rainfall adds atmospheric salt to the sea and increases surface salinity
C. Evaporation removes dissolved sodium chloride from the ocean and makes the water fresher
D. Neither evaporation nor precipitation has any measurable effect on seawater salt content
choices: A. High evaporation removes fresh water and raises salinity, while heavy precipitation adds fresh water and lowers salinity
B. Heavy rainfall adds atmospheric salt to the sea and increases surface salinity
C. Evaporation removes dissolved sodium chloride from the ocean and makes the water fresher
D. Neither evaporation nor precipitation has any measurable effect on seawater salt content
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. High evaporation removes fresh water and raises salinity, while heavy precipitation adds fresh water and lowers salinity
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Evaporation leaves salts behind in the sea and increases salinity, whereas precipitation dilutes seawater with fresh rain or snow and lowers salinity (p. 31).

pamphlet_excerpts: Drifting Marine Plankton Wanderers: The term plankton comes from the Greek word planktos, which means "wanderer." Plankton includes marine plants and animals that drift with the currents (p. 45).
Swimmers and Bottom Dwellers: Because they drift, plankton differ from nekton, animals that actively swim or lie on or burrow into the seafloor, such as clams and worms (p. 45).
Contrast With Large Seaweeds: They also differ from marine plants such as large seaweeds (p. 45).
Microscopic Plankton Cell Size: Plankton cells are seldom larger in diameter than a few tenths of an inch (p. 45).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Distinguish Plankton From Seaweeds: They also differ from marine plants such as large seaweeds (p. 45).
Step 2 - Measure Microscopic Plankton Cells: Plankton cells are seldom larger in diameter than a few tenths of an inch (p. 45).
Step 3 - Trace Marine Food Chains: Plankton forms the basis of all major ocean food chains (p. 45).

Step 4 - Examine Floating Plankton Adaptations: However, because of their small size, long spines, shell extension, and the ability to float, these drifters have adapted in different ways to slow (p. 45).

requirements.description: Describe some of the biologically important properties of seawater. Define benthos, nekton, and plankton. Name some of the plants and animals that make up each of these groups. Describe the place and importance of phytoplankton in the oceanic food chain.

requirements.lead_text: Do ONE of the following:
requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a plankton net. Tow the net by a dock, wade with it, hold it in a current, or tow it from a rowboat. Do this for about 20 minutes. Save the sample. Examine it under a microscope or high-power glass. Identify the three most common types of plankton in the sample. Note: May be done in lakes or streams. (b) Make a series of models (clay or plaster and wood) of a volcanic island. Show the growth of an atoll from a fringing reef through a barrier reef. Describe the Darwinian theory of coral reef formation. (c) Measure the water temperature at the surface, midwater, and bottom of a body of water four times daily for five consecutive days. You may measure depth with a rock tied to a line. Make a Secchi disk to measure turbidity (how much suspended sedimentation is in the water). Measure the air temperature. Note the cloud cover and roughness of the water. Show your findings (air and water temperature, turbidity) on a graph. Tell how the water temperature changes with air temperature. (d) Make a model showing the inshore sediment movement by littoral currents, tidal movement, and wave action. Include such formations as high and low waterlines, low-tide terrace, berm, and coastal cliffs. Show how offshore bars are built up and torn down. (e) Make a wave generator. Show reflection and refraction of waves. Show how groins, jetties, and breakwaters affect these patterns. (f) With your counselor's and parent or guardian's approval and permission, track and monitor satellite images available on the internet for a specific location for three weeks. Describe what you have learned to your counselor.

Towering Internal Wave Heights: The resulting waves can reach heights above 300 feet (91 meters), much higher than typical surface waves (p. 23).
Nutrient and Temperature Mixing: Internal waves can influence the amount and diversity of nutrients available and the water temperature in an area (p. 23).
Submersible Navigation Hazards Underwater: They can also hinder the monitoring of underwater environments and endanger submersibles (p. 23).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Monitor Nutrient and Temperature Shifts: Internal waves can influence the amount and diversity of nutrients available and the water temperature in an area (p. 23).
Step 2 - Account for Submersible Hazards: They can also hinder the monitoring of underwater environments and endanger submersibles (p. 23).
Step 3 - Time Semidiurnal High Tides: On most ocean shores, high tide occurs regularly every 12 hours, 25 minutes (p. 23).
Step 4 - Log Daily Tidal Delays: This means each new tide, high orlow, occurs a little later each day (p. 23).

requirements.description: Do ONE of the following: (a) Make a plankton net. Tow the net by a dock, wade with it, hold it in a current, or tow it from a rowboat. Do this for about 20 minutes. Save the sample. Examine it under a microscope or high-power glass. Identify the three most common types of plankton in the sample. Note: May be done in lakes or streams. (b) Make a series of models (clay or plaster and wood) of a volcanic island. Show the growth of an atoll from a fringing reef through a barrier reef. Describe the Darwinian theory of coral reef formation. (c) Measure the water temperature at the surface, midwater, and bottom of a body of water four times daily for five consecutive days. You may measure depth with a rock tied to a line. Make a Secchi disk to measure turbidity (how much suspended sedimentation is in the water). Measure the air temperature. Note the cloud cover and roughness of the water. Show your findings (air and water temperature, turbidity) on a graph. Tell how the water temperature changes with air temperature. (d) Make a model showing the inshore sediment movement by littoral currents, tidal movement, and wave action. Include such formations as high and low waterlines, low-tide terrace, berm, and coastal cliffs. Show how offshore bars are built up and torn down. (e) Make a wave generator. Show reflection and refraction of waves. Show how groins, jetties, and breakwaters affect these patterns. (f) With your counselor's and parent or guardian's approval and permission, track and monitor satellite images available on the internet for a specific location for three weeks. Describe what you have learned to your counselor.

pamphlet_excerpts: Diverse Marine Life Habitats: A rich assortment of living things calls the ocean home (p. 36).
Microscopic to Giant Organisms: Big and small, long and short, multicolored and drab, active and inactive, sea life ranges from microscopic plankton to the largest creatures on Earth (p. 36).
Bioluminescent Deep Sea Organisms: Some organisms even light up, like ghostly neon lights (p. 36).
Scientific Ocean Ecological Zones: The sea is so vast that scientists have divided it into zones (p. 36).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Observe Bioluminescent Sea Life: Some organisms even light up, like ghostly neon lights (p. 36).
Step 2 - Classify Major Ocean Zones: The sea is so vast that scientists have divided it into zones (p. 36).
Step 3 - Map Open Pelagic Waters: The pelagic zone includes all the environments of the ocean above the bottom, or living in open oceans or seas rather than in waters next to land (p. 36).
Step 4 - Separate Neritic and Oceanic Zones: It is divided into an inshore neritic zone (the zone of shallow water adjoining the seacoast) and the open-sea oceanic zone (p. 36).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do marine phytoplankton and the global ocean interact with Earth's atmosphere to support life and regulate climate?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do marine phytoplankton and the global ocean interact with Earth's atmosphere to support life and regulate climate?
options: A. Deep-sea hydrothermal vents produce most atmospheric oxygen, while surface currents reflect all incoming solar heat back into space.
B. Marine phytoplankton generate at least half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen through photosynthesis, while ocean waters absorb vast amounts of solar heat and carbon dioxide.
C. Saltwater evaporation removes carbon dioxide from the ocean and locks it permanently into stratospheric clouds.
D. Ocean tides generate geothermal heat that warms polar air masses without transferring moisture to the atmosphere.
choices: A. Deep-sea hydrothermal vents produce most atmospheric oxygen, while surface currents reflect all incoming solar heat back into space.
B. Marine phytoplankton generate at least half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen through photosynthesis, while ocean waters absorb vast amounts of solar heat and carbon dioxide.
C. Saltwater evaporation removes carbon dioxide from the ocean and locks it permanently into stratospheric clouds.
D. Ocean tides generate geothermal heat that warms polar air masses without transferring moisture to the atmosphere.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Marine phytoplankton generate at least half of Earth's atmospheric oxygen through photosynthesis, while ocean waters absorb vast amounts of solar heat and carbon dioxide.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Microscopic marine phytoplankton produce over half of the world's oxygen and anchor marine food webs, while the ocean stores and redistributes solar heat and absorbs atmospheric carbon dioxide.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do the trade winds and westerlies work together to shape surface circulation in each ocean basin?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do the trade winds and westerlies work together to shape surface circulation in each ocean basin?
options: A. They cancel each other out so that mid-ocean waters remain completely still
B. They push surface waters in opposite latitudinal bands, creating large circular current patterns
C. They force all ocean water to flow exclusively from the poles straight to the equator
D. They heat the ocean floor directly to generate vertical volcanic plumes
choices: A. They cancel each other out so that mid-ocean waters remain completely still
B. They push surface waters in opposite latitudinal bands, creating large circular current patterns
C. They force all ocean water to flow exclusively from the poles straight to the equator
D. They heat the ocean floor directly to generate vertical volcanic plumes
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. They push surface waters in opposite latitudinal bands, creating large circular current patterns
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Trade winds blowing from the east near the equator and westerlies blowing from the west in the temperate zone cause currents in each ocean basin to move in a circular pattern (p. 32).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What happens to a deep-water swell wave as it enters shallow water and forms a breaker?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What happens to a deep-water swell wave as it enters shallow water and forms a breaker?
options: A. The wave speeds up and stretches out until it flattens silently onto the sand
B. The bottom of the wave slows down from friction with the seafloor while the top pitches forward and collapses
C. Cold groundwater rises from the beach sand to push the wave back out to sea
D. Surface tension locks the wave crest in place so it cannot topple over
choices: A. The wave speeds up and stretches out until it flattens silently onto the sand
B. The bottom of the wave slows down from friction with the seafloor while the top pitches forward and collapses
C. Cold groundwater rises from the beach sand to push the wave back out to sea
D. Surface tension locks the wave crest in place so it cannot topple over
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. The bottom of the wave slows down from friction with the seafloor while the top pitches forward and collapses
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): When a wave reaches shallow water where depth is less than half its wavelength, friction with the bottom slows the wave base, increasing height and steepness until the crest pitches forward as surf (p. 27).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How did submerged flat-topped undersea mountains known as guyots get their shape?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How did submerged flat-topped undersea mountains known as guyots get their shape?
options: A. Heavy deep-sea currents scraped the tops off underwater sand dunes
B. Submarines and dredging vessels leveled the peaks for navigation safety
C. Wave action eroded and flattened exposed volcanic seamount peaks during lower Ice Age sea levels
D. Tectonic plates pulled the mountain summits apart into wide rift valleys
choices: A. Heavy deep-sea currents scraped the tops off underwater sand dunes
B. Submarines and dredging vessels leveled the peaks for navigation safety
C. Wave action eroded and flattened exposed volcanic seamount peaks during lower Ice Age sea levels
D. Tectonic plates pulled the mountain summits apart into wide rift valleys
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Wave action eroded and flattened exposed volcanic seamount peaks during lower Ice Age sea levels
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): During the last Ice Age, lower sea levels exposed volcanic seamount peaks to surface wave action that eroded and flattened their tops before melting glaciers submerged them again as guyots (p. 14).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do differences in evaporation and precipitation affect the salinity of surface ocean water?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do differences in evaporation and precipitation affect the salinity of surface ocean water?
options: A. High evaporation removes fresh water and raises salinity, while heavy precipitation adds fresh water and lowers salinity
B. Heavy rainfall adds atmospheric salt to the sea and increases surface salinity
C. Evaporation removes dissolved sodium chloride from the ocean and makes the water fresher
D. Neither evaporation nor precipitation has any measurable effect on seawater salt content
choices: A. High evaporation removes fresh water and raises salinity, while heavy precipitation adds fresh water and lowers salinity
B. Heavy rainfall adds atmospheric salt to the sea and increases surface salinity
C. Evaporation removes dissolved sodium chloride from the ocean and makes the water fresher
D. Neither evaporation nor precipitation has any measurable effect on seawater salt content
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. High evaporation removes fresh water and raises salinity, while heavy precipitation adds fresh water and lowers salinity
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Evaporation leaves salts behind in the sea and increases salinity, whereas precipitation dilutes seawater with fresh rain or snow and lowers salinity (p. 31).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which group of marine organisms consists of microscopic plants and animals that drift with ocean currents and form the base of ocean food chains?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which group of marine organisms consists of microscopic plants and animals that drift with ocean currents and form the base of ocean food chains?
options: A. Benthos
B. Nekton
C. Holdfast seaweeds
D. Plankton
choices: A. Benthos
B. Nekton
C. Holdfast seaweeds
D. Plankton
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Plankton
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Plankton, from the Greek word for wanderer, includes microscopic drifting plants (phytoplankton) and animals (zooplankton) that form the basis of all major ocean food chains (p. 45).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why do high and low tides on most ocean shores occur a little later each day?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why do high and low tides on most ocean shores occur a little later each day?
options: A. Winds slow down the rotation of ocean basins during the afternoon
B. High tide occurs regularly every 12 hours and 25 minutes, following the moon's orbit as Earth rotates
C. Internal waves block tidal water from reaching the beach until sunset
D. Groins and jetties delay the arrival of tidal water by several hours
choices: A. Winds slow down the rotation of ocean basins during the afternoon
B. High tide occurs regularly every 12 hours and 25 minutes, following the moon's orbit as Earth rotates
C. Internal waves block tidal water from reaching the beach until sunset
D. Groins and jetties delay the arrival of tidal water by several hours
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. High tide occurs regularly every 12 hours and 25 minutes, following the moon's orbit as Earth rotates
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): On most ocean shores, high tide occurs regularly every 12 hours and 25 minutes, which means each new high or low tide occurs a little later each day (p. 23).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What college education is typically recommended for a student preparing for a career as an oceanographer?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What college education is typically recommended for a student preparing for a career as an oceanographer?
options: A. A six-month commercial boat captain certificate only
B. A four-year undergraduate degree and at least a two-year master's degree
C. A two-year associate degree in recreational scuba diving
D. No formal college degree is needed if you live near a beach
choices: A. A six-month commercial boat captain certificate only
B. A four-year undergraduate degree and at least a two-year master's degree
C. A two-year associate degree in recreational scuba diving
D. No formal college degree is needed if you live near a beach
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. A four-year undergraduate degree and at least a two-year master's degree
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): An aspiring oceanographer's education should include a four-year undergraduate degree in science or oceanography and at least two more years for a master's degree (p. 57).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do marine scientists divide the pelagic zone of the ocean?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do marine scientists divide the pelagic zone of the ocean?
options: A. Into the inshore neritic zone adjoining the seacoast and the open-sea oceanic zone
B. Into the freshwater river zone and the underground aquifer zone
C. Into the trade wind zone and the westerly wind belt
D. Into the guyot peak zone and the basal tic rock basin
choices: A. Into the inshore neritic zone adjoining the seacoast and the open-sea oceanic zone
B. Into the freshwater river zone and the underground aquifer zone
C. Into the trade wind zone and the westerly wind belt
D. Into the guyot peak zone and the basal tic rock basin
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Into the inshore neritic zone adjoining the seacoast and the open-sea oceanic zone
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The pelagic zone encompasses all ocean water environments above the seafloor and is divided into the shallow inshore neritic zone and the open-sea oceanic zone (p. 36).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
quiz_item.question: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
options: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
choices: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Magnetic declination is the angular difference between true north (shown on the map) and magnetic north (where the compass needle points); failing to adjust for it causes significant navigation errors.

pamphlet_excerpts: Aligning the Compass Bezel: Rotate the bezel until the orienting arrow or north-south lines lie parallel to and in the same direction as the magnetic north-south lines on the map (p. 10).
Reading the Bearing Index: Read the bearing directly opposite of the bearing index (p. 10).
Converting Map and Compass: If the magnetic north-south lines are not drawn on the map, convert the language of the compass to that of the map (p. 10).
Adjusting for Magnetic Declination: Always add the number of degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Convert Map Compass Angles: If the magnetic north-south lines are not drawn on the map, convert the language of the compass to that of the map (p. 10).
Step 2 - Add or Subtract Declination: Always add the number of degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination (p. 10).
Step 3 - Read Exact Degree Bearings: The bearing is 244 degrees from "A" to "B." (Points "A" and "B" can be seen in the top photo on page 21.) (p. 10).
Step 4 - Navigate With Thumb Compasses: The thumb compass rides on the thumb and simplifies map orientation and direction finding while you are on the move (p. 10).

pamphlet_excerpts: Meaning of Map Orientation: Using a Map and Compass Together Orienting a Map With a Compass Orienting a map means aligning it with the terrain (p. 19).
Limits of Visual Alignment: You can do this visually, but it is easier to make errors that way (p. 19).
Precision of Compass Alignment: A more accurate way of aligning the map and terrain is to use a compass (p. 19).
Setting Bezel to North: First, rotate the compass bezel until Nor 360 degrees is lined up with the direction-of-travel arrow (p. 19).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Choose Compass Over Sight: A more accurate way of aligning the map and terrain is to use a compass (p. 19).
Step 2 - Set Bezel to North: First, rotate the compass bezel until Nor 360 degrees is lined up with the direction-of-travel arrow (p. 19).
Step 3 - Align Edge With Meridian: Next, set the compass down on the map, with the compass edge along one of the north-south magnetic lines and the direction-of-travel arrow pointing (p. 19).
Step 4 - Rotate Map and Compass: Rotate the map and the compass together until the compass needle matches the direction-of-travel arrow (p. 19).

B. Turn the bezel until the orienting arrow points due east
C. Walk 100 paces forward while holding the map vertical
D. Rotate the map and compass together until the compass needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow
choices: A. Fold the map in half along the equator line
B. Turn the bezel until the orienting arrow points due east
C. Walk 100 paces forward while holding the map vertical
D. Rotate the map and compass together until the compass needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Rotate the map and compass together until the compass needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Rotating the map and compass together until the magnetic needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow aligns the map accurately with the surrounding terrain (p. 19).

common_misconception_pair.misconception: Your 100-meter pace count stays exactly the same whether you are walking calmly or running at full speed.
common_misconception_pair.fact: Stride length and speed change between walking and running, so orienteers must mentally adjust both their pace count and time whenever they switch speeds (p. 26).

pamphlet_excerpts: Adjusting for Speed Changes: Every timeorienteers switch from walking to running or the reverse, they must mentally adjust the pace and time as well (p. 26).
Counting Paces and Time: Once you have laid out the course, start at the beginning and walk the length of it, counting the number of paces and recording the time it takes you to reach (p. 26).
Baseline Per Hundred Meters: This is your walking pace and time per 100 meters (p. 26).
Averaging Multiple Pace Trials: You will get a more accurate measure if you walk the course two or more times and then divide the total paces and minutes by the total meters walked (p. 26).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Record Hundred Meter Baseline: This is your walking pace and time per 100 meters (p. 26).
Step 2 - Average Multiple Course Runs: You will get a more accurate measure if you walk the course two or more times and then divide the total paces and minutes by the total meters walked (p. 26).
Step 3 - Account for Uneven Ground: This is particularly important if the course is on uneven ground (p. 26).
Step 4 - Measure Running Pace Speed: Judging Distance on the Ground Running Pace/Time Foot speed is important in orienteering, especially for competitive orienteering (p. 26).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How can you get the most accurate baseline measurement for your 100-meter walking or running pace?
quiz_item.question: How can you get the most accurate baseline measurement for your 100-meter walking or running pace?
options: A. Estimate your stride length indoors using a ruler and multiply by 100
B. Walk a 10-meter driveway once and multiply the result by 10
C. Cover the 100-meter course two or more times, especially on uneven ground, and divide total paces and time by total meters
D. Copy the pace count of another Scout who is approximately your height
choices: A. Estimate your stride length indoors using a ruler and multiply by 100
B. Walk a 10-meter driveway once and multiply the result by 10
C. Cover the 100-meter course two or more times, especially on uneven ground, and divide total paces and time by total meters
D. Copy the pace count of another Scout who is approximately your height
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Cover the 100-meter course two or more times, especially on uneven ground, and divide total paces and time by total meters
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Repeating the 100-meter course multiple times and averaging the total paces and minutes over the total distance provides a reliable baseline, particularly on uneven ground (p. 26).

common_misconception_pair.misconception: When navigating to a control located directly on a road or stream, you should always aim straight at the control.
common_misconception_pair.fact: If you aim straight at a control on a linear feature and miss it slightly, you will not know which way to turn, whereas aiming off deliberately to one side tells you the exact direction to turn (p. 38).

pamphlet_excerpts: Turning at Linear Features: If you arrive at the linear feature and do not see the control, you will then know which way to turn to find (p. 38).
Avoiding Direction Uncertainty: In this map, it would be easy to reach the road and not be sure what direction the control lies (p. 38).
Deliberate Aiming Off Strategy: To prevent this, you can deliberately aim a few meters south of the control so you know to turn north when you get to the road (p. 38).
Mental Picture of Terrain: Keep a clear mental picture of the terrain that you will pass (p. 38).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Aim Off to One Side: To prevent this, you can deliberately aim a few meters south of the control so you know to turn north when you get to the road (p. 38).
Step 2 - Visualize Upcoming Terrain Shapes: Keep a clear mental picture of the terrain that you will pass (p. 38).
Step 3 - Read Map Every Few Seconds: Read the map every few seconds, think beyond your location, and plan ahead (p. 38).
Step 4 - Plan Ahead After Controls: The best way to practice reading ahead is to take time at the beginning of the course and after each control to make sure you understand (p. 38).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why would an orienteer deliberately aim a few meters south of a control located along a north-south road?
quiz_item.question: Why would an orienteer deliberately aim a few meters south of a control located along a north-south road?
options: A. To compensate for a broken compass bezel during the race
B. To guarantee that upon reaching the road, they know to turn north to find the control
C. To avoid having to punch the control card at that station
D. To add extra distance so their pace count reaches an even number
choices: A. To compensate for a broken compass bezel during the race
B. To guarantee that upon reaching the road, they know to turn north to find the control
C. To avoid having to punch the control card at that station
D. To add extra distance so their pace count reaches an even number
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. To guarantee that upon reaching the road, they know to turn north to find the control
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): This technique, called aiming off, ensures that when you hit the linear feature (the road), you know with certainty which direction to turn to reach the control (p. 38).

pamphlet_excerpts: Orienteering USA Governing Body: Orienteering USA is the ruling body for sanctioned orienteering events in the United States (p. 35).
Official Rules and Conduct: Its rule book is comprehensive and addresses the technicalities of holding an event, as well as conduct that is expected of the participants (p. 35).
Consulting the Rule Book: A few general rules are provided below, but for detailed information, it is best to consult the rule book or to contact the OUSA (p. 35).
Fairness and Prior Knowledge: Competitors who have prior knowledge of the course that will give them an unfair advantage should not participate (p. 35).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Review Official OUSA Rules: A few general rules are provided below, but for detailed information, it is best to consult the rule book or to contact the OUSA (p. 35).
Step 2 - Screen Out Unfair Advantages: Competitors who have prior knowledge of the course that will give them an unfair advantage should not participate (p. 35).
Step 3 - Prohibit Pre-Event Course Inspection: Investigation of the course before an event is forbidden (p. 35).
Step 4 - Enforce Compass-Only Navigation: The use of any navigational aid other than a compass is prohibited for navigation during a race (p. 35).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When taking a bearing from a topographic map in an area with a 12-degree west magnetic declination, why must you account for declination before following your compass in the field?
options: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
choices: A. Because contour lines on a topographic map shift position seasonally as soil moisture changes.
B. Because a baseplate compass needle always points toward the geographic North Pole rather than magnetic north.
C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
D. Because metal control flags placed at orienteering checkpoints reverse the polarity of the compass housing.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Because map grid lines align with true north while the compass needle points to magnetic north, and ignoring a 12-degree difference will pull you far off course over distance.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Magnetic declination is the angular difference between true north (shown on the map) and magnetic north (where the compass needle points); failing to adjust for it causes significant navigation errors.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do index contour lines on an orienteering map differ from those on a standard topographic map?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do index contour lines on an orienteering map differ from those on a standard topographic map?
options: A. They are drawn as dotted blue lines to indicate seasonal water flow
B. They only appear at the exact summit of conical mountains
C. They are thicker to guide the eye but do not have elevation numbers printed on them
D. They point directly toward magnetic north across the map sheet
choices: A. They are drawn as dotted blue lines to indicate seasonal water flow
B. They only appear at the exact summit of conical mountains
C. They are thicker to guide the eye but do not have elevation numbers printed on them
D. They point directly toward magnetic north across the map sheet
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. They are thicker to guide the eye but do not have elevation numbers printed on them
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): On orienteering maps, index contour lines are thicker than intermediate contours to guide your eye, though they omit printed elevation numbers (p. 14).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: If your map does not have magnetic north-south lines drawn on it, how do you adjust a map bearing for magnetic declination?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: If your map does not have magnetic north-south lines drawn on it, how do you adjust a map bearing for magnetic declination?
options: A. Add the degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination
B. Subtract the degrees of error for both east and west declination
C. Multiply the contour interval by the magnetic variation angle
D. Point the direction-of-travel arrow south before rotating the bezel
choices: A. Add the degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination
B. Subtract the degrees of error for both east and west declination
C. Multiply the contour interval by the magnetic variation angle
D. Point the direction-of-travel arrow south before rotating the bezel
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Add the degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): To convert from true north on the map to magnetic north on the compass, always add the degrees of error for west declination and subtract for east declination (p. 10).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When orienting a map using a compass, what do you do after setting the bezel to 360 degrees and placing the compass edge along a magnetic north-south line?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When orienting a map using a compass, what do you do after setting the bezel to 360 degrees and placing the compass edge along a magnetic north-south line?
options: A. Fold the map in half along the equator line
B. Turn the bezel until the orienting arrow points due east
C. Walk 100 paces forward while holding the map vertical
D. Rotate the map and compass together until the compass needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow
choices: A. Fold the map in half along the equator line
B. Turn the bezel until the orienting arrow points due east
C. Walk 100 paces forward while holding the map vertical
D. Rotate the map and compass together until the compass needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Rotate the map and compass together until the compass needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Rotating the map and compass together until the magnetic needle aligns with the direction-of-travel arrow aligns the map accurately with the surrounding terrain (p. 19).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How can you get the most accurate baseline measurement for your 100-meter walking or running pace?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How can you get the most accurate baseline measurement for your 100-meter walking or running pace?
options: A. Estimate your stride length indoors using a ruler and multiply by 100
B. Walk a 10-meter driveway once and multiply the result by 10
C. Cover the 100-meter course two or more times, especially on uneven ground, and divide total paces and time by total meters
D. Copy the pace count of another Scout who is approximately your height
choices: A. Estimate your stride length indoors using a ruler and multiply by 100
B. Walk a 10-meter driveway once and multiply the result by 10
C. Cover the 100-meter course two or more times, especially on uneven ground, and divide total paces and time by total meters
D. Copy the pace count of another Scout who is approximately your height
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Cover the 100-meter course two or more times, especially on uneven ground, and divide total paces and time by total meters
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Repeating the 100-meter course multiple times and averaging the total paces and minutes over the total distance provides a reliable baseline, particularly on uneven ground (p. 26).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Why would an orienteer deliberately aim a few meters south of a control located along a north-south road?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Why would an orienteer deliberately aim a few meters south of a control located along a north-south road?
options: A. To compensate for a broken compass bezel during the race
B. To guarantee that upon reaching the road, they know to turn north to find the control
C. To avoid having to punch the control card at that station
D. To add extra distance so their pace count reaches an even number
choices: A. To compensate for a broken compass bezel during the race
B. To guarantee that upon reaching the road, they know to turn north to find the control
C. To avoid having to punch the control card at that station
D. To add extra distance so their pace count reaches an even number
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. To guarantee that upon reaching the road, they know to turn north to find the control
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): This technique, called aiming off, ensures that when you hit the linear feature (the road), you know with certainty which direction to turn to reach the control (p. 38).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the recommended first step when planning and mapping an area to set up a new orienteering course?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the recommended first step when planning and mapping an area to set up a new orienteering course?

B. Print control description sheets before selecting the park location
C. Invite competitors to start running while you place the markers ahead of them
D. Spend a half-day scouting the area with a notebook to note terrain, vegetation, features, and hazards
choices: A. Hang all control bags randomly in the woods and measure the distances afterward
B. Print control description sheets before selecting the park location
C. Invite competitors to start running while you place the markers ahead of them
D. Spend a half-day scouting the area with a notebook to note terrain, vegetation, features, and hazards

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Thorough preliminary reconnaissance with a notebook lets you identify terrain features, hazards, and good control sites so you can plot and refine a safe working course (p. 30).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to Orienteering USA rules, which of the following actions is prohibited for competitors in an orienteering event?
options: A. Carrying a whistle for emergency signaling
B. Investigating the course before the event or using a GPS device for navigation
C. Using a thumb compass instead of a rectangular baseplate compass
D. Wearing long pants and gaiters to protect against brush and ticks
choices: A. Carrying a whistle for emergency signaling
B. Investigating the course before the event or using a GPS device for navigation

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Orienteering USA rules forbid pre-event investigation of the course and prohibit any navigational aid other than a compass during competition (p. 35).

quiz_item.question: When setting up an extension ladder to scrape, prime, and paint an exterior wall, how should you position the base of the ladder according to the 4-to-1 rule?
options: A. Place the base of the ladder 1 foot away from the wall for every 4 feet of vertical height to the upper support point, on firm level ground.
B. Place the base 4 feet away from the wall for every 1 foot of vertical height so you can lean backward while rolling paint.
C. Set the ladder rails flush against the siding and tie the top rung to a rain gutter with twine.
D. Extend the ladder to its maximum length with zero overlap between sections and prop one leg on loose bricks.
choices: A. Place the base of the ladder 1 foot away from the wall for every 4 feet of vertical height to the upper support point, on firm level ground.
B. Place the base 4 feet away from the wall for every 1 foot of vertical height so you can lean backward while rolling paint.
C. Set the ladder rails flush against the siding and tie the top rung to a rain gutter with twine.

quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Place the base of the ladder 1 foot away from the wall for every 4 feet of vertical height to the upper support point, on firm level ground.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): The 4-to-1 ladder safety rule places the base 1 foot out from the wall for every 4 feet of working height, providing a stable 75-degree climbing angle that prevents tipping backward or sliding out.

pamphlet_excerpts: Understanding Paint Sheen: Sheen is a critical characteristic that refers to the degree of shine or gloss of any coating or surface (p. 43).
Existing Sheen Impact: The sheen currently on the surface can determine the amount of surface preparation required (p. 43).
Durability and Appearance: The abrasion resistance, chemical resistance, and overall beauty of the painted area (p. 43).
Full Sheen Spectrum: The typical full sheen range, from lowest to highest, includes flat or matte, eggshell or low luster, satin or pearl, semi gloss, and high or full gloss (p. 43).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Evaluate Durability Needs: The abrasion resistance, chemical resistance, and overall beauty of the painted area (p. 43).
Step 2 - Compare Gloss Levels: The typical full sheen range, from lowest to highest, includes flat or matte, eggshell or low luster, satin or pearl, semi gloss, and high or full gloss (p. 43).
Step 3 - Check Manufacturer Standards: Because there are no industry wide standard definitions of these terms, gloss levels may vary from one manufacturer to another (p. 43).
Step 4 - Match Sheen to Surface: The type of sheen you choose will depend on what you are painting (p. 43).

common_misconception_pair.fact: Applying primer is the final stage of surface preparation that seals porous material, protects the substrate, and ensures the topcoat adheres properly (p. 51).

pamphlet_excerpts: Primer as Final Prep: Applying primer, the first coat of paint, also is the last stage of surface preparation (p. 51).
Bonding and Sealing Functions: The primer makes the next coat stick to the surface, protects the substrate, and seals the surface (p. 51).
Substrate-Specific Primers: There are different primers for wood, concrete and masonry, plaster and drywall, steel, and other metals (p. 51).
Indoor and Outdoor Wood Primers: Wood primers are available in oil-based or water-based products and can be used indoors or outdoors (p. 51).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Select Substrate Primer: There are different primers for wood, concrete and masonry, plaster and drywall, steel, and other metals (p. 51).
Step 2 - Prime Bare Wood Surfaces: Wood primers are available in oil-based or water-based products and can be used indoors or outdoors (p. 51).
Step 3 - Apply Alkali-Resistant Masonry Primer: Exterior masonry surfaces are often highly alkaline, so be sure to use primers on surfaces that are alkali-resistant (p. 51).
Step 4 - Remove Loose Plaster Dust: Make sure primers for plaster surfaces are alkali-resistant and that plaster dust is removed first (p. 51).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Why must you choose a specialized primer when preparing exterior masonry or plaster surfaces for painting?
quiz_item.question: Why must you choose a specialized primer when preparing exterior masonry or plaster surfaces for painting?
options: A. Masonry and plaster surfaces are completely nonporous and reject water-based coatings.
B. Standard wood primers dry too slowly when exposed to concrete and brick.
C. Masonry primers eliminate the need to patch cracks or apply a topcoat.
D. Exterior masonry and plaster are often highly alkaline, requiring an alkali-resistant primer after dust removal.
choices: A. Masonry and plaster surfaces are completely nonporous and reject water-based coatings.
B. Standard wood primers dry too slowly when exposed to concrete and brick.
C. Masonry primers eliminate the need to patch cracks or apply a topcoat.
D. Exterior masonry and plaster are often highly alkaline, requiring an alkali-resistant primer after dust removal.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Exterior masonry and plaster are often highly alkaline, requiring an alkali-resistant primer after dust removal.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Masonry and plaster contain alkaline compounds that degrade ordinary primers, so painters must remove surface dust and apply an alkali-resistant primer (p. 51).
