quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Your patrol rolls two solid spheres of the exact same size and shape down an inclined ramp from rest: one made of aluminum and one made of heavy brass. Neglecting air resistance, how do their accelerations down the ramp compare?
quiz_item.question: Your patrol rolls two solid spheres of the exact same size and shape down an inclined ramp from rest: one made of aluminum and one made of heavy brass. Neglecting air resistance, how do their accelerations down the ramp compare?
options: A. The heavier brass sphere accelerates twice as fast because it has more gravitational mass.
B. Both spheres accelerate down the ramp at the same rate because gravitational acceleration and rotational inertia scale proportionally with mass for identical solid spheres.
C. The lighter aluminum sphere reaches the bottom first because it has less friction.
D. Neither sphere rolls unless the ramp angle exceeds 45 degrees.
choices: A. The heavier brass sphere accelerates twice as fast because it has more gravitational mass.
B. Both spheres accelerate down the ramp at the same rate because gravitational acceleration and rotational inertia scale proportionally with mass for identical solid spheres.
C. The lighter aluminum sphere reaches the bottom first because it has less friction.
D. Neither sphere rolls unless the ramp angle exceeds 45 degrees.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Both spheres accelerate down the ramp at the same rate because gravitational acceleration and rotational inertia scale proportionally with mass for identical solid spheres.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Since both gravitational force and moment of inertia are proportional to mass (I = 2/5 m r^2), mass cancels out of the equation of motion on an incline.

quiz_item.question: Which statement best defines the science of physics and how its branches relate to the natural world?
options: A. It is the study of classifying rocks, minerals, and tectonic plate boundaries on Earth.
B. It is the study of how matter and energy interact across space and time, from subatomic particles to the cosmos.
C. It is the practice of mixing chemical reagents to synthesize new plastics and medicines.
D. It is a branch of mathematics that only calculates abstract geometry without testing physical objects.
choices: A. It is the study of classifying rocks, minerals, and tectonic plate boundaries on Earth.
B. It is the study of how matter and energy interact across space and time, from subatomic particles to the cosmos.
C. It is the practice of mixing chemical reagents to synthesize new plastics and medicines.
D. It is a branch of mathematics that only calculates abstract geometry without testing physical objects.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. It is the study of how matter and energy interact across space and time, from subatomic particles to the cosmos.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Physics investigates the fundamental interactions between matter and energy across all scales of space and time, forming the foundation for mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, optics, and quantum science (p. 10).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: What happens to energy and matter when a mechanical wave travels across the surface of a quiet pond?
quiz_item.question: What happens to energy and matter when a mechanical wave travels across the surface of a quiet pond?
options: A. Water molecules travel outward from the center all the way to the shoreline at the speed of the wave.
B. Potential energy is destroyed at each wave crest and recreated from nothing at each trough.
C. Energy travels outward across the pond while individual water molecules oscillate mostly up and down in place.
D. Gravity stops acting on the water surface until the wave vibrations completely die out.
choices: A. Water molecules travel outward from the center all the way to the shoreline at the speed of the wave.
B. Potential energy is destroyed at each wave crest and recreated from nothing at each trough.
C. Energy travels outward across the pond while individual water molecules oscillate mostly up and down in place.
D. Gravity stops acting on the water surface until the wave vibrations completely die out.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Energy travels outward across the pond while individual water molecules oscillate mostly up and down in place.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transporting the bulk matter of the medium, which simply oscillates around its resting position (p. 17).

requirements.req_text: Hands-On Experimentation. Conduct THREE physics experiments, selecting from the following options. Each experiment must include: a hypothesis, materials used, safety precautions, observations, and conclusions based on results. Explain how each experiment demonstrates key physics principles. For each experiment, be sure to try variations/variables to test your hypothesis. (A) Option A: Newton's Laws in Action: Balloon-Powered Car. Make and test a balloon-powered car to show how force and motion interact. (B) Option B: Momentum: Stacked Ball Drop. Drop different-sized stacked balls to show momentum. (C) Option C: Centrifugal Force. Make spinning toys to demonstrate centrifugal force. (D) Option D: Centripetal Force. Swing a water bucket or tray filled with water glasses to demonstrate centripetal force. (E) Option E: Balance. Explore center of gravity, inertia, and harmonic motion using a Tweety Bopper. (F) Option F: Visualize Sound. Visualize Chladni patterns using a tonoscope. (G) Option G: Cartesian Diver. Demonstrate buoyancy and the ideal gas law with Cartesian divers. (H) Option H: Air Pressure: Bernoulli's principle and the Coandă Effect. Balance different objects in a stream of air. (I) Option I: Electromagnet. Make an electromagnet and explore how to increase its strength.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In the Cartesian diver experiment, why does the diver sink to the bottom when you squeeze the sides of the sealed plastic bottle?
quiz_item.question: In the Cartesian diver experiment, why does the diver sink to the bottom when you squeeze the sides of the sealed plastic bottle?
options: A. Squeezing the bottle heats the water, which makes the liquid less dense than the plastic diver.
B. Squeezing creates a magnetic field at the bottom of the bottle that pulls the diver downward.
C. Squeezing removes gravity from the upper half of the bottle and concentrates it at the base.
D. Increased pressure compresses the air pocket inside the diver, increasing its overall density above the density of water.
choices: A. Squeezing the bottle heats the water, which makes the liquid less dense than the plastic diver.
B. Squeezing creates a magnetic field at the bottom of the bottle that pulls the diver downward.
C. Squeezing removes gravity from the upper half of the bottle and concentrates it at the base.
D. Increased pressure compresses the air pocket inside the diver, increasing its overall density above the density of water.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Increased pressure compresses the air pocket inside the diver, increasing its overall density above the density of water.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): By Pascal's principle and the ideal gas law, squeezing the bottle transmits pressure throughout the water and compresses the trapped air bubble, reducing buoyancy so the diver sinks (p. 25).

requirements.description: Hands-On Experimentation. Conduct THREE physics experiments, selecting from the following options. Each experiment must include: a hypothesis, materials used, safety precautions, observations, and conclusions based on results. Explain how each experiment demonstrates key physics principles. For each experiment, be sure to try variations/variables to test your hypothesis. (A) Option A: Newton's Laws in Action: Balloon-Powered Car. Make and test a balloon-powered car to show how force and motion interact. (B) Option B: Momentum: Stacked Ball Drop. Drop different-sized stacked balls to show momentum. (C) Option C: Centrifugal Force. Make spinning toys to demonstrate centrifugal force. (D) Option D: Centripetal Force. Swing a water bucket or tray filled with water glasses to demonstrate centripetal force. (E) Option E: Balance. Explore center of gravity, inertia, and harmonic motion using a Tweety Bopper. (F) Option F: Visualize Sound. Visualize Chladni patterns using a tonoscope. (G) Option G: Cartesian Diver. Demonstrate buoyancy and the ideal gas law with Cartesian divers. (H) Option H: Air Pressure: Bernoulli's principle and the Coandă Effect. Balance different objects in a stream of air. (I) Option I: Electromagnet. Make an electromagnet and explore how to increase its strength.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How does a Scouting block-and-tackle pulley system help a patrol raise a heavy pioneering tower?
quiz_item.question: How does a Scouting block-and-tackle pulley system help a patrol raise a heavy pioneering tower?
options: A. It multiplies mechanical advantage so Scouts pull with less force over a longer rope distance while conserving total work.
B. It eliminates gravitational potential energy so the timber weighs less at the top of the lift.
C. It creates extra mechanical energy inside the pulley wheels so less rope needs to be pulled.
D. It converts static friction directly into upward magnetic lift along the hemp rope.
choices: A. It multiplies mechanical advantage so Scouts pull with less force over a longer rope distance while conserving total work.
B. It eliminates gravitational potential energy so the timber weighs less at the top of the lift.
C. It creates extra mechanical energy inside the pulley wheels so less rope needs to be pulled.
D. It converts static friction directly into upward magnetic lift along the hemp rope.
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. It multiplies mechanical advantage so Scouts pull with less force over a longer rope distance while conserving total work.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): A pulley system provides mechanical advantage by distributing the load across multiple supporting rope segments, reducing required effort force while increasing pull distance (p. 32).

requirements.req_text: The Future of Physics. Physicists try to explain the universe and apply these concepts to novel technologies. Discuss one option with your counselor: (A) Option A: Unsolved Mysteries of Physics. Discuss the following with your counselor: (a) Dark Matter & Dark Energy. Scientists know it exists, but what is it? (b) Black Holes & Wormholes. Can we harness their energy or travel through them? (B) Option B: Quantum Mechanics & Computing. Discuss the following with your counselor: (a) Quantum Computers. How can super fast computers be made of atoms instead of microchips? (b) Quantum Entanglement. Can we communicate instantly across space? (C) Option C: Space Exploration & Astrophysics. Discuss the following with your counselor: (a) Colonizing Mars. How can physics help humans live on other planets? (b) Interstellar Travel. Can we reach other stars with warp drives or solar sails? (D) Option D: Advanced Theories & Future Discoveries. Discuss the following with your counselor: (a) Time Travel. Is it possible under extreme conditions? (b) Artificial Gravity. Can we create Earth-like gravity in space stations?

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How do astrophysicists distinguish the role of dark matter from the role of dark energy in the universe?
quiz_item.question: How do astrophysicists distinguish the role of dark matter from the role of dark energy in the universe?
options: A. Dark matter pushes galaxies apart while dark energy pulls planets into circular orbits.
B. Dark matter provides extra gravitational attraction holding galaxies together, while dark energy drives the accelerated expansion of space.
C. Dark matter is made of ordinary black holes that glow in X-rays, while dark energy is frozen hydrogen gas.
D. Dark matter only exists inside Earth laboratories, while dark energy only exists inside our solar system.
choices: A. Dark matter pushes galaxies apart while dark energy pulls planets into circular orbits.
B. Dark matter provides extra gravitational attraction holding galaxies together, while dark energy drives the accelerated expansion of space.
C. Dark matter is made of ordinary black holes that glow in X-rays, while dark energy is frozen hydrogen gas.
D. Dark matter only exists inside Earth laboratories, while dark energy only exists inside our solar system.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Dark matter provides extra gravitational attraction holding galaxies together, while dark energy drives the accelerated expansion of space.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Observations of galaxy rotation speeds reveal unseen gravitational mass called dark matter, while distant supernovae show that dark energy is accelerating cosmic expansion (p. 34).

requirements.description: The Future of Physics. Physicists try to explain the universe and apply these concepts to novel technologies. Discuss one option with your counselor: (A) Option A: Unsolved Mysteries of Physics. Discuss the following with your counselor: (a) Dark Matter & Dark Energy. Scientists know it exists, but what is it? (b) Black Holes & Wormholes. Can we harness their energy or travel through them? (B) Option B: Quantum Mechanics & Computing. Discuss the following with your counselor: (a) Quantum Computers. How can super fast computers be made of atoms instead of microchips? (b) Quantum Entanglement. Can we communicate instantly across space? (C) Option C: Space Exploration & Astrophysics. Discuss the following with your counselor: (a) Colonizing Mars. How can physics help humans live on other planets? (b) Interstellar Travel. Can we reach other stars with warp drives or solar sails? (D) Option D: Advanced Theories & Future Discoveries. Discuss the following with your counselor: (a) Time Travel. Is it possible under extreme conditions? (b) Artificial Gravity. Can we create Earth-like gravity in space stations?

requirements.req_text: Engineering and Physics Challenge. Solve a simple engineering problem using physics-based reasoning. Define the problem, allowable materials, and safety constraints. You may enlist friends or family in completing your challenge. All plans must be approved in advance by your counselor. Do ONE of the following options: (A) Option A: Fastest Pinewood Derby Car. Build pinewood derby cars using physics principles to get the fastest time on the track. (B) Option B: Rube Goldberg Machine. Build a machine using household materials to perform a simple task. You can use examples of tasks from the annual Rube Goldberg competition, or you can create your own task: (C) Option C: Egg Drop Challenge. Explore the physics of energy and momentum by building a structure using household materials to prevent an egg from breaking when dropped from a significant height. The location of the egg drop must be approved by your counselor. (D) Option D: Water Bottle Rockets. Explore propulsion and Newton's Third Law. The challenge is to land an air pressured rocket, using water as a propellant, exactly at a specific distance (for example, 70 m) from launch point, three times, with extra points for flight duration. (E) Option E: Design your Own Physics Challenge. Create a physics challenge with your counselor's approval.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: According to the impulse-momentum theorem, how does a collapsible crumple zone keep a raw egg from cracking in the Egg Drop Challenge?
quiz_item.question: According to the impulse-momentum theorem, how does a collapsible crumple zone keep a raw egg from cracking in the Egg Drop Challenge?
options: A. It increases the mass of the egg at the moment of impact so gravity stops pulling on it.
B. It makes the container bounce upward faster than it hit the ground to double the impact force.
C. It extends the duration of the collision impact, which decreases the peak force acting on the egg shell.
D. It prevents the falling container from gaining any kinetic energy during its descent.
choices: A. It increases the mass of the egg at the moment of impact so gravity stops pulling on it.
B. It makes the container bounce upward faster than it hit the ground to double the impact force.
C. It extends the duration of the collision impact, which decreases the peak force acting on the egg shell.
D. It prevents the falling container from gaining any kinetic energy during its descent.
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. It extends the duration of the collision impact, which decreases the peak force acting on the egg shell.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Because impulse equals force multiplied by time, extending the stopping time with a deformable crumple zone significantly lowers the peak force experienced by the egg (p. 42).

requirements.description: Engineering and Physics Challenge. Solve a simple engineering problem using physics-based reasoning. Define the problem, allowable materials, and safety constraints. You may enlist friends or family in completing your challenge. All plans must be approved in advance by your counselor. Do ONE of the following options: (A) Option A: Fastest Pinewood Derby Car. Build pinewood derby cars using physics principles to get the fastest time on the track. (B) Option B: Rube Goldberg Machine. Build a machine using household materials to perform a simple task. You can use examples of tasks from the annual Rube Goldberg competition, or you can create your own task: (C) Option C: Egg Drop Challenge. Explore the physics of energy and momentum by building a structure using household materials to prevent an egg from breaking when dropped from a significant height. The location of the egg drop must be approved by your counselor. (D) Option D: Water Bottle Rockets. Explore propulsion and Newton's Third Law. The challenge is to land an air pressured rocket, using water as a propellant, exactly at a specific distance (for example, 70 m) from launch point, three times, with extra points for flight duration. (E) Option E: Design your Own Physics Challenge. Create a physics challenge with your counselor's approval.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Your patrol rolls two solid spheres of the exact same size and shape down an inclined ramp from rest: one made of aluminum and one made of heavy brass. Neglecting air resistance, how do their accelerations down the ramp compare?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Your patrol rolls two solid spheres of the exact same size and shape down an inclined ramp from rest: one made of aluminum and one made of heavy brass. Neglecting air resistance, how do their accelerations down the ramp compare?
options: A. The heavier brass sphere accelerates twice as fast because it has more gravitational mass.
B. Both spheres accelerate down the ramp at the same rate because gravitational acceleration and rotational inertia scale proportionally with mass for identical solid spheres.
C. The lighter aluminum sphere reaches the bottom first because it has less friction.
D. Neither sphere rolls unless the ramp angle exceeds 45 degrees.
choices: A. The heavier brass sphere accelerates twice as fast because it has more gravitational mass.
B. Both spheres accelerate down the ramp at the same rate because gravitational acceleration and rotational inertia scale proportionally with mass for identical solid spheres.
C. The lighter aluminum sphere reaches the bottom first because it has less friction.
D. Neither sphere rolls unless the ramp angle exceeds 45 degrees.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Both spheres accelerate down the ramp at the same rate because gravitational acceleration and rotational inertia scale proportionally with mass for identical solid spheres.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Since both gravitational force and moment of inertia are proportional to mass (I = 2/5 m r^2), mass cancels out of the equation of motion on an incline.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which statement best defines the science of physics and how its branches relate to the natural world?
options: A. It is the study of classifying rocks, minerals, and tectonic plate boundaries on Earth.
B. It is the study of how matter and energy interact across space and time, from subatomic particles to the cosmos.
C. It is the practice of mixing chemical reagents to synthesize new plastics and medicines.
D. It is a branch of mathematics that only calculates abstract geometry without testing physical objects.
choices: A. It is the study of classifying rocks, minerals, and tectonic plate boundaries on Earth.
B. It is the study of how matter and energy interact across space and time, from subatomic particles to the cosmos.
C. It is the practice of mixing chemical reagents to synthesize new plastics and medicines.
D. It is a branch of mathematics that only calculates abstract geometry without testing physical objects.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. It is the study of how matter and energy interact across space and time, from subatomic particles to the cosmos.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Physics investigates the fundamental interactions between matter and energy across all scales of space and time, forming the foundation for mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, optics, and quantum science (p. 10).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What happens to energy and matter when a mechanical wave travels across the surface of a quiet pond?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What happens to energy and matter when a mechanical wave travels across the surface of a quiet pond?
options: A. Water molecules travel outward from the center all the way to the shoreline at the speed of the wave.
B. Potential energy is destroyed at each wave crest and recreated from nothing at each trough.
C. Energy travels outward across the pond while individual water molecules oscillate mostly up and down in place.
D. Gravity stops acting on the water surface until the wave vibrations completely die out.
choices: A. Water molecules travel outward from the center all the way to the shoreline at the speed of the wave.
B. Potential energy is destroyed at each wave crest and recreated from nothing at each trough.
C. Energy travels outward across the pond while individual water molecules oscillate mostly up and down in place.
D. Gravity stops acting on the water surface until the wave vibrations completely die out.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Energy travels outward across the pond while individual water molecules oscillate mostly up and down in place.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Waves transfer energy from one place to another without transporting the bulk matter of the medium, which simply oscillates around its resting position (p. 17).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: In the Cartesian diver experiment, why does the diver sink to the bottom when you squeeze the sides of the sealed plastic bottle?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: In the Cartesian diver experiment, why does the diver sink to the bottom when you squeeze the sides of the sealed plastic bottle?
options: A. Squeezing the bottle heats the water, which makes the liquid less dense than the plastic diver.
B. Squeezing creates a magnetic field at the bottom of the bottle that pulls the diver downward.
C. Squeezing removes gravity from the upper half of the bottle and concentrates it at the base.
D. Increased pressure compresses the air pocket inside the diver, increasing its overall density above the density of water.
choices: A. Squeezing the bottle heats the water, which makes the liquid less dense than the plastic diver.
B. Squeezing creates a magnetic field at the bottom of the bottle that pulls the diver downward.
C. Squeezing removes gravity from the upper half of the bottle and concentrates it at the base.
D. Increased pressure compresses the air pocket inside the diver, increasing its overall density above the density of water.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Increased pressure compresses the air pocket inside the diver, increasing its overall density above the density of water.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): By Pascal's principle and the ideal gas law, squeezing the bottle transmits pressure throughout the water and compresses the trapped air bubble, reducing buoyancy so the diver sinks (p. 25).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does a Scouting block-and-tackle pulley system help a patrol raise a heavy pioneering tower?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does a Scouting block-and-tackle pulley system help a patrol raise a heavy pioneering tower?
options: A. It multiplies mechanical advantage so Scouts pull with less force over a longer rope distance while conserving total work.
B. It eliminates gravitational potential energy so the timber weighs less at the top of the lift.
C. It creates extra mechanical energy inside the pulley wheels so less rope needs to be pulled.
D. It converts static friction directly into upward magnetic lift along the hemp rope.
choices: A. It multiplies mechanical advantage so Scouts pull with less force over a longer rope distance while conserving total work.
B. It eliminates gravitational potential energy so the timber weighs less at the top of the lift.
C. It creates extra mechanical energy inside the pulley wheels so less rope needs to be pulled.
D. It converts static friction directly into upward magnetic lift along the hemp rope.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. It multiplies mechanical advantage so Scouts pull with less force over a longer rope distance while conserving total work.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): A pulley system provides mechanical advantage by distributing the load across multiple supporting rope segments, reducing required effort force while increasing pull distance (p. 32).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How do astrophysicists distinguish the role of dark matter from the role of dark energy in the universe?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How do astrophysicists distinguish the role of dark matter from the role of dark energy in the universe?
options: A. Dark matter pushes galaxies apart while dark energy pulls planets into circular orbits.
B. Dark matter provides extra gravitational attraction holding galaxies together, while dark energy drives the accelerated expansion of space.
C. Dark matter is made of ordinary black holes that glow in X-rays, while dark energy is frozen hydrogen gas.
D. Dark matter only exists inside Earth laboratories, while dark energy only exists inside our solar system.
choices: A. Dark matter pushes galaxies apart while dark energy pulls planets into circular orbits.
B. Dark matter provides extra gravitational attraction holding galaxies together, while dark energy drives the accelerated expansion of space.
C. Dark matter is made of ordinary black holes that glow in X-rays, while dark energy is frozen hydrogen gas.
D. Dark matter only exists inside Earth laboratories, while dark energy only exists inside our solar system.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Dark matter provides extra gravitational attraction holding galaxies together, while dark energy drives the accelerated expansion of space.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Observations of galaxy rotation speeds reveal unseen gravitational mass called dark matter, while distant supernovae show that dark energy is accelerating cosmic expansion (p. 34).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: According to the impulse-momentum theorem, how does a collapsible crumple zone keep a raw egg from cracking in the Egg Drop Challenge?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: According to the impulse-momentum theorem, how does a collapsible crumple zone keep a raw egg from cracking in the Egg Drop Challenge?
options: A. It increases the mass of the egg at the moment of impact so gravity stops pulling on it.
B. It makes the container bounce upward faster than it hit the ground to double the impact force.
C. It extends the duration of the collision impact, which decreases the peak force acting on the egg shell.
D. It prevents the falling container from gaining any kinetic energy during its descent.
choices: A. It increases the mass of the egg at the moment of impact so gravity stops pulling on it.
B. It makes the container bounce upward faster than it hit the ground to double the impact force.
C. It extends the duration of the collision impact, which decreases the peak force acting on the egg shell.
D. It prevents the falling container from gaining any kinetic energy during its descent.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. It extends the duration of the collision impact, which decreases the peak force acting on the egg shell.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Because impulse equals force multiplied by time, extending the stopping time with a deformable crumple zone significantly lowers the peak force experienced by the egg (p. 42).

B. Managing hospital cafeteria budgets and scheduling ambulance fleet maintenance.

D. Calibrating radiation therapy equipment and ensuring accurate dose delivery and imaging safety for patients.
choices: A. Prescribing antibiotics and performing emergency orthopedic surgeries in the operating room.
B. Managing hospital cafeteria budgets and scheduling ambulance fleet maintenance.
C. Designing tectonic earthquake sensors for deep-ocean geological surveys.
D. Calibrating radiation therapy equipment and ensuring accurate dose delivery and imaging safety for patients.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Calibrating radiation therapy equipment and ensuring accurate dose delivery and imaging safety for patients.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Medical physicists apply nuclear and electromagnetic physics to calibrate imaging systems and plan safe, precise radiation treatments for patients (p. 47).

Premier Ropework Skill Priority: Very often, the ability to do a neat job of splicing is placed on the top of the skills list ofropework (p. 11).

Three Fundamental Rope Splices: There are three basic types of splices that are typically made on three-strand twisted rope, an eye splice, a back splice, and a short splice (p. 11).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Approach Splicing with Confidence: Making splices is not really all that hard (p. 11).
Step 2 - Select the Proper Splice: There are three basic types of splices that are typically made on three-strand twisted rope, an eye splice, a back splice, and a short splice (p. 11).
Step 3 - Unlay and Weave Strands: The process in all three splices is tounlay the strands at the end of the rope, then weave them over and under back into the rope to form (p. 11).
Step 4 - Replace Bulky Rope Knots: Knots are more bulky than an eye splice or short splice (p. 11).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When tensioning a pioneering structure with a block-and-tackle or rope tackle under heavy load, why must Scouts never stand inside the bight of a rope or in the line of pull?
quiz_item.question: When tensioning a pioneering structure with a block-and-tackle or rope tackle under heavy load, why must Scouts never stand inside the bight of a rope or in the line of pull?
options: A. Standing on the rope increases friction inside the pulley sheaves and wears out natural manila fibers.
B. Body weight near the anchor stake loosens square lashings on the main A-frame spars.
C. Standing in the bight prevents the signal caller from seeing hand signals from the anchor crew.
D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
choices: A. Standing on the rope increases friction inside the pulley sheaves and wears out natural manila fibers.
B. Body weight near the anchor stake loosens square lashings on the main A-frame spars.
C. Standing in the bight prevents the signal caller from seeing hand signals from the anchor crew.
D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): A rope or anchor under tension stores dangerous kinetic energy; staying clear of the bight (loop) and the direct line of pull prevents getting caught or struck if the line parts or an anchor pulls free.

pamphlet_excerpts: Functional Patrol Table Surface: This small table is functional and provides a convenient raised surface for personal or patrol use (p. 67).
Shear and Crosspiece Lashings: Lash the top of each pair of legs with as hear lashing, and lash on the 2 1/2- to 3-foot cross piece with tight square lashings (p. 67).
Uniform Crosspiece Height Placement: Lash on each cross piece at the same place on each of the legs, about 2 1/2 feet up from the bottom (p. 67).
Angled Anchor Stake Positioning: On each side of the stave, about 5 feet out, hammer in a sturdy stake at a 20-degree angle, with the notch facing (p. 67).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Lash Matching Leg Crosspieces: Lash on each cross piece at the same place on each of the legs, about 2 1/2 feet up from the bottom (p. 67).
Step 2 - Drive Angled Anchor Stakes: On each side of the stave, about 5 feet out, hammer in a sturdy stake at a 20-degree angle, with the notch facing (p. 67).
Step 3 - Tension Guys with Tackle: Attach each end of the 20-foot rope to a stake with a rope tackle, then pull each A-frame upright (p. 67).
Step 4 - Secure A-Frames with Hitches: The clove hitches will hold the A-frames in a tight, stable position (p. 67).

pamphlet_excerpts: Finger Safety During Frapping: When lifting a spar to facilitate the frapping of atripod or shear lashing, always ensure the person working the rope doesn't injure their fingers (p. 9).
Scheduled Crew Alignment Breaks: Take regular breaks to discuss the work in progress and ensure everyone understands what is required of them (p. 9).
Heavy Mallet Handling Caution: Use extra care when using heavy mallets to pound in pioneering stakes (p. 9).
Heeling In Structure Legs: For safety, heel in the legs of a structure by setting them in holes approximately 4 to 6 inches deep (p. 9).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Swing Heavy Mallets Safely: Use extra care when using heavy mallets to pound in pioneering stakes (p. 9).
Step 2 - Dig Four-Inch Footing Holes: For safety, heel in the legs of a structure by setting them in holes approximately 4 to 6 inches deep (p. 9).
Step 3 - Follow Specified Material Strengths: If the design calls for a certain size and type of rope or spar, do not substitute anything of lesser strength (p. 9).
Step 4 - Test Completed Structure Thoroughly: Before allowing general use, run a complete test tosee everything is working correctly (p. 9).

common_misconception_pair.fact: Because a back splice weaves the strands back into the standing part, it thickens the end of the rope, making whipping a better choice when the line must fit through small blocks (p. 52).

pamphlet_excerpts: Unlaying Sufficient Rope Strands: Unlay more than sufficient to make the splice and spread the strands evenly (p. 52).
Temporary Strand End Whipping: With pieces of string or some tape, temporarily whip the ends of each strand (p. 52).
Forming the Crown Knot: Make a crown knot by bending each end over its neighbor in turn, going the same way round as the lay of the rope (p. 52).
Over-and-Under Strand Tucking: Tuck each end in turn over the adjoining main strand and under the next (p. 52).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Tie Initial Crown Knot: Make a crown knot by bending each end over its neighbor in turn, going the same way round as the lay of the rope (p. 52).
Step 2 - Tuck Strands: Tuck each end in turn over the adjoining main strand and under the next (p. 52).
Step 3 - Complete Three Full Tucks: Continue over and under one in turn at least three times (p. 52).
Step 4 - Join Ropes Without Knots: A short splice can be used in place of a knot to join two ropes or the ends of the same rope together (p. 52).

common_misconception_pair.misconception: To make a three-strand rope hold together, you twist the individual strands and the final combined rope in the exact same rotational direction.
common_misconception_pair.fact: Rope stays tightly laid because the three strands are twisted in one direction while the combined strands are laid together in the opposite direction, creating balanced counter-tension (p. 47).

pamphlet_excerpts: Proper Whipping Length Ratio: Make the whipping as long as the diameter of the rope (p. 13).

Alternating Front-and-Back Half Knots: Continue by taking the two ends of the whipping cord around the back of the rope (away from you), and tie another half knot identical to the first (see) (p. 13).
Tight Repeated Half Knots: Keep repeating the half knots, front and back, pulling each one tight, until the whipping has been formed (p. 13).
Square Knot Finishing Trim: The West Country whipping is finished with a square knot and the excess cord is trimmed (p. 13).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Repeat Tight Half Knots: Keep repeating the half knots, front and back, pulling each one tight, until the whipping has been formed (p. 13).
Step 2 - Finish with Square Knot: The West Country whipping is finished with a square knot and the excess cord is trimmed (p. 13).
Step 3 - Align Knots Snugly Together: Tie each half knot either right over left or left over right so that the knots lay neatly together and snug against the previous knot to form a smooth (p. 13).
Step 4 - Protect Rope Ends Early: Sail maker's knew that alittle extra effort spent whipping the ends of the ropes would make their work much easier in the long haul (p. 13).

pamphlet_excerpts: Single-Trestle Dual-Walkway Bridge: This simple bridge uses a single trestle and two walkways (p. 84).
Extended Trestle Handrail Legs: The legs of the trestle are extended above the walkways to provide away to attach handrails (p. 84).
Trestle Leg Spar Dimensions: The legs for the trestle are spars that are about 3 inches in diameter and 8 to 10 feet long (p. 84).
Accounting for Creek Depth: When choosing these spars, take into account the depth of the creek you're crossing (p. 84).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Select Three-Inch Leg Spars: The legs for the trestle are spars that are about 3 inches in diameter and 8 to 10 feet long (p. 84).
Step 2 - Measure Creek Crossing Depth: When choosing these spars, take into account the depth of the creek you're crossing (p. 84).
Step 3 - Set Transom Above Banks: The distance from the base of the legs to the top ledger (transom) on the trestle should be about 1 foot higher than the level of the banks (p. 84).
Step 4 - Join Trestles with Spreaders: It's formed by building two trestles with top handrails, and joining them on each side with three spreaders and a diagonal support (p. 84).

pamphlet_excerpts: Simple Strop Lashing Method: A strop lashing is easy to tie (p. 10).
Midpoint Wraps and Knot: Halve the rope, place the midpoint behind what you'relashing, wrap both ends around the spars a few times and finish with asquare knot (p. 10).
Four Identical A-Frame Subassemblies: Build four identical A-frames using the 8-foot spars for the two legs and 6-foot spars for the ledger (p. 10).
Matching Ledger Height Alignment: Make sure the ledgers of each A-frame cross the legs at the same height and that the tips of the legs intersect at an equal distance from the tops (p. 10).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Assemble Four Matching A-Frames: Build four identical A-frames using the 8-foot spars for the two legs and 6-foot spars for the ledger (p. 10).
Step 2 - Align Ledgers and Tips: Make sure the ledgers of each A-frame cross the legs at the same height and that the tips of the legs intersect at an equal distance from the tops (p. 10).
Step 3 - Tie Three Square Lashings: Lash each A-frame together with three tight square lashings (p. 10).
Step 4 - Join Paired A-Frame Sections: When you have four identical A-frames, lash two of them together (p. 10).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When tensioning a pioneering structure with a block-and-tackle or rope tackle under heavy load, why must Scouts never stand inside the bight of a rope or in the line of pull?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When tensioning a pioneering structure with a block-and-tackle or rope tackle under heavy load, why must Scouts never stand inside the bight of a rope or in the line of pull?
options: A. Standing on the rope increases friction inside the pulley sheaves and wears out natural manila fibers.
B. Body weight near the anchor stake loosens square lashings on the main A-frame spars.
C. Standing in the bight prevents the signal caller from seeing hand signals from the anchor crew.
D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
choices: A. Standing on the rope increases friction inside the pulley sheaves and wears out natural manila fibers.
B. Body weight near the anchor stake loosens square lashings on the main A-frame spars.
C. Standing in the bight prevents the signal caller from seeing hand signals from the anchor crew.
D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. If a strained rope, lashing, or anchor fails or slips, the rope can snap back violently across the bight or recoil along the line of pull, causing severe injury.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): A rope or anchor under tension stores dangerous kinetic energy; staying clear of the bight (loop) and the direct line of pull prevents getting caught or struck if the line parts or an anchor pulls free.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: In a flowering vascular plant, what are the distinct roles of xylem and phloem tissues inside the roots, stems, and leaves?
quiz_item.question: In a flowering vascular plant, what are the distinct roles of xylem and phloem tissues inside the roots, stems, and leaves?
options: A. Xylem produces pollen grains in the anther, while phloem captures sunlight in the epidermis.
B. Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots to the leaves, while phloem distributes sugars produced during photosynthesis throughout the plant.
C. Xylem carries sugars downward from flowers to the soil, while phloem absorbs carbon dioxide through root hairs.
D. Xylem and phloem are reproductive organs located inside the pistil that fertilize ovules.
choices: A. Xylem produces pollen grains in the anther, while phloem captures sunlight in the epidermis.
B. Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots to the leaves, while phloem distributes sugars produced during photosynthesis throughout the plant.
C. Xylem carries sugars downward from flowers to the soil, while phloem absorbs carbon dioxide through root hairs.
D. Xylem and phloem are reproductive organs located inside the pistil that fertilize ovules.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Xylem transports water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots to the leaves, while phloem distributes sugars produced during photosynthesis throughout the plant.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Vascular plants rely on xylem to conduct water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots and phloem to transport photosynthetic sugars (food) to growing tissues and storage organs.

B. They chew through thick seed coats so dormant seeds can sprout in spring
C. They inject chlorophyll into flower petals to start photosynthesis
D. They loosen compacted clay around deep taproots during dry weather
choices: A. They carry pollen from the male anthers to the female pistils so fertilization and seed production can occur
B. They chew through thick seed coats so dormant seeds can sprout in spring
C. They inject chlorophyll into flower petals to start photosynthesis
D. They loosen compacted clay around deep taproots during dry weather
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. They carry pollen from the male anthers to the female pistils so fertilization and seed production can occur
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): As honeybees and other insects forage among blossoms, they transfer pollen grains to the pistil, enabling fertilization and the development of fertile seeds and fruit (p. 21).

pamphlet_excerpts: Fast-Draining Sandy Soil: As a result, water drains away quickly and sandy soils tend to be dry, with a lot of air (p. 22).
Tightly Packed Clay Particles: Clay particles are very small and flat so they pack together very closely, leaving only tiny spaces between them (p. 22).
Pore Space Water Retention: Smaller spaces are good at holding onto water but are so small that there is little air (p. 22).
Moisture and Nutrient Availability: Nutrients often follow water, so sandy soils are not only drier but have fewer nutrients, and clay soils are moister and have more nutrients (p. 22).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Compare Pore Space Sizes: Smaller spaces are good at holding onto water but are so small that there is little air (p. 22).
Step 2 - Assess Soil Nutrient Retention: Nutrients often follow water, so sandy soils are not only drier but have fewer nutrients, and clay soils are moister and have more nutrients (p. 22).
Step 3 - Inspect Clumped Soil Particles: Soil particles tend to cling together to form larger clumps of soil (p. 22).
Step 4 - Identify Peds and Aggregates: These clusters are called peds or aggregates, and the way they group together is the soil structure (p. 22).

pamphlet_excerpts: Sweet Potato Water Setup: Put a fresh sweet potato in a glass jar filled with water (p. 29).
Balancing With Rim Toothpicks: Stick toothpicks in the side of the sweet potato, with the ends of the toothpicks extending over the jar rimto balance the potato, so it is partially (p. 29).
Warm Sunny Window Placement: Set the jar in a warm, sunny spot such as a window ledge (p. 29).
Weekly Fresh Water Changes: Replace the water in the jar once a week, making sure the water level doesn't drop below the bottom of the potato (p. 29).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Place Jar in Sunlight: Set the jar in a warm, sunny spot such as a window ledge (p. 29).
Step 2 - Refresh Water Every Week: Replace the water in the jar once a week, making sure the water level doesn't drop below the bottom of the potato (p. 29).
Step 3 - Observe New Roots and Leaves: In two to three weeks, roots will appear on the submerged portion of the sweet potato, and leaves will sprout above the water line (p. 29).
Step 4 - Maintain Growing Leafy Vines: If you keep filling the jar with water, these leaves will develop into vines that can grow up to several feet long over four to six months (p. 29).

D. After a full year in the dark

pamphlet_excerpts: Costly Crop Weed Competition: Farmers spend billions every year to control the hundreds of weed species that compete with crop plants for nutrients and moisture (p. 47).
Common Field Crop Weeds: Here are a few of the most common weeds that infest field crops (p. 47).
Rapidly Spreading Sowthistle Roots: There are several varieties of sowthistle, all of which have strong roots that spread rapidly (p. 47).
Dandelion-Like Yellow Blossoms: The sow thistle has a bright yellow flower similar to dandelions (p. 47).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Check Spreading Weed Roots: There are several varieties of sowthistle, all of which have strong roots that spread rapidly (p. 47).
Step 2 - Identify Yellow Sowthistle Blooms: The sow thistle has a bright yellow flower similar to dandelions (p. 47).
Step 3 - Spot Four-Petaled Wild Mustard: Wild mustard, also known as charlockmustard, is easily recognized by its four petals that form a cross (p. 47).
Step 4 - Inspect Notched Hairy Leaves: The leaves of wild mustard are lobed, or notched, with small hairs on the underside of the leaves (p. 47).

requirements.lead_text: Choose ONE of the following options and complete each requirement:
requirements.req_text: Choose ONE of the following options and complete each requirement: (a) Option A, Agronomy. Do ALL of the following: (1) Describe how to prepare a seedbed. (2) Make and use a seed germination tester to test 50 seeds of four of the following plants: corn, cotton, alfalfa, soybeans, clover, wheat, rice, rye, or barley. Determine the percentage of live seeds. (3) Explain one important insect pest and one important disease that damage each of the following: corn, small grains, and cotton. Collect and name five weeds that compete with crops in your locality. Tell how to control these weeds without harming people, wildlife, or useful insects. (4) On a map of the United States, identify the chief regions where corn, cotton, forage crops, small grain crops, and oil crops grow. Tell how the climate and location of these regions make them leaders in the production of these crops. (5) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Corn (1) Grow a plot of corn and have your plot inspected by your counselor. Record seed variety or experimental code number. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial corn farming and the contributions that corn makes to today's food and fuel supply. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage corn, and explain how it affects corn production and how it is controlled. (5) (b) Cotton (1) Grow a plot of cotton and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial cotton farming, and about the uses of cotton fiber and seed and the economic value of this crop. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage cotton, and explain how it affects cotton production and how it is controlled. (5) (c) Forage Crops (1) Collect, count, and label samples of each for display: perennial grasses, annual grasses, legumes, and broadleaf weeds. Indicate how each grass and legume is used. Keep a log of the site where you found each sample and share it with your counselor. (2) Explain how legumes can be used to enrich the soil and how they may deplete it under certain conditions. Explain how livestock may enrich or deplete the soil. (3) Name five poisonous plants that are dangerous to livestock, and tell the different ways of using forage crops as feed for livestock. (5) (d) Small Grains (1) Give production figures for small grain crops listed in the U. S. Statistical Report or Agricultural Statistics Handbook for the latest year available. (2) Help in harvesting a crop of grain. Tell how to reduce harvesting losses and about modern methods of growing one small grain crop. (3) Visit a grain elevator, flour mill, cereal plant, feed or seed company. Talk with the operator. Take notes, and describe the processes used and tell your patrol, troop, or class about your visit. (5) (e) Oil Crops (1) Grow a plot of soybeans and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of growing soybeans on a commercial scale, and discuss the contributions soybeans make to our food supply. (3) Explain why a hard frost can be dangerous to soybeans just after emergence. (b) Option B, Horticulture. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit one of the following places and tell what you learned about horticulture there: public garden, arboretum, retail nursery, wholesale nursery, production greenhouse, or conservatory greenhouse. (2) Explain the following terms: hardiness zone, shade tolerance, pH, moisture requirement, native habitat, texture, cultivar, ultimate size, disease resistance, habit, evergreen, deciduous, annual, and perennial. Find out what hardiness zone you live in and list 10 landscape plants you like that are suitable for your climate, giving the common name and scientific name for each. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Explain the difference between vegetative and sexual propagation methods, and tell some horticultural advantages of each. Grow a plant from a stem or root cutting or graft. (b) Transplant 12 seedlings or rooted cuttings to larger containers and grow them for at least one month. (c) Demonstrate good pruning techniques and tell why pruning is important. (d) After obtaining permission, plant a tree or shrub properly in an appropriate site. (4) Do the following: (a) Explain the importance of good landscape design and selection of plants that are suitable for particular sites and conditions. (b) Tell why it is important to know how big a plant will grow. (c) Tell why slower-growing landscape plants are sometimes a better choice than faster-growing varieties. (5) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Bedding Plants (1) Grow bedding plants appropriate for your area in pots or flats from seed or cuttings in a manufactured soil mix. Explain why you chose the mix and tell what is in it. (2) Transplant plants to a bed in the landscape and maintain the bed until the end of the growing season. Record your activities, observations, materials used, and costs. (3) Demonstrate mulching, fertilizing, watering, weeding, and deadheading, and tell how each practice helps your plants. (4) Tell some differences between gardening with annuals and perennials. (5) (b) Fruit, Berry, and Nut Crops (1) Plant five fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants that are suited to your area. Take full care of fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants through one season. (2) Prune a tree, vine, or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) Demonstrate one type of graft and tell why this method is useful. (4) Describe how one fruit, nut, or berry crop is processed for use. (5) (c) Woody Ornamentals (1) Plant five or more trees or shrubs in a landscape setting. Take full care of the trees or shrubs you have planted for one growing season. (2) Prune a tree or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) List 10 trees (in addition to those listed in general requirement 6 above) and tell your counselor how each is used in the landscape. Give the common and scientific names. (4) Describe the size, texture, color, flowers, leaves, fruit, hardiness, cultural requirements, and any special characteristics that make each type of tree or shrub attractive or interesting. (5) Tell five ways trees help improve the quality of our environment. (5) (d) Home Gardening (1) Design and plant a garden or landscape that is at least 10 by 10 feet. (2) Plant 10 or more different types of plants in your garden. Tell why you selected particular varieties of vegetables and flowers. Take care of the plants in your garden for one season. (3) Demonstrate soil preparation, staking, watering, weeding, mulching, composting, fertilizing, pest management, and pruning. Tell why each technique is used. (4) Tell four types of things you could provide to make your home landscape or park a better place for birds and wildlife. List the common and scientific names of 10 kinds of native plants that are beneficial to birds and wildlife in your area. (c) Option C, Field Botany. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit a park, forest, Scout camp, or other natural area near your home. While you are there: (a) Determine which species of plants are the largest and which are the most abundant. Note whether they cast shade on other plants. (b) Using information from maps, textbooks, or the internet, describe the environmental factors that may influence the presence of plants on your site, including latitude, climate, air and soil temperature, soil type and pH, geology, hydrology, and topography. (c) Record any differences in the types of plants you see at the edge of a forest, near water, in burned areas, or near a road or railroad. (2) Select a study site that is at least 100 by 100 feet. Make a list of 10 woody plants (trees and shrubs) and 10 non-woody plants in the study site. Find out which of these are native plants and which are exotic (or non-native). (3) Tell how an identification key works and use a simple key to identify 10 kinds of plants (in addition to those in general requirement 5 above). Tell the difference between common and scientific names and tell why scientific names are important. (4) After gaining permission, collect, identify, press, mount, and label 10 different plants that are common in your area. Tell why voucher specimens are important for documentation of a field botanist's discoveries. (5) Obtain a list of rare plants of your state. Tell what is being done to protect rare plants and natural areas in your state. Write a paragraph about one of the rare plants in your state. (6) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (a) Tree Inventory (1) Identify the trees of your neighborhood, a park, a section of your town, or a Scout camp. (2) Collect, press, and label leaves, flowers, or fruits to document your inventory. (3) List the types of trees by scientific name and give common names. Note the number and size (diameter at 4½ feet above ground) of trees observed and determine the largest of each species in your study area. (4) Show two or more people how to use a leaf or twig key to identify at least five species of trees or shrubs. (b) Transect Study (1) Visit two sites, at least one of which is different from the one you visited for Field Botany requirement 1. (2) Use the transect method to study the two different kinds of plant communities. The transects should be at least 500 feet long. (3) At each site, record observations about the soil and other influencing factors AND do the following. Then make a graph or chart to show the results of your studies. (a) Identify each tree within 10 feet of the transect line. (b) Measure the diameter of each tree at 4½ feet above the ground, and map and list each tree. (c) Nested Plot (1) Visit two sites, at least one of which is different from the one you visited for Field Botany requirement 1. (2) Mark off nested plots and inventory two different kinds of plant communities. (3) At each site, record observations about the soil and other influencing factors AND do the following. Then make a graph or chart to show the results of your studies. (a) Identify, measure, and map each tree in a 100-by-100-foot plot. (Measure the diameter of each tree larger than 3 inches in diameter at 4½ feet above the ground.) (b) Identify and count all trees and shrubs in a 10-by-10-foot plot within each of the larger areas. (c) Identify and count all broad-leaved plants (trees, shrubs, vines, and herbaceous plants) and all plants (wildflowers, ferns, grasses, mosses, etc.) of a 4-by-4-foot plot within the 10-by-10-foot plot. Note: If individual plants like ferns, grasses, and mosses cannot be clearly distinguished, make a reasonable estimate of area (square inches of cover) for each species and record that as an estimate within the 4 x 4 subplot. (d) Herbarium Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit an herbarium at a university, park, or botanical garden; OR, visit an herbarium website (with your parent or guardian's permission). (2) Tell how the specimens are arranged and how they are used by researchers. If possible, observe voucher specimens of a plant that is rare in your state. (3) Tell how a voucher specimen is mounted and prepared for permanent storage. Tell how specimens should be handled so that they will not be damaged. (4) Tell about the tools and references used by botanists in an herbarium. (e) Plant Conservation Organization Visit (1) Write ahead and arrange to visit a private conservation organization or government agency that is concerned with protecting rare plants and natural areas. (2) Tell about the activities of the organization in studying and protecting rare plants and natural areas. (3) If possible, visit a nature preserve managed by the organization. Tell about land management practices such as controlled burning, or measures to eradicate invasive (non-native) plants or other threats to the plants that are native to the area.

children.sub_req_text: Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Corn (1) Grow a plot of corn and have your plot inspected by your counselor. Record seed variety or experimental code number. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial corn farming and the contributions that corn makes to today's food and fuel supply. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage corn, and explain how it affects corn production and how it is controlled. (5) (b) Cotton (1) Grow a plot of cotton and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial cotton farming, and about the uses of cotton fiber and seed and the economic value of this crop. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage cotton, and explain how it affects cotton production and how it is controlled. (5) (c) Forage Crops (1) Collect, count, and label samples of each for display: perennial grasses, annual grasses, legumes, and broadleaf weeds. Indicate how each grass and legume is used. Keep a log of the site where you found each sample and share it with your counselor. (2) Explain how legumes can be used to enrich the soil and how they may deplete it under certain conditions. Explain how livestock may enrich or deplete the soil. (3) Name five poisonous plants that are dangerous to livestock, and tell the different ways of using forage crops as feed for livestock. (5) (d) Small Grains (1) Give production figures for small grain crops listed in the U. S. Statistical Report or Agricultural Statistics Handbook for the latest year available. (2) Help in harvesting a crop of grain. Tell how to reduce harvesting losses and about modern methods of growing one small grain crop. (3) Visit a grain elevator, flour mill, cereal plant, feed or seed company. Talk with the operator. Take notes, and describe the processes used and tell your patrol, troop, or class about your visit. (5) (e) Oil Crops (1) Grow a plot of soybeans and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of growing soybeans on a commercial scale, and discuss the contributions soybeans make to our food supply. (3) Explain why a hard frost can be dangerous to soybeans just after emergence.

Determine the percentage of live seeds. (3) Explain one important insect pest and one important disease that damage each of the following: corn, small grains, and cotton. Collect and name five weeds that compete with crops in your locality. Tell how to control these weeds without harming people, wildlife, or useful insects. (4) On a map of the United States, identify the chief regions where corn, cotton, forage crops, small grain crops, and oil crops grow. Tell how the climate and location of these regions make them leaders in the production of these crops. (5) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Corn (1) Grow a plot of corn and have your plot inspected by your counselor. Record seed variety or experimental code number. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial corn farming and the contributions that corn makes to today's food and fuel supply. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage corn, and explain how it affects corn production and how it is controlled. (5) (b) Cotton (1) Grow a plot of cotton and have your plot inspected by your counselor. (2) Tell about modern methods of commercial cotton farming, and about the uses of cotton fiber and seed and the economic value of this crop. (3) Tell about an insect that can damage cotton, and explain how it affects cotton production and how it is controlled. sub_requirements.text: Option B, Horticulture. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit one of the following places and tell what you learned about horticulture there: public garden, arboretum, retail nursery, wholesale nursery, production greenhouse, or conservatory greenhouse. (2) Explain the following terms: hardiness zone, shade tolerance, pH, moisture requirement, native habitat, texture, cultivar, ultimate size, disease resistance, habit, evergreen, deciduous, annual, and perennial. Find out what hardiness zone you live in and list 10 landscape plants you like that are suitable for your climate, giving the common name and scientific name for each. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Explain the difference between vegetative and sexual propagation methods, and tell some horticultural advantages of each. Grow a plant from a stem or root cutting or graft. (b) Transplant 12 seedlings or rooted cuttings to larger containers and grow them for at least one month. (c) Demonstrate good pruning techniques and tell why pruning is important. (d) After obtaining permission, plant a tree or shrub properly in an appropriate site. (4) Do the following: (a) Explain the importance of good landscape design and selection of plants that are suitable for particular sites and conditions. (b) Tell why it is important to know how big a plant will grow. (c) Tell why slower-growing landscape plants are sometimes a better choice than faster-growing varieties. (5) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Bedding Plants (1) Grow bedding plants appropriate for your area in pots or flats from seed or cuttings in a manufactured soil mix. Explain why you chose the mix and tell what is in it. (2) Transplant plants to a bed in the landscape and maintain the bed until the end of the growing season. Record your activities, observations, materials used, and costs. (3) Demonstrate mulching, fertilizing, watering, weeding, and deadheading, and tell how each practice helps your plants. (4) Tell some differences between gardening with annuals and perennials. (5) (b) Fruit, Berry, and Nut Crops (1) Plant five fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants that are suited to your area. Take full care of fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants through one season. (2) Prune a tree, vine, or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) Demonstrate one type of graft and tell why this method is useful. (4) Describe how one fruit, nut, or berry crop is processed for use. (5) (c) Woody Ornamentals (1) Plant five or more trees or shrubs in a landscape setting. Take full care of the trees or shrubs you have planted for one growing season. (2) Prune a tree or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) List 10 trees (in addition to those listed in general requirement 6 above) and tell your counselor how each is used in the landscape. Give the common and scientific names. (4) Describe the size, texture, color, flowers, leaves, fruit, hardiness, cultural requirements, and any special characteristics that make each type of tree or shrub attractive or interesting. (5) Tell five ways trees help improve the quality of our environment. (5) (d) Home Gardening (1) Design and plant a garden or landscape that is at least 10 by 10 feet. (2) Plant 10 or more different types of plants in your garden. Tell why you selected particular varieties of vegetables and flowers. Take care of the plants in your garden for one season. (3) Demonstrate soil preparation, staking, watering, weeding, mulching, composting, fertilizing, pest management, and pruning. Tell why each technique is used. (4) Tell four types of things you could provide to make your home landscape or park a better place for birds and wildlife. List the common and scientific names of 10 kinds of native plants that are beneficial to birds and wildlife in your area.

children.text: Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Bedding Plants (1) Grow bedding plants appropriate for your area in pots or flats from seed or cuttings in a manufactured soil mix. Explain why you chose the mix and tell what is in it. (2) Transplant plants to a bed in the landscape and maintain the bed until the end of the growing season. Record your activities, observations, materials used, and costs. (3) Demonstrate mulching, fertilizing, watering, weeding, and deadheading, and tell how each practice helps your plants. (4) Tell some differences between gardening with annuals and perennials. (5) (b) Fruit, Berry, and Nut Crops (1) Plant five fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants that are suited to your area. Take full care of fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants through one season. (2) Prune a tree, vine, or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) Demonstrate one type of graft and tell why this method is useful. (4) Describe how one fruit, nut, or berry crop is processed for use. (5) (c) Woody Ornamentals (1) Plant five or more trees or shrubs in a landscape setting. Take full care of the trees or shrubs you have planted for one growing season. (2) Prune a tree or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) List 10 trees (in addition to those listed in general requirement 6 above) and tell your counselor how each is used in the landscape. Give the common and scientific names. (4) Describe the size, texture, color, flowers, leaves, fruit, hardiness, cultural requirements, and any special characteristics that make each type of tree or shrub attractive or interesting. (5) Tell five ways trees help improve the quality of our environment. (5) (d) Home Gardening (1) Design and plant a garden or landscape that is at least 10 by 10 feet. (2) Plant 10 or more different types of plants in your garden. Tell why you selected particular varieties of vegetables and flowers. Take care of the plants in your garden for one season. children.sub_req_text: Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Bedding Plants (1) Grow bedding plants appropriate for your area in pots or flats from seed or cuttings in a manufactured soil mix. Explain why you chose the mix and tell what is in it. (2) Transplant plants to a bed in the landscape and maintain the bed until the end of the growing season. Record your activities, observations, materials used, and costs. (3) Demonstrate mulching, fertilizing, watering, weeding, and deadheading, and tell how each practice helps your plants. (4) Tell some differences between gardening with annuals and perennials. (5) (b) Fruit, Berry, and Nut Crops (1) Plant five fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants that are suited to your area. Take full care of fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants through one season. (2) Prune a tree, vine, or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) Demonstrate one type of graft and tell why this method is useful. (4) Describe how one fruit, nut, or berry crop is processed for use. (2) Prune a tree or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) List 10 trees (in addition to those listed in general requirement 6 above) and tell your counselor how each is used in the landscape. Give the common and scientific names. (4) Describe the size, texture, color, flowers, leaves, fruit, hardiness, cultural requirements, and any special characteristics that make each type of tree or shrub attractive or interesting. (5) Tell five ways trees help improve the quality of our environment. (5) (d) Home Gardening (1) Design and plant a garden or landscape that is at least 10 by 10 feet. (2) Plant 10 or more different types of plants in your garden. Tell why you selected particular varieties of vegetables and flowers. Take care of the plants in your garden for one season. (3) Demonstrate soil preparation, staking, watering, weeding, mulching, composting, fertilizing, pest management, and pruning. Tell why each technique is used. sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Horticulture. Do ALL of the following: (1) Visit one of the following places and tell what you learned about horticulture there: public garden, arboretum, retail nursery, wholesale nursery, production greenhouse, or conservatory greenhouse. (2) Explain the following terms: hardiness zone, shade tolerance, pH, moisture requirement, native habitat, texture, cultivar, ultimate size, disease resistance, habit, evergreen, deciduous, annual, and perennial. Find out what hardiness zone you live in and list 10 landscape plants you like that are suitable for your climate, giving the common name and scientific name for each. (3) Do ONE of the following: (a) Explain the difference between vegetative and sexual propagation methods, and tell some horticultural advantages of each. Grow a plant from a stem or root cutting or graft. (b) Transplant 12 seedlings or rooted cuttings to larger containers and grow them for at least one month. (c) Demonstrate good pruning techniques and tell why pruning is important. (d) After obtaining permission, plant a tree or shrub properly in an appropriate site. (4) Do the following: (a) Explain the importance of good landscape design and selection of plants that are suitable for particular sites and conditions. (b) Tell why it is important to know how big a plant will grow. (c) Tell why slower-growing landscape plants are sometimes a better choice than faster-growing varieties. (5) Do ALL of the requirements in ONE of the following alternatives: (5) (a) Bedding Plants (1) Grow bedding plants appropriate for your area in pots or flats from seed or cuttings in a manufactured soil mix. Explain why you chose the mix and tell what is in it. (2) Transplant plants to a bed in the landscape and maintain the bed until the end of the growing season. Record your activities, observations, materials used, and costs. (3) Demonstrate mulching, fertilizing, watering, weeding, and deadheading, and tell how each practice helps your plants. (4) Tell some differences between gardening with annuals and perennials. (5) (b) Fruit, Berry, and Nut Crops (1) Plant five fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants that are suited to your area. Take full care of fruit or nut trees, grapevines, or berry plants through one season. (2) Prune a tree, vine, or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) Demonstrate one type of graft and tell why this method is useful. (4) Describe how one fruit, nut, or berry crop is processed for use. (5) (c) Woody Ornamentals (1) Plant five or more trees or shrubs in a landscape setting. Take full care of the trees or shrubs you have planted for one growing season. (2) Prune a tree or shrub properly. Explain why pruning is necessary. (3) List 10 trees (in addition to those listed in general requirement 6 above) and tell your counselor how each is used in the landscape. Give the common and scientific names. (4) Describe the size, texture, color, flowers, leaves, fruit, hardiness, cultural requirements, and any special characteristics that make each type of tree or shrub attractive or interesting. (5) Tell five ways trees help improve the quality of our environment. (5) (d) Home Gardening (1) Design and plant a garden or landscape that is at least 10 by 10 feet. (2) Plant 10 or more different types of plants in your garden. Tell why you selected particular varieties of vegetables and flowers. Take care of the plants in your garden for one season. (3) Demonstrate soil preparation, staking, watering, weeding, mulching, composting, fertilizing, pest management, and pruning. Tell why each technique is used. (4) Tell four types of things you could provide to make your home landscape or park a better place for birds and wildlife. List the common and scientific names of 10 kinds of native plants that are beneficial to birds and wildlife in your area.
