quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When hand sewing a flat button onto a shirt or jacket, why do tailors place a toothpick or pin across the top of the button while stitching?
quiz_item.question: When hand sewing a flat button onto a shirt or jacket, why do tailors place a toothpick or pin across the top of the button while stitching?
options: A. To keep the needle from dulling against the plastic rim of the button
B. To create slack for wrapping a thread shank underneath the button
C. To measure the exact distance between the buttonholes on the placket
D. To lock the quilter's knot on the front side of the garment
choices: A. To keep the needle from dulling against the plastic rim of the button
B. To create slack for wrapping a thread shank underneath the button
C. To measure the exact distance between the buttonholes on the placket
D. To lock the quilter's knot on the front side of the garment
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. To create slack for wrapping a thread shank underneath the button
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Stitching over a pin or toothpick creates controlled slack that you wrap with thread beneath the button to form a sturdy shank, giving the buttonhole fabric space to sit flat when buttoned (p. 13).

requirements.description: Hand Sewing. Do the following: (a) Assemble a basic sewing and repair kit and explain the purpose of each item. (b) Thread a needle and tie a quilter's or tailor's knot in a piece of fabric. (c) Demonstrate the following sewing techniques, including when and why each is used: (1) Running stitch (2) Back stitch (3) Hem stitch (4) Whip stitch. (d) Sew a patch on your uniform or other fabric. (e) Sew a button onto an item. (f) Upcycle by practicing visible mending to patch a piece of clothing or material.

requirements.lead_text: Choose ONE of the following options and complete each requirement:
requirements.req_text: Choose ONE of the following options and complete each requirement: (A) Machine Sewing (a) Provide a brief overview of the evolution of the sewing machine (b) Read your machine manual and do the following: (1) Explain the parts of a sewing machine and their functions. (2) Thread the machine and the bobbin. (3) Explain how to properly clean and oil the machine and change the needle. (c) Identify other tools you will need for machine sewing. Demonstrate the following sewing techniques, including when and why each is used: (1) Pinning (2) Sewing in a straight line (3) Back stitch (4) Basting stitch (5) Gathering stitch (6) Unpicking or seam ripping. (d) Do the following using a sewing machine: (1) Sew a Scout patch on your uniform or other fabric. (2) Repair a tear or small hole in fabric using a patch or darning technique. (e) Sew ONE item from this list using a pattern, using THREE or more techniques from requirement 3(c): (1) Drawstring backpack (2) Camp utensil holder (3) Storage bag for tent stakes or school supplies (4) Pillowcase (5) An item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor. (B) Knitting (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of knitting. (b) Explain the tools used when knitting. Demonstrate the ability to read a pattern, including deciphering symbols. (c) Using knitting needles, demonstrate how to tie a slip knot, cast on and bind off. (d) Demonstrate the following stitches: (1) Knit stitch (2) Purl stitch. (e) Knit a small item such as a dishcloth, scarf, or an item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor, using ONE of the following stitch patterns with at least two colors of yarn: (1) Garter stitch (2) Stockinette stitch (3) Ribbing. (C) Crochet (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of crochet OR the history of Amigurumi. (b) Explain the tools used when crocheting. Demonstrate the ability to read a pattern, including deciphering symbols. (c) Demonstrate how to tie a slip knot and how to hold a crochet hook and yarn to crochet. (d) Demonstrate the following stitches in a small practice piece: (1) Single crochet (2) Double crochet (3) Half-double crochet. (e) Crochet a small item such as a dishcloth, scrub, or an item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor, using at least two colors of yarn. (D) Hand Embroidery (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of hand embroidery. (b) Explain the tools used in hand embroidery. (c) Embroider a small sampler of your own design or from a purchased kit or embroider a temporary patch for your uniform. Include SIX of the following basic stitches: running stitch, back stitch, stem stitch, chain stitch, surface couching, blanket stitch, herringbone stitch, chevron stitch, feather stitch, weave stitch, seed stitch, French knots, fishbone stitch, satin stitch, cross stitch. (E) Appliqué (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of hand appliqué. (b) In a small sample, demonstrate how to do appliqué by hand using the following methods: needle turn or freezer paper using an invisible (ladder) stitch or blanket stitch. (c) (c) In a small sample, demonstrate machine appliqué using a raw edge fusible technique and a blanket stitch. (d) Appliqué a design onto a T-shirt by hand or machine or reverse appliqué a shape by hand sewing. (F) Quilting (a) Research historical quilts and show your counselor examples of types of quilts that interest you. Discuss how they were made. (b) Explain the tools used when quilting and how to use them safely. Discuss why accuracy is important in traditional quilting. Sew an accurate ¼" seam. (c) Using scraps of cotton quilting fabric, sort into light, medium and dark colors. Choose a focus fabric and find a group of fabrics that would work well in a scrap quilt. Demonstrate how the value and scale of a printed fabric can create interest. (d) Using three copies of a quilting design, color blocks to achieve different quilt designs. Show your counselor your designs and which one is your favorite. (e) Make a small quilt (12" square plus borders): (1) Using a rotary cutter, cut fabric into strips and pieces to make a four patch, rail fence block pattern, or design of your choice. Sew together on a machine or by hand using a ¼" seam allowance and press flat. Cut and add borders. (2) Make a sandwich with backing and batting. Baste. (3) Hand quilt with a running stitch or big stitch. (4) Label your quilt. Explain why this is important. (5) Bind to finish the edge of the quilt.

quiz_item.correct_answer: C. The feed dogs beneath the needle plate and the presser foot above

requirements.description: Choose ONE of the following options and complete each requirement: (A) Machine Sewing (a) Provide a brief overview of the evolution of the sewing machine (b) Read your machine manual and do the following: (1) Explain the parts of a sewing machine and their functions. (2) Thread the machine and the bobbin. (3) Explain how to properly clean and oil the machine and change the needle. (c) Identify other tools you will need for machine sewing. Demonstrate the following sewing techniques, including when and why each is used: (1) Pinning (2) Sewing in a straight line (3) Back stitch (4) Basting stitch (5) Gathering stitch (6) Unpicking or seam ripping. (d) Do the following using a sewing machine: (1) Sew a Scout patch on your uniform or other fabric. (2) Repair a tear or small hole in fabric using a patch or darning technique. (e) Sew ONE item from this list using a pattern, using THREE or more techniques from requirement 3(c): (1) Drawstring backpack (2) Camp utensil holder (3) Storage bag for tent stakes or school supplies (4) Pillowcase (5) An item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor. (B) Knitting (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of knitting. (b) Explain the tools used when knitting. Demonstrate the ability to read a pattern, including deciphering symbols. (c) Using knitting needles, demonstrate how to tie a slip knot, cast on and bind off. (d) Demonstrate the following stitches: (1) Knit stitch (2) Purl stitch. (e) Knit a small item such as a dishcloth, scarf, or an item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor, using ONE of the following stitch patterns with at least two colors of yarn: (1) Garter stitch (2) Stockinette stitch (3) Ribbing. (C) Crochet (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of crochet OR the history of Amigurumi. (b) Explain the tools used when crocheting. Demonstrate the ability to read a pattern, including deciphering symbols. (c) Demonstrate how to tie a slip knot and how to hold a crochet hook and yarn to crochet. (d) Demonstrate the following stitches in a small practice piece: (1) Single crochet (2) Double crochet (3) Half-double crochet. (e) Crochet a small item such as a dishcloth, scrub, or an item of your own choosing, approved in advance by your counselor, using at least two colors of yarn. (D) Hand Embroidery (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of hand embroidery. (b) Explain the tools used in hand embroidery. (c) Embroider a small sampler of your own design or from a purchased kit or embroider a temporary patch for your uniform. Include SIX of the following basic stitches: running stitch, back stitch, stem stitch, chain stitch, surface couching, blanket stitch, herringbone stitch, chevron stitch, feather stitch, weave stitch, seed stitch, French knots, fishbone stitch, satin stitch, cross stitch. (E) Appliqué (a) Provide a brief overview of the history of hand appliqué. (b) In a small sample, demonstrate how to do appliqué by hand using the following methods: needle turn or freezer paper using an invisible (ladder) stitch or blanket stitch. (c) (c) In a small sample, demonstrate machine appliqué using a raw edge fusible technique and a blanket stitch. (d) Appliqué a design onto a T-shirt by hand or machine or reverse appliqué a shape by hand sewing. (F) Quilting (a) Research historical quilts and show your counselor examples of types of quilts that interest you. Discuss how they were made. (b) Explain the tools used when quilting and how to use them safely. Discuss why accuracy is important in traditional quilting. Sew an accurate ¼" seam. (c) Using scraps of cotton quilting fabric, sort into light, medium and dark colors. Choose a focus fabric and find a group of fabrics that would work well in a scrap quilt. Demonstrate how the value and scale of a printed fabric can create interest. (d) Using three copies of a quilting design, color blocks to achieve different quilt designs. Show your counselor your designs and which one is your favorite. (e) Make a small quilt (12" square plus borders): (1) Using a rotary cutter, cut fabric into strips and pieces to make a four patch, rail fence block pattern, or design of your choice. Sew together on a machine or by hand using a ¼" seam allowance and press flat. Cut and add borders. (2) Make a sandwich with backing and batting. Baste. (3) Hand quilt with a running stitch or big stitch. (4) Label your quilt. Explain why this is important. (5) Bind to finish the edge of the quilt.

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When examining a traditional quilt at a textile exhibition, what are the three distinct layers held together by the quilting stitches?
quiz_item.question: When examining a traditional quilt at a textile exhibition, what are the three distinct layers held together by the quilting stitches?
options: A. The warp threads, the weft threads, and the selvedge edge
B. The paper pattern, the fusible interfacing, and the outer canvas lining
C. The embroidery hoop, the monk's cloth foundation, and the yarn fringe
D. The decorative pieced top, the insulating middle batting, and the fabric backing
choices: A. The warp threads, the weft threads, and the selvedge edge
B. The paper pattern, the fusible interfacing, and the outer canvas lining
C. The embroidery hoop, the monk's cloth foundation, and the yarn fringe
D. The decorative pieced top, the insulating middle batting, and the fabric backing
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. The decorative pieced top, the insulating middle batting, and the fabric backing
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): A quilt sandwich consists of three layers: the decorative top (often pieced or appliqued), the warm inner batting, and the bottom backing fabric, all joined by hand or machine quilting stitches (p. 23).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: While sewing a heavy canvas Merit Badge sash repair on a sewing machine, the needle hits a thick seam and snaps. What is the mandatory safety and machine procedure before replacing the needle?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: While sewing a heavy canvas Merit Badge sash repair on a sewing machine, the needle hits a thick seam and snaps. What is the mandatory safety and machine procedure before replacing the needle?
options: A. Keep your foot on the presser-foot speed controller while reaching into the needle bar.

B. Turn off and unplug the sewing machine first, locate all broken needle fragments so none remain in the fabric, and insert a fresh heavy-duty needle with the flat shank side facing the correct direction.
C. Leave the broken needle tip inside the canvas and sew over it.
D. Hold the replacement needle between your lips while loosening the needle clamp screw with power on.
choices: A. Keep your foot on the presser-foot speed controller while reaching into the needle bar.

B. Turn off and unplug the sewing machine first, locate all broken needle fragments so none remain in the fabric, and insert a fresh heavy-duty needle with the flat shank side facing the correct direction.
C. Leave the broken needle tip inside the canvas and sew over it.
D. Hold the replacement needle between your lips while loosening the needle clamp screw with power on.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Turn off and unplug the sewing machine first, locate all broken needle fragments so none remain in the fabric, and insert a fresh heavy-duty needle with the flat shank side facing the correct direction.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Turning off power prevents accidental foot-pedal activation while fingers are near the needle bar, and recovering broken needle tips prevents puncture injuries.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When hand sewing a flat button onto a shirt or jacket, why do tailors place a toothpick or pin across the top of the button while stitching?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When hand sewing a flat button onto a shirt or jacket, why do tailors place a toothpick or pin across the top of the button while stitching?
options: A. To keep the needle from dulling against the plastic rim of the button
B. To create slack for wrapping a thread shank underneath the button
C. To measure the exact distance between the buttonholes on the placket
D. To lock the quilter's knot on the front side of the garment
choices: A. To keep the needle from dulling against the plastic rim of the button
B. To create slack for wrapping a thread shank underneath the button
C. To measure the exact distance between the buttonholes on the placket
D. To lock the quilter's knot on the front side of the garment
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. To create slack for wrapping a thread shank underneath the button
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Stitching over a pin or toothpick creates controlled slack that you wrap with thread beneath the button to form a sturdy shank, giving the buttonhole fabric space to sit flat when buttoned (p. 13).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which pair of sewing machine components works together to move the fabric forward by one stitch length after each needle penetration?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which pair of sewing machine components works together to move the fabric forward by one stitch length after each needle penetration?
options: A. The bobbin winder spindle and the upper thread spool pin
B. The tension dial and the thread take-up lever
C. The feed dogs beneath the needle plate and the presser foot above
D. The flywheel clutch and the reverse stitch button
choices: A. The bobbin winder spindle and the upper thread spool pin
B. The tension dial and the thread take-up lever
C. The feed dogs beneath the needle plate and the presser foot above
D. The flywheel clutch and the reverse stitch button
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. The feed dogs beneath the needle plate and the presser foot above
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): The toothed feed dogs rise through slots in the throat plate to grip the underside of the fabric against the downward pressure of the presser foot, advancing the material evenly between stitches (p. 16).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When examining a traditional quilt at a textile exhibition, what are the three distinct layers held together by the quilting stitches?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When examining a traditional quilt at a textile exhibition, what are the three distinct layers held together by the quilting stitches?
options: A. The warp threads, the weft threads, and the selvedge edge
B. The paper pattern, the fusible interfacing, and the outer canvas lining
C. The embroidery hoop, the monk's cloth foundation, and the yarn fringe
D. The decorative pieced top, the insulating middle batting, and the fabric backing
choices: A. The warp threads, the weft threads, and the selvedge edge
B. The paper pattern, the fusible interfacing, and the outer canvas lining
C. The embroidery hoop, the monk's cloth foundation, and the yarn fringe
D. The decorative pieced top, the insulating middle batting, and the fabric backing
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. The decorative pieced top, the insulating middle batting, and the fabric backing
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): A quilt sandwich consists of three layers: the decorative top (often pieced or appliqued), the warm inner batting, and the bottom backing fabric, all joined by hand or machine quilting stitches (p. 23).

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): Charitable organizations and hospitals publish specific construction guidelines covering washable fibers, exact dimensions, and fragrance-free handling to protect recipients (p. 29).

requirements.req_text: Do the following: (a) Explain what a projectile is, and why any device that shoots a projectile at high speed must be handled with care and respect, and used only in approved locations. (b) Explain the basic rules of safe gun handling that apply to all firearms. (c) Describe how you would react if a friend visiting your home asked to see your or your family's firearm. (d) Explain the need for, types, and use of eye protection and hearing protection. (e) Explain the main points of the laws for owning and using guns in your community and state. (f) Explain how hunting is related to the wise use of renewable wildlife resources. (g) Successfully complete a state hunter education course, or obtain a copy of the hunting laws for your state, then do the following: (1) Explain the main points of hunting laws in your state, and any special laws on the use of guns and ammunition, AND (2) List the kinds of wildlife that can be legally hunted in your state. (h) Explain to your counselor the proper hygienic guidelines followed while shooting. (i) List and explain three shotgun sports. Identify places in your community where you could practice these sports, and explain how you can join or be a part of range and target activities. (j) Discuss with your counselor a list of sources you could contact for information on firearms and their use.

pamphlet_excerpts: Universal Shooting Sportsmanship Standards: Sportsmanship applies to all of shooting, whether recreational, competitive, or hunting (p. 57).
Preventing Litter and Destruction: Do not litter the area with trash. Be careful of the target, both for safety and also to avoid senseless destruction (p. 57).
Protecting Public Utility Property: Do not shoot power line insulators, pipeline valves, signs, or similar property (p. 57).
Ethical Field Hunting Courtesy: Confine your shots to proper targets. When hunting in the field, give fellow hunters a fair chance at game (p. 57).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Never Shoot Public Property: Do not shoot power line insulators, pipeline valves, signs, or similar property (p. 57).

Step 3 - Practice Fair Range Courtesy: Do not take unfair advantage of another shooter in any way (p. 57).
Step 4 - Value Ethical Outdoor Stewardship: The accomplishment of taking game during the hunt is only part of the experience (p. 57).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Before loading a 12-gauge shotgun on the range, why must you check the barrel for obstructions and verify that no smaller 20-gauge shell is mixed into your ammunition pouch?
quiz_item.question: Before loading a 12-gauge shotgun on the range, why must you check the barrel for obstructions and verify that no smaller 20-gauge shell is mixed into your ammunition pouch?
options: A. A 20-gauge shell has a wider brass rim that refuses to enter a 12-gauge receiver.
B. Mixing gauges causes the clay target thrower to release targets at the wrong angle.
C. A 20-gauge shell contains black powder that corrodes modern smokeless-powder chokes.
D. A 20-gauge shell dropped into a 12-gauge chamber will slide partway down the barrel and lodge out of sight; if a 12-gauge shell is then loaded and fired behind it, the barrel will burst.
choices: A. A 20-gauge shell has a wider brass rim that refuses to enter a 12-gauge receiver.
B. Mixing gauges causes the clay target thrower to release targets at the wrong angle.
C. A 20-gauge shell contains black powder that corrodes modern smokeless-powder chokes.
D. A 20-gauge shell dropped into a 12-gauge chamber will slide partway down the barrel and lodge out of sight; if a 12-gauge shell is then loaded and fired behind it, the barrel will burst.
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. A 20-gauge shell dropped into a 12-gauge chamber will slide partway down the barrel and lodge out of sight; if a 12-gauge shell is then loaded and fired behind it, the barrel will burst.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): A 20-gauge shell is narrow enough to slip past a 12-gauge chamber and lodge in the forcing cone, creating a catastrophic '12/20 burst' obstruction if a 12-gauge shell is chambered and fired behind it.

requirements.description: Do the following: (a) Explain what a projectile is, and why any device that shoots a projectile at high speed must be handled with care and respect, and used only in approved locations. (b) Explain the basic rules of safe gun handling that apply to all firearms. (c) Describe how you would react if a friend visiting your home asked to see your or your family's firearm. (d) Explain the need for, types, and use of eye protection and hearing protection. (e) Explain the main points of the laws for owning and using guns in your community and state. (f) Explain how hunting is related to the wise use of renewable wildlife resources. (g) Successfully complete a state hunter education course, or obtain a copy of the hunting laws for your state, then do the following: (1) Explain the main points of hunting laws in your state, and any special laws on the use of guns and ammunition, AND (2) List the kinds of wildlife that can be legally hunted in your state. (h) Explain to your counselor the proper hygienic guidelines followed while shooting. (i) List and explain three shotgun sports. Identify places in your community where you could practice these sports, and explain how you can join or be a part of range and target activities. (j) Discuss with your counselor a list of sources you could contact for information on firearms and their use.

requirements.lead_text: Working under the supervision of a certified National Rifle Association (NRA) Shotgun instructor and a certified range safety officer, at a nationally authorized camp property or at a commercial firearm range (as defined in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual ), do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Working under the supervision of a certified National Rifle Association (NRA) Shotgun instructor and a certified range safety officer, at a nationally authorized camp property or at a commercial firearm range (as defined in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual ), do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Shotgun Shooting (Modern Shotshell Type). Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify and explain the principal parts of a shotgun, action types, and how they function. (2) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a shotgun. (3) Identify the parts of a shotgun shell and their functions. (4) Identify the various gauges of shotguns. Explain which you would choose for a particular use and why. (5) Identify the causes of a shotgun's failure to fire, and explain what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are. Explain and demonstrate proper preventive measures, and the procedures to follow in response to each. (6) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot a shotgun on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (7) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning a shotgun, and identify the materials needed. (8) Demonstrate how to clean a shotgun properly and safely. (9) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a shotgun. (10) Shoot a moving target with a shotgun using the four fundamentals of firing a shot, position, mount, vision, and movement. Shooting score required: Hit at least 12 out of 25 targets (48%) in two 25-target groups. The two groups need not be shot in consecutive order. A minimum of 50 shots must be fired. Shooting skill rules: Targets may be thrown by a hand trap, manual mechanical trap, or on any trap or skeet field. If using a hand trap or manual mechanical trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the right and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. If throwing left-handed with a hand trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the left and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. All targets should be thrown at a reasonable speed and in the same direction. Targets should be generally thrown so as to climb in the air after leaving the trap. Scores may be fired at any time, either in formal competition or in practice, but only under approved supervision and at an approved range as noted in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual. Modern, age-appropriate, target shotgun models, 12-, 16-, or 20-gauge, may be used. Only commercially manufactured ammunition may be used. Reloads may not be used in Scouting America range and target activities. Shooters must shoot in rounds of 25. Rounds need not be shot continuously or on the same day. The term "round" refers to a single series of 25 shots. If using a trap field, shoot station 3 with traps set to throw straightaway targets. If using a skeet field, shoot station 7 low house. (b) Option B, Muzzleloading Shotgun Shooting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Discuss with your counselor a brief history of the development of the muzzleloading shotgun. (2) Identify principal parts of muzzleloading shotguns and discuss how they function. (3) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a muzzleloading shotgun. (4) Identify the various grades of black powder and explain their proper and safe use. (5) Discuss proper safety procedures pertaining to black powder storage. (6) Discuss proper components of a load. (7) Identify proper procedures and accessories used for safely loading a muzzleloading shotgun. (8) Identify the causes of a muzzleloading shotgun's failure to fire, and explain what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are. Explain and demonstrate proper preventive measures, and the procedures to follow in response to each. (9) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot a muzzleloading shotgun on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (10) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning a muzzleloading shotgun, and identify the materials needed. (11) Demonstrate how to clean a muzzleloading shotgun properly and safely. (12) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a muzzleloading shotgun. (13) Shoot a moving target with a muzzleloading shotgun using the four fundamentals of firing a shot, position, mount, vision, and movement. Shooting score required: Hit at least 5 out of 15 targets in each of two 15-target groups. The two groups need not be shot in consecutive order. A minimum of 30 shots must be fired. Shooting skill rules: Targets may be thrown by a hand trap, manual mechanical trap, or on any trap or skeet field. If using a hand trap or manual mechanical trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the right and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. If throwing left-handed with a hand trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the left and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. All targets should be thrown at a reasonable speed and in the same direction. Targets should be generally thrown so as to climb in the air after leaving the trap. Scores may be fired at any time, either in formal competition or in practice, but only under approved supervision and at an approved range as noted in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual. A 10 gauge or smaller muzzleloading rifle in appropriate size for the participant may be used. Matchlock, wheellock, or flintlock firearms are not approved. Standard clay targets customarily used for trap and skeet are to be used. On a standard trap field, the shooter should be positioned 8 yards behind the trap house. The trap should be set to throw only straightaway targets. If using a skeet field, shoot station 7 low house.

children.text: Shoot a moving target with a shotgun using the four fundamentals of firing a shot, position, mount, vision, and movement. Shooting score required: Hit at least 12 out of 25 targets (48%) in two 25-target groups. The two groups need not be shot in consecutive order. A minimum of 50 shots must be fired. Shooting skill rules: Targets may be thrown by a hand trap, manual mechanical trap, or on any trap or skeet field. If using a hand trap or manual mechanical trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the right and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. If throwing left-handed with a hand trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the left and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. All targets should be thrown at a reasonable speed and in the same direction. Targets should be generally thrown so as to climb in the air after leaving the trap. Scores may be fired at any time, either in formal competition or in practice, but only under approved supervision and at an approved range as noted in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual. Modern, age-appropriate, target shotgun models, 12-, 16-, or 20-gauge, may be used. Only commercially manufactured ammunition may be used. Reloads may not be used in Scouting America range and target activities. Shooters must shoot in rounds of 25. Rounds need not be shot continuously or on the same day. The term "round" refers to a single series of 25 shots. If using a trap field, shoot station 3 with traps set to throw straightaway targets. If using a skeet field, shoot station 7 low house.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Shotgun Shooting (Modern Shotshell Type). Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify and explain the principal parts of a shotgun, action types, and how they function. (2) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a shotgun. (3) Identify the parts of a shotgun shell and their functions. (4) Identify the various gauges of shotguns. Explain which you would choose for a particular use and why. (5) Identify the causes of a shotgun's failure to fire, and explain what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are. Explain and demonstrate proper preventive measures, and the procedures to follow in response to each. (6) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot a shotgun on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (7) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning a shotgun, and identify the materials needed. (8) Demonstrate how to clean a shotgun properly and safely. (9) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a shotgun. (10) Shoot a moving target with a shotgun using the four fundamentals of firing a shot, position, mount, vision, and movement. Shooting score required: Hit at least 12 out of 25 targets (48%) in two 25-target groups. The two groups need not be shot in consecutive order. A minimum of 50 shots must be fired. Shooting skill rules: Targets may be thrown by a hand trap, manual mechanical trap, or on any trap or skeet field. If using a hand trap or manual mechanical trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the right and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. If throwing left-handed with a hand trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the left and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. All targets should be thrown at a reasonable speed and in the same direction. Targets should be generally thrown so as to climb in the air after leaving the trap. Scores may be fired at any time, either in formal competition or in practice, but only under approved supervision and at an approved range as noted in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual. Modern, age-appropriate, target shotgun models, 12-, 16-, or 20-gauge, may be used. Only commercially manufactured ammunition may be used. Reloads may not be used in Scouting America range and target activities. Shooters must shoot in rounds of 25. Rounds need not be shot continuously or on the same day. The term "round" refers to a single series of 25 shots. If using a trap field, shoot station 3 with traps set to throw straightaway targets. If using a skeet field, shoot station 7 low house.

sub_requirements.label: (b)
sub_requirements.text: Option B, Muzzleloading Shotgun Shooting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Discuss with your counselor a brief history of the development of the muzzleloading shotgun. (2) Identify principal parts of muzzleloading shotguns and discuss how they function. (3) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a muzzleloading shotgun. (4) Identify the various grades of black powder and explain their proper and safe use. (5) Discuss proper safety procedures pertaining to black powder storage. (6) Discuss proper components of a load. (7) Identify proper procedures and accessories used for safely loading a muzzleloading shotgun. (8) Identify the causes of a muzzleloading shotgun's failure to fire, and explain what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are. Explain and demonstrate proper preventive measures, and the procedures to follow in response to each. (9) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot a muzzleloading shotgun on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (10) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning a muzzleloading shotgun, and identify the materials needed. (11) Demonstrate how to clean a muzzleloading shotgun properly and safely. (12) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a muzzleloading shotgun. (13) Shoot a moving target with a muzzleloading shotgun using the four fundamentals of firing a shot, position, mount, vision, and movement. Shooting score required: Hit at least 5 out of 15 targets in each of two 15-target groups. The two groups need not be shot in consecutive order. A minimum of 30 shots must be fired. Shooting skill rules: Targets may be thrown by a hand trap, manual mechanical trap, or on any trap or skeet field. If using a hand trap or manual mechanical trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the right and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. If throwing left-handed with a hand trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the left and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. All targets should be thrown at a reasonable speed and in the same direction. Targets should be generally thrown so as to climb in the air after leaving the trap. Scores may be fired at any time, either in formal competition or in practice, but only under approved supervision and at an approved range as noted in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual. A 10 gauge or smaller muzzleloading rifle in appropriate size for the participant may be used. Matchlock, wheellock, or flintlock firearms are not approved. Standard clay targets customarily used for trap and skeet are to be used. On a standard trap field, the shooter should be positioned 8 yards behind the trap house. The trap should be set to throw only straightaway targets. If using a skeet field, shoot station 7 low house.

children.text: Shoot a moving target with a muzzleloading shotgun using the four fundamentals of firing a shot, position, mount, vision, and movement. Shooting score required: Hit at least 5 out of 15 targets in each of two 15-target groups. The two groups need not be shot in consecutive order. A minimum of 30 shots must be fired. Shooting skill rules: Targets may be thrown by a hand trap, manual mechanical trap, or on any trap or skeet field. If using a hand trap or manual mechanical trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the right and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. If throwing left-handed with a hand trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the left and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. All targets should be thrown at a reasonable speed and in the same direction. Targets should be generally thrown so as to climb in the air after leaving the trap. Scores may be fired at any time, either in formal competition or in practice, but only under approved supervision and at an approved range as noted in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual. A 10 gauge or smaller muzzleloading rifle in appropriate size for the participant may be used. Matchlock, wheellock, or flintlock firearms are not approved. Standard clay targets customarily used for trap and skeet are to be used. On a standard trap field, the shooter should be positioned 8 yards behind the trap house. The trap should be set to throw only straightaway targets. If using a skeet field, shoot station 7 low house.

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option B, Muzzleloading Shotgun Shooting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Discuss with your counselor a brief history of the development of the muzzleloading shotgun. (2) Identify principal parts of muzzleloading shotguns and discuss how they function. (3) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a muzzleloading shotgun. (4) Identify the various grades of black powder and explain their proper and safe use. (5) Discuss proper safety procedures pertaining to black powder storage. (6) Discuss proper components of a load. (7) Identify proper procedures and accessories used for safely loading a muzzleloading shotgun. (8) Identify the causes of a muzzleloading shotgun's failure to fire, and explain what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are. Explain and demonstrate proper preventive measures, and the procedures to follow in response to each. (12) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a muzzleloading shotgun. pamphlet_excerpts: Counting Standard Skeet Rounds: If you've been counting, you have noticed that this accounts for only 24 shots (p. 47).
Twenty-Fifth Option Shot Rule: In skeet, the remaining shot is either a repeat of the shooter's first missed target or, if all 24 targets have been broken, a repeat of the last shot (p. 47).
Approved Skeet Shotgun Gauges: Skeet may be shot with any gauge shotgun, 12 gauge or smaller, capable of firing two shots in quick succession (p. 47).
Close-Range Chokes and Shot: Since it is a close-range sport, guns with skeet or improved cylinder chokes using No. 8 or No. 9 shot are preferred (p. 47).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Select Approved Shotgun Gauge: Skeet may be shot with any gauge shotgun, 12 gauge or smaller, capable of firing two shots in quick succession (p. 47).
Step 2 - Pair Choke With Shot: Since it is a close-range sport, guns with skeet or improved cylinder chokes using No. 8 or No. 9 shot are preferred (p. 47).
Step 3 - Follow Standard Skeet Rules: Formal competitive skeet shooting events are held throughout the United States under the direction of the National Skeet Shooting Association (p. 47).
Step 4 - Match Bore To Event: Most formal competitions have separate events for the 12 gauge, 20 gauge, 28 gauge, and .410 bore shotguns (p. 47).

requirements.description: Working under the supervision of a certified National Rifle Association (NRA) Shotgun instructor and a certified range safety officer, at a nationally authorized camp property or at a commercial firearm range (as defined in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual ), do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Shotgun Shooting (Modern Shotshell Type). Do ALL of the following: (1) Identify and explain the principal parts of a shotgun, action types, and how they function. (2) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a shotgun. (3) Identify the parts of a shotgun shell and their functions. (4) Identify the various gauges of shotguns. Explain which you would choose for a particular use and why. (5) Identify the causes of a shotgun's failure to fire, and explain what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are. Explain and demonstrate proper preventive measures, and the procedures to follow in response to each. (6) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot a shotgun on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (7) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning a shotgun, and identify the materials needed. (8) Demonstrate how to clean a shotgun properly and safely. (9) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a shotgun. (10) Shoot a moving target with a shotgun using the four fundamentals of firing a shot, position, mount, vision, and movement. Shooting score required: Hit at least 12 out of 25 targets (48%) in two 25-target groups. The two groups need not be shot in consecutive order. A minimum of 50 shots must be fired. Shooting skill rules: Targets may be thrown by a hand trap, manual mechanical trap, or on any trap or skeet field. If using a hand trap or manual mechanical trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the right and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. If throwing left-handed with a hand trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the left and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. All targets should be thrown at a reasonable speed and in the same direction. Targets should be generally thrown so as to climb in the air after leaving the trap. Scores may be fired at any time, either in formal competition or in practice, but only under approved supervision and at an approved range as noted in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual. Modern, age-appropriate, target shotgun models, 12-, 16-, or 20-gauge, may be used. Only commercially manufactured ammunition may be used. Reloads may not be used in Scouting America range and target activities. Shooters must shoot in rounds of 25. Rounds need not be shot continuously or on the same day. The term "round" refers to a single series of 25 shots. If using a trap field, shoot station 3 with traps set to throw straightaway targets. If using a skeet field, shoot station 7 low house. (b) Option B, Muzzleloading Shotgun Shooting. Do ALL of the following: (1) Discuss with your counselor a brief history of the development of the muzzleloading shotgun. (2) Identify principal parts of muzzleloading shotguns and discuss how they function. (3) Identify and demonstrate the rules for safely storing and handling a muzzleloading shotgun. (4) Identify the various grades of black powder and explain their proper and safe use. (5) Discuss proper safety procedures pertaining to black powder storage. (6) Discuss proper components of a load. (7) Identify proper procedures and accessories used for safely loading a muzzleloading shotgun. (8) Identify the causes of a muzzleloading shotgun's failure to fire, and explain what a misfire, hangfire, and squib fire are. Explain and demonstrate proper preventive measures, and the procedures to follow in response to each. (9) Demonstrate the knowledge, skills, and attitude necessary to safely shoot a muzzleloading shotgun on a range, including understanding and following range procedures and commands. (10) Explain the basic safety rules for cleaning a muzzleloading shotgun, and identify the materials needed. (11) Demonstrate how to clean a muzzleloading shotgun properly and safely. (12) Discuss what points you would consider in selecting a muzzleloading shotgun. (13) Shoot a moving target with a muzzleloading shotgun using the four fundamentals of firing a shot, position, mount, vision, and movement. Shooting score required: Hit at least 5 out of 15 targets in each of two 15-target groups. The two groups need not be shot in consecutive order. A minimum of 30 shots must be fired. Shooting skill rules: Targets may be thrown by a hand trap, manual mechanical trap, or on any trap or skeet field. If using a hand trap or manual mechanical trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the right and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. If throwing left-handed with a hand trap, the trap operator should be at least 5 feet to the left and 3 feet to the rear of the shooter. All targets should be thrown at a reasonable speed and in the same direction. Targets should be generally thrown so as to climb in the air after leaving the trap. Scores may be fired at any time, either in formal competition or in practice, but only under approved supervision and at an approved range as noted in the Scouting America National Range and Target Activities Manual. A 10 gauge or smaller muzzleloading rifle in appropriate size for the participant may be used. Matchlock, wheellock, or flintlock firearms are not approved. Standard clay targets customarily used for trap and skeet are to be used. On a standard trap field, the shooter should be positioned 8 yards behind the trap house. The trap should be set to throw only straightaway targets. If using a skeet field, shoot station 7 low house.

patrol_quiz_bank.question: Before loading a 12-gauge shotgun on the range, why must you check the barrel for obstructions and verify that no smaller 20-gauge shell is mixed into your ammunition pouch?
options: A. A 20-gauge shell has a wider brass rim that refuses to enter a 12-gauge receiver.
B. Mixing gauges causes the clay target thrower to release targets at the wrong angle.
C. A 20-gauge shell contains black powder that corrodes modern smokeless-powder chokes.
D. A 20-gauge shell dropped into a 12-gauge chamber will slide partway down the barrel and lodge out of sight; if a 12-gauge shell is then loaded and fired behind it, the barrel will burst.
choices: A. A 20-gauge shell has a wider brass rim that refuses to enter a 12-gauge receiver.

patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. A 20-gauge shell dropped into a 12-gauge chamber will slide partway down the barrel and lodge out of sight; if a 12-gauge shell is then loaded and fired behind it, the barrel will burst.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): A 20-gauge shell is narrow enough to slip past a 12-gauge chamber and lodge in the forcing cone, creating a catastrophic '12/20 burst' obstruction if a 12-gauge shell is chambered and fired behind it.

quiz_item.question: What is the universal international distress call in Morse code, and what pattern of audible or visual signals is recognized worldwide as an emergency call for help?
options: A. Four short flashes followed by two long whistle blasts, repeated once every hour.
B. SOS in Morse code (three dots, three dashes, three dots), or three of any signal such as three whistle blasts, three signal fires, or three flashes of light.
C. A single continuous horn blast lasting ten seconds or waving a green flag overhead.
D. Two short whistle blasts repeated every thirty seconds, which means all clear in wilderness navigation.
choices: A. Four short flashes followed by two long whistle blasts, repeated once every hour.
B. SOS in Morse code (three dots, three dashes, three dots), or three of any signal such as three whistle blasts, three signal fires, or three flashes of light.
C. A single continuous horn blast lasting ten seconds or waving a green flag overhead.
D. Two short whistle blasts repeated every thirty seconds, which means all clear in wilderness navigation.
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. SOS in Morse code (three dots, three dashes, three dots), or three of any signal such as three whistle blasts, three signal fires, or three flashes of light.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Three of anything (three whistle blasts, three fires or smoke columns, three light flashes) and Morse code SOS (three dots, three dashes, three dots) are universally recognized emergency distress signals.

common_misconception_pair.fact: The universal distress signal consists of three repeats of any sound, light flash, or visual marker, such as three whistle blasts, three signal fires, or three flashes of a mirror (p. 8).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: When constructing a large ground-to-air distress symbol in an open clearing, what does a giant letter "V" communicate to search aircraft?
quiz_item.question: When constructing a large ground-to-air distress symbol in an open clearing, what does a giant letter "V" communicate to search aircraft?
options: A. The party has found safe shelter and requires no assistance
B. The group is moving north toward the nearest paved road
C. The survivors on the ground require general search-and-rescue assistance
D. A helicopter can safely land directly on top of the marked spot
choices: A. The party has found safe shelter and requires no assistance
B. The group is moving north toward the nearest paved road
C. The survivors on the ground require general search-and-rescue assistance
D. A helicopter can safely land directly on top of the marked spot
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. The survivors on the ground require general search-and-rescue assistance
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): In international ground-to-air emergency signaling, a large V constructed on open ground means "Require assistance," while an X means "Require medical assistance" (p. 8).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How is a dash timed relative to a dot when transmitting a clear message in international Morse code?
quiz_item.question: How is a dash timed relative to a dot when transmitting a clear message in international Morse code?
options: A. Three times the duration of a single dot, with three-dot pauses between letters
B. Twice the duration of a single dot, with no pause needed between individual letters
C. Five times the duration of a single dot, sent only over electrical telegraph wires
D. Equal in length to a dot, distinguished only by using a higher audio pitch
choices: A. Three times the duration of a single dot, with three-dot pauses between letters
B. Twice the duration of a single dot, with no pause needed between individual letters
C. Five times the duration of a single dot, sent only over electrical telegraph wires
D. Equal in length to a dot, distinguished only by using a higher audio pitch
quiz_item.correct_answer: A. Three times the duration of a single dot, with three-dot pauses between letters
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In international Morse code timing, a dash is three times as long as a dot, the pause between letters is three dot-lengths, and the pause between words is seven dot-lengths (p. 6).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Because semaphore uses the same arm angles for the letters A through J as it does for the digits 1 through 0, how does a sender indicate that numbers are being transmitted?
quiz_item.question: Because semaphore uses the same arm angles for the letters A through J as it does for the digits 1 through 0, how does a sender indicate that numbers are being transmitted?
options: A. Switch from red-and-yellow flags to blue-and-white flags before signaling numbers
B. Wave both flags in a continuous figure-eight above the head during each digit
C. Kneel on one knee so the receiver knows the clock positions represent digits
D. Send the dedicated "numerals" position first, then send the "letters" signal when returning to text
choices: A. Switch from red-and-yellow flags to blue-and-white flags before signaling numbers
B. Wave both flags in a continuous figure-eight above the head during each digit
C. Kneel on one knee so the receiver knows the clock positions represent digits
D. Send the dedicated "numerals" position first, then send the "letters" signal when returning to text
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Send the dedicated "numerals" position first, then send the "letters" signal when returning to text
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): In semaphore, letters and numbers share the same arm angles, so the sender must flash the "numerals" signal before sending digits and the "letters" (or "J") signal to return to text (p. 8).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: How does standard six-dot Braille distinguish a capital letter from a lowercase letter?
quiz_item.question: How does standard six-dot Braille distinguish a capital letter from a lowercase letter?
options: A. By embossing the raised dots twice as large as standard lowercase dots
B. By placing a special capital-indicator cell (dot 6) immediately before the letter
C. By inverting the six-dot cell upside down for every uppercase character
D. By using an eight-dot cell for capitals and a four-dot cell for lowercase letters
choices: A. By embossing the raised dots twice as large as standard lowercase dots
B. By placing a special capital-indicator cell (dot 6) immediately before the letter
C. By inverting the six-dot cell upside down for every uppercase character
D. By using an eight-dot cell for capitals and a four-dot cell for lowercase letters
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. By placing a special capital-indicator cell (dot 6) immediately before the letter
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): In Braille, capital letters use the same cell patterns as lowercase letters but are preceded by a special cell with a single dot in position 6 (the capital indicator) (p. 6).

quiz_item.question: When directing a heavy-equipment or crane operator, what does extending both arms horizontally with palms down and moving them rapidly back and forth mean?
options: A. Raise the load slowly while swinging the boom to the operator's left
B. Lower the boom while holding the load height constant
C. Shut down the engine and secure the cab for the end of the shift
D. Execute an immediate Emergency Stop of all equipment movement
choices: A. Raise the load slowly while swinging the boom to the operator's left
B. Lower the boom while holding the load height constant
C. Shut down the engine and secure the cab for the end of the shift
D. Execute an immediate Emergency Stop of all equipment movement
quiz_item.correct_answer: D. Execute an immediate Emergency Stop of all equipment movement
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (D): In standard heavy-equipment and crane hand signaling, extending both arms horizontally with palms down and moving them back and forth signals an immediate "Emergency Stop" (p. 9).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: On a standard topographical map, what do symbols and lines printed in brown ink represent?
quiz_item.question: On a standard topographical map, what do symbols and lines printed in brown ink represent?
options: A. Unpaved backcountry dirt roads and seasonal four-wheel-drive tracks
B. Contour lines and relief features showing terrain elevation and shape
C. Dense woodland canopy, national forest boundaries, and scrub brush
D. Intermittent desert streams, dry washes, and seasonal marshlands
choices: A. Unpaved backcountry dirt roads and seasonal four-wheel-drive tracks
B. Contour lines and relief features showing terrain elevation and shape
C. Dense woodland canopy, national forest boundaries, and scrub brush
D. Intermittent desert streams, dry washes, and seasonal marshlands
quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Contour lines and relief features showing terrain elevation and shape
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): On standard U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) topographical maps, brown is used for contour lines representing terrain elevation and relief features, while blue represents water and green represents vegetation (p. 9).

common_misconception_pair.misconception: A substitution cipher where every letter of the alphabet is replaced by a unique random symbol is impossible to crack without the key.
common_misconception_pair.fact: Simple monoalphabetic substitution ciphers preserve the underlying letter frequencies of the language, allowing crypt analysts to crack them easily by counting how often letters like E, T, A, and O appear (p. 7).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: Which of the following is an example of a transposition cipher rather than a substitution cipher?
quiz_item.question: Which of the following is an example of a transposition cipher rather than a substitution cipher?
options: A. Replacing every letter in the message with the letter three places ahead in the alphabet
B. Swapping each letter for a tic-tac-toe grid shape containing a dot in the Pigpen cipher
C. Writing the message in rows inside a grid and reading the letters out column by column
D. Looking up whole words in a two-part codebook and replacing each word with a five-digit number
choices: A. Replacing every letter in the message with the letter three places ahead in the alphabet
B. Swapping each letter for a tic-tac-toe grid shape containing a dot in the Pigpen cipher
C. Writing the message in rows inside a grid and reading the letters out column by column
D. Looking up whole words in a two-part codebook and replacing each word with a five-digit number
quiz_item.correct_answer: C. Writing the message in rows inside a grid and reading the letters out column by column
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A transposition cipher (such as a rail fence or columnar cipher) keeps the original plain text letters intact but scrambles their positions according to a geometric pattern or key (p. 7).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: What is the universal international distress call in Morse code, and what pattern of audible or visual signals is recognized worldwide as an emergency call for help?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: What is the universal international distress call in Morse code, and what pattern of audible or visual signals is recognized worldwide as an emergency call for help?
options: A. Four short flashes followed by two long whistle blasts, repeated once every hour.
B. SOS in Morse code (three dots, three dashes, three dots), or three of any signal such as three whistle blasts, three signal fires, or three flashes of light.
C. A single continuous horn blast lasting ten seconds or waving a green flag overhead.
D. Two short whistle blasts repeated every thirty seconds, which means all clear in wilderness navigation.
choices: A. Four short flashes followed by two long whistle blasts, repeated once every hour.
B. SOS in Morse code (three dots, three dashes, three dots), or three of any signal such as three whistle blasts, three signal fires, or three flashes of light.
C. A single continuous horn blast lasting ten seconds or waving a green flag overhead.
D. Two short whistle blasts repeated every thirty seconds, which means all clear in wilderness navigation.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. SOS in Morse code (three dots, three dashes, three dots), or three of any signal such as three whistle blasts, three signal fires, or three flashes of light.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Three of anything (three whistle blasts, three fires or smoke columns, three light flashes) and Morse code SOS (three dots, three dashes, three dots) are universally recognized emergency distress signals.

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When constructing a large ground-to-air distress symbol in an open clearing, what does a giant letter "V" communicate to search aircraft?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When constructing a large ground-to-air distress symbol in an open clearing, what does a giant letter "V" communicate to search aircraft?
options: A. The party has found safe shelter and requires no assistance
B. The group is moving north toward the nearest paved road
C. The survivors on the ground require general search-and-rescue assistance
D. A helicopter can safely land directly on top of the marked spot
choices: A. The party has found safe shelter and requires no assistance
B. The group is moving north toward the nearest paved road
C. The survivors on the ground require general search-and-rescue assistance
D. A helicopter can safely land directly on top of the marked spot
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. The survivors on the ground require general search-and-rescue assistance
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): In international ground-to-air emergency signaling, a large V constructed on open ground means "Require assistance," while an X means "Require medical assistance" (p. 8).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How is a dash timed relative to a dot when transmitting a clear message in international Morse code?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How is a dash timed relative to a dot when transmitting a clear message in international Morse code?
options: A. Three times the duration of a single dot, with three-dot pauses between letters
B. Twice the duration of a single dot, with no pause needed between individual letters
C. Five times the duration of a single dot, sent only over electrical telegraph wires
D. Equal in length to a dot, distinguished only by using a higher audio pitch
choices: A. Three times the duration of a single dot, with three-dot pauses between letters
B. Twice the duration of a single dot, with no pause needed between individual letters
C. Five times the duration of a single dot, sent only over electrical telegraph wires
D. Equal in length to a dot, distinguished only by using a higher audio pitch
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Three times the duration of a single dot, with three-dot pauses between letters
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In international Morse code timing, a dash is three times as long as a dot, the pause between letters is three dot-lengths, and the pause between words is seven dot-lengths (p. 6).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Because semaphore uses the same arm angles for the letters A through J as it does for the digits 1 through 0, how does a sender indicate that numbers are being transmitted?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Because semaphore uses the same arm angles for the letters A through J as it does for the digits 1 through 0, how does a sender indicate that numbers are being transmitted?
options: A. Switch from red-and-yellow flags to blue-and-white flags before signaling numbers
B. Wave both flags in a continuous figure-eight above the head during each digit
C. Kneel on one knee so the receiver knows the clock positions represent digits
D. Send the dedicated "numerals" position first, then send the "letters" signal when returning to text
choices: A. Switch from red-and-yellow flags to blue-and-white flags before signaling numbers
B. Wave both flags in a continuous figure-eight above the head during each digit
C. Kneel on one knee so the receiver knows the clock positions represent digits
D. Send the dedicated "numerals" position first, then send the "letters" signal when returning to text
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Send the dedicated "numerals" position first, then send the "letters" signal when returning to text
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): In semaphore, letters and numbers share the same arm angles, so the sender must flash the "numerals" signal before sending digits and the "letters" (or "J") signal to return to text (p. 8).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: How does standard six-dot Braille distinguish a capital letter from a lowercase letter?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: How does standard six-dot Braille distinguish a capital letter from a lowercase letter?
options: A. By embossing the raised dots twice as large as standard lowercase dots
B. By placing a special capital-indicator cell (dot 6) immediately before the letter
C. By inverting the six-dot cell upside down for every uppercase character
D. By using an eight-dot cell for capitals and a four-dot cell for lowercase letters
choices: A. By embossing the raised dots twice as large as standard lowercase dots
B. By placing a special capital-indicator cell (dot 6) immediately before the letter
C. By inverting the six-dot cell upside down for every uppercase character
D. By using an eight-dot cell for capitals and a four-dot cell for lowercase letters
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. By placing a special capital-indicator cell (dot 6) immediately before the letter
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): In Braille, capital letters use the same cell patterns as lowercase letters but are preceded by a special cell with a single dot in position 6 (the capital indicator) (p. 6).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When a troop leader raises the silent Scout sign during an assembly or hike, what action should Scouts take?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When a troop leader raises the silent Scout sign during an assembly or hike, what action should Scouts take?
options: A. Form two parallel lines for an immediate equipment inspection
B. Scatter immediately to take cover from approaching severe weather
C. Come to quiet attention and listen to the leader speaking
D. Double-time jog toward the leader to form a tight semicircle
choices: A. Form two parallel lines for an immediate equipment inspection
B. Scatter immediately to take cover from approaching severe weather
C. Come to quiet attention and listen to the leader speaking
D. Double-time jog toward the leader to form a tight semicircle
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: C. Come to quiet attention and listen to the leader speaking
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): Raising the Scout sign silently alerts the troop or patrol to come to attention and stop talking, following the principle that the signal is passed along visually without shouting (p. 7).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: Which traditional woodcraft trail sign is used to warn following hikers of "Danger" or "Caution ahead"?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: Which traditional woodcraft trail sign is used to warn following hikers of "Danger" or "Caution ahead"?
options: A. Three rocks stacked vertically or three clumps of grass tied together
B. A single small pebble balanced on top of a larger base rock with a side stone on the right
C. Two twigs crossed in an X shape directly across the center of the footpath
D. A forked stick driven upright into the dirt with a longer stick resting in the fork
choices: A. Three rocks stacked vertically or three clumps of grass tied together
B. A single small pebble balanced on top of a larger base rock with a side stone on the right
C. Two twigs crossed in an X shape directly across the center of the footpath
D. A forked stick driven upright into the dirt with a longer stick resting in the fork
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: A. Three rocks stacked vertically or three clumps of grass tied together
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (A): In traditional woodcraft trail signs, three rocks stacked on top of one another or three tufts of grass tied together warn hikers of danger or important caution ahead (p. 7).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: When directing a heavy-equipment or crane operator, what does extending both arms horizontally with palms down and moving them rapidly back and forth mean?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: When directing a heavy-equipment or crane operator, what does extending both arms horizontally with palms down and moving them rapidly back and forth mean?
options: A. Raise the load slowly while swinging the boom to the operator's left
B. Lower the boom while holding the load height constant
C. Shut down the engine and secure the cab for the end of the shift
D. Execute an immediate Emergency Stop of all equipment movement
choices: A. Raise the load slowly while swinging the boom to the operator's left
B. Lower the boom while holding the load height constant
C. Shut down the engine and secure the cab for the end of the shift
D. Execute an immediate Emergency Stop of all equipment movement
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Execute an immediate Emergency Stop of all equipment movement
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): In standard heavy-equipment and crane hand signaling, extending both arms horizontally with palms down and moving them back and forth signals an immediate "Emergency Stop" (p. 9).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: On a standard topographical map, what do symbols and lines printed in brown ink represent?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: On a standard topographical map, what do symbols and lines printed in brown ink represent?

B. Contour lines and relief features showing terrain elevation and shape
C. Dense woodland canopy, national forest boundaries, and scrub brush
D. Intermittent desert streams, dry washes, and seasonal marshlands

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): On standard U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) topographical maps, brown is used for contour lines representing terrain elevation and relief features, while blue represents water and green represents vegetation (p. 9).

pamphlet_excerpts: Common Foot Friction Blisters: In skating, blisters are most likely to occur on the feet (p. 89).
Early Hot Spot Detection: Skaters should be attentive to any tenderness or sensitive areas ("hot spots") that indicate the start of a blister (p. 89).
Boot Lacing and Sock Adjustments: You may be able to adjust lacing or socks to avoid friction on the sensitive area (p. 89).
Recognizing Physical Fatigue Limits: Listen to your body and quit for the day (p. 89).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Adjust Laces and Socks: You may be able to adjust lacing or socks to avoid friction on the sensitive area (p. 89).
Step 2 - Stop Skating When Fatigued: Listen to your body and quit for the day (p. 89).
Step 3 - Apply Preventive Protective Tape: If you have no choice but to continue the activity, follow preventive steps such as taping and the use of commercial skin tougheners (p. 89).
Step 4 - Monitor and Treat for Shock: When a person is injured or under great stress, the circulatory system may fail to provide enough blood to all parts of the body (p. 89).

quiz_item.scenario_prompt: While skating on an outdoor winter pond, a skater breaks through thin ice into frigid water 30 feet from shore. How should your patrol respond safely?
quiz_item.question: While skating on an outdoor winter pond, a skater breaks through thin ice into frigid water 30 feet from shore. How should your patrol respond safely?
options: A. Skate out to the edge of the ice hole in a group to pull the skater up by both hands.

B. Stay off the thin ice, call for emergency help, lie flat near shore to spread weight, and extend a long reach/throw aid (branch, hockey stick, or rope) while coaching the skater to kick horizontally onto firm ice and roll away from the hole.
C. Instruct the skater to remove their skates and winter jacket in the water before trying to climb out.
D. Have one Scout walk upright to the rim of the broken ice hole carrying a heavy wooden bench.

quiz_item.correct_answer: B. Stay off the thin ice, call for emergency help, lie flat near shore to spread weight, and extend a long reach/throw aid (branch, hockey stick, or rope) while coaching the skater to kick horizontally onto firm ice and roll away from the hole.
quiz_item.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Walking or skating up to an ice breakthrough hole causes the ice edge to collapse under rescuers; follow Reach-Throw protocol and keep clothing/skates on for buoyancy and traction.

requirements.description: Do the following: (a) Explain to your counselor the most likely hazards associated with skating and what you should do to anticipate, help prevent, mitigate, and respond to these hazards. (b) Show that you know first aid for injuries or illnesses that could occur while skating, including hypothermia, frostbite, lacerations, abrasions, fractures, sprains and strains, concussions, blisters, heat-related reactions, and shock.

requirements.lead_text: Working under the supervision of an experienced adult, do ONE of the following options:
requirements.req_text: Working under the supervision of an experienced adult, do ONE of the following options: (a) Option A, Ice Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety and courtesy guidelines for ice skating. (2) Discuss preparations that must be taken when skating outdoors on natural ice. Explain how to make an ice rescue. (3) Discuss the parts and functions of the different types of ice skates. (4) Describe the proper way to carry ice skates at the rink and for travel. (5) Describe how to store ice skates for long periods of time, such as seasonal storage. (6) Skate forward at least 40 feet and come to a complete stop. Use either a two-foot snowplow stop or a one-foot snowplow stop. (7) After skating forward, glide forward on two feet, then on one foot, first right and then left. (8) Starting from a T position, stroke forward around the test area, avoiding the use of toe picks if wearing figure skates. (9) Glide backward on two feet for at least two times the skater's height. (10) Skate backward for at least 20 feet on two skates. (11) After gaining forward speed, glide forward on two feet, making a turn of 180 degrees around a cone, first to the right and then to the left. (12) Perform forward crossovers in a figure-eight pattern. (13) Explain to your counselor the safety considerations for participating in an ice-skating race. (14) Perform a hockey stop. (b) Option B, Roller Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and etiquette guidelines for roller skating. (2) Discuss the parts of a roller skate and their functions. (3) Describe five essential steps to good roller skate care. (4) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet in both directions around the rink and demonstrate proper techniques for stopping. (5) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (6) Perform a forward crossover. (7) Skate backward for at least 40 feet on two skates, then for at least 15 feet on one skate. (8) Skate forward in a slalom pattern for at least 40 feet on two skates, then for at least 20 feet on one skate. (9) Skate backward in a slalom pattern for at least 15 feet on two skates. (10) Shuttle skate once around the rink, bending twice along the way, without stopping. (11) Perform a series of two consecutive spins on skates, OR hop, skip, and jump on skates for at least 10 feet. (12) Perform a stepover. (13) While skating, dribble a basketball at least 40 feet, then back to your starting position, OR push a hockey ball with a stick at least 40 feet, then back to your starting position. (c) Option C, In-Line Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety rules and courtesy guidelines for in-line skating. (2) Describe the parts of an in-line skate and their functions. (3) Describe the required and recommended safety equipment for in-line skating. (4) Explain four essential steps to good in-line skate care. (5) Skate forward with smooth, linked strokes on two feet for at least 100 feet. (6) Skate forward and glide at least 15 feet on one skate, then on the other skate. (7) Stop on command on flat pavement using the heel brake. (8) Perform a forward crossover. (9) Perform a series of forward, linked swizzles for at least 40 feet. (10) Skate backward for at least 40 feet in a series of linked, backward swizzles. (11) From a strong pace, perform a lunge turn around an object predetermined by your counselor. (12) Perform a mohawk. (13) Perform a series of at least four one-footed downhill slaloms on pavement with a gentle slope. (14) Describe how to pass a pedestrian or another skater from behind. (15) Describe at least three ways to avoid an unforeseen obstacle while skating. (16) Describe two ways to get on and off a curb, and demonstrate at least one of these methods. (d) Option D, Skateboarding. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the history and evolution of skateboarding. (2) Describe the benefits of skateboarding (physical fitness, balance, coordination, perseverance, and creativity). (3) Explain the safety rules and courtesy guidelines for skateboarding, including right-of-way and communication signals and warnings. (4) Explain the protective gear needed to skate safely, including helmet, knee pads, elbow pads, and wrist guards, and show how to wear them correctly. (5) Describe the two main styles of skateboarding (street and vert), and describe common skatepark features (ramps, manual pad, rails, spine, etc.). (6) Explain skateboard anatomy (deck, trucks, wheels, hardware, etc.). (7) Build a board by assembling all pieces (deck, wheels, trucks, hardware, and grip tape) in the proper order. (8) Explain skateboard maintenance (cleaning, adjusting bolts, and replacing parts). (9) Explain the difference between regular and goofy stance, and demonstrate your preferred stance. (10) Demonstrate how to push, cruise, and carve on flat ground. (11) Show at least two braking and stopping techniques. (12) Do a basic ollie and at least one variation. (13) Show how to drop-in from coping. (14) Demonstrate THREE skateboarding tricks from the following types: (a) Flat ground tricks (b) Flip and shove-it tricks (c) Grind and slide tricks (d) Air and grab tricks (e) Footplant tricks

sub_requirements.sub_req_text: Option A, Ice Skating. Do ALL of the following: (1) Explain the general safety and courtesy guidelines for ice skating. (2) Discuss preparations that must be taken when skating outdoors on natural ice. Explain how to make an ice rescue. (3) Discuss the parts and functions of the different types of ice skates. (4) Describe the proper way to carry ice skates at the rink and for travel. (5) Describe how to store ice skates for long periods of time, such as seasonal storage. (6) Skate forward at least 40 feet and come to a complete stop. Use either a two-foot snowplow stop or a one-foot snowplow stop. (7) After skating forward, glide forward on two feet, then on one foot, first right and then left. (8) Starting from a T position, stroke forward around the test area, avoiding the use of toe picks if wearing figure skates. (9) Glide backward on two feet for at least two times the skater's height. (10) Skate backward for at least 20 feet on two skates. (11) After gaining forward speed, glide forward on two feet, making a turn of 180 degrees around a cone, first to the right and then to the left. (12) Perform forward crossovers in a figure-eight pattern. (13) Explain to your counselor the safety considerations for participating in an ice-skating race. (14) Perform a hockey stop.
